Why, then, has he now carved these woodblocks again? It is precisely to place a cangue upon a neck already in shackles and add more ropes to those already bound, so that they may penetrate and liberate themselves.
A man of spiritual acuity will, upon seeing this, immediately know its point of rest; they would not seek the profound within this record.
Exquisite! To seek it in words and phrases is simply to bore through tortoise shells and strike at roof tiles as one pleases.

Regarding the Chan Master Guang of Dongshan, whom the monastic communities called Guang Wuxin: he was a native of Zizhou.

When he first traveled to study under various masters, he asked Master Yungai Zhi, "What was the underlying meaning of Xinghua’s striking the karmadāna? Zhi descended from his meditation seat and extended both hands.
Guang stuck out his tongue to show him and struck his meditation mat once. Zhi said, "This is moved by the power of the wind.
He then took these words and asked Master Shishuang Lin, "What do you think? Lin said, "How do you understand it? Guang likewise struck his meditation mat once.
Lín said, "What a fine sitting mat! It is simply that you do not know where it lands. He then asked Zhēnjìng, "What is your intention? Guǎng also struck a sitting mat.
Zhēnjìng said, "He strikes, and you strike as well. At this, Guǎng attained great enlightenment. Consequently, Zhēnjìng composed a verse, saying:
"If a man of spirit should sever [delusions] but does not sever them himself, Xīnghuà acts on behalf of others with thorough penetration."
"You base Chinese! From now on, let your own eyes open according to the teaching. He was then bound with a staff, fined, and expelled from the monastery.
Several men, including Ciming, Langya, and Dayu, took their leave of Fenyang; they vied with one another, refusing to serve as the leader of the procession.
Fenyang said, "This journey cannot be determined by seniority in ordination. Listen to this verse of mine: 'The headless bird, the city of Jizhou.'"
The halberds and spears were leveled; the General passed beneath the forest on a single horse. Inside the city of Yuanzhou, there was a clamor and hubbub.
Ciming stepped forward from the ranks and said, "Chu-yuan, who are you to dare claim this seal of certification? He then led the assembly in prostrations.
When Zen Master Zhantang Zhun first visited Zhenjing, Zhenjing asked, "Where have you recently come from? Zhun replied, "Dayang.
Zhenjing asked, "Where did you spend the summer retreat? Zhun replied, "Dawei. Zhenjing asked, "Whom did you attend to there? Zhun replied, "The Prefecture of Xingyuan."
Jing (Zhaozhou) extended his hand and said, "How is my hand like the Buddha’s hand? Zhun was at a loss for words.
Jing said, "Just now, in your every response, you were one by one spiritual, bright, and true. Yet as soon as you spoke of the 'Buddha's hand,' it became an obstruction.
Tell me, where does the sickness lie? Zhun said, "I do not understand. Jing said, "Everything is already established; who else would you have to understand it?"
At Huanglong Mountain in Hongzhou, father and son have transmitted the dharma-vessel. The current Abbot Xin possesses clear and penetrating insight;

however, because his karmic conditions did not coincide with those of the world, few monastics followed him. Nevertheless, he renovated the entire monastery in accordance with the established regulations of the monastic community.
When someone asked the reason for this, Xin replied: "Since the time when those who merely 'talk about Chan' appeared, the monastery has been completed. [I] went to Nanchang."
Chen Qi requested that Chan Master Jicui Nan be appointed as the Dharma-transmitting abbot. The Prefect approved his request.
Several years later, Nan passed away at Xinhuasi and was interred in the mountains. One night, Nan suddenly dreamed of a divine being who said, "Qi has gone to guard the stupa.
Upon waking, he did not take it seriously. One day, while sitting in the abbot’s quarters, he again saw the person from the previous dream, who said, "Go and guard [the stupa]."
[He established] a stupa. He then interrogated the spirit, who said, "A successor has already arrived. Before long, a person came bearing a clay statue.
[The Master] then ordered that a separate image of the Local Deity (Tǔdì) be fashioned, and moved the former one to guard the new stupa of the Mountain Lord.
The monk Xian had long studied under Xuedou. When it was intended that he be appointed as the abbot of Jinge Monastery, Xian heard of this;

that night, he secretly inscribed two verses on the wall of the abbot’s quarters and immediately fled. The verses read: "It is not that I lack the mind to continue the ancestral lamp, But I am ashamed that my Way has not yet matched that of Neng of Lingnan.
At the third watch, beneath the moon, I leave the mountain caves; With lingering, wordless affection, I look back upon the azure peaks. He further said:
For more than thirty years throughout the four seas, he sought teachers and chose companions without a moment’s rest.

This morning, having reached the ground of no-mind, he was instead driven out of the mountains by that very no-mind. Later, Xian entered the world at Kaixian Temple and became a successor to Master Deshan Yuan.
He continued the correspondence with Xuedou. When the old woman before the mountain saw the special messenger, she joyfully asked, "Head Seat Xian?"
He went out to see him off. "For whom are you burning incense? the messenger asked. "For Master Yuanchu of Deshan," he replied.
The old woman scolded him, saying, "Xuedou shook out his bowels of excrement to preach Zen for you; how can you be so ungrateful and disloyal?"
The elder Yunju Shun often ridiculed Chan Master Tianyi Huai for preaching "entangling vines" (ge-teng) Chan.
One day, upon hearing that Huai had passed away, he joined his palms before the Dharma seat and said, "I am glad; the entangling vine stake has finally been toppled.
Xiu Yuanthong was then in the assembly serving as the *karmadāna* (venerable of duties). Seeing him constantly rebuking and scolding [the master], he said to his colleagues: "I..."
"I must settle this old fellow once and for all. That night during the formal assembly (yècān), as before, [Huì] reviled him with harsh words.
Xiu stepped out from the crowd and said in a stern voice, "Have you not seen what is said in the *Nirvāṇa-samādhi-sūtra*? Shùn suddenly said, "I have long kept the great assembly standing;
I humbly pray that you all take care of yourselves," and he then returned to his quarters. Xiu remarked, "This old fellow has eyes all over his body; he has truly rebuked Master Huì."

Chan Master Datong Ben used his words to answer the "Seamless Pagoda" koan, saying: "Mist and clouds arise from its front and back; stars and moon circle its rafters and beams."
Chun resided at Yuelu Monastery. He was diligent in disciplining his body. Once, while walking in meditation along the palace steps one night, he lost his footing and fell.
A nearby monk helped him up; he remained dazed and unconscious, unable to distinguish people or affairs. Even the writings he had composed throughout his life, he could no longer understand.
When Chan Master Zhao of Doushuai first traveled abroad, he passed through Yuelu and heard an elder monk speak of Chun’s condition. Zhao...

He was startled and said, "In this life I have practiced Chan, yet I have not clarified the mind-ground; I am just like Chun. If even a single stumble brings such a state as this, how much more so when one is separated from the body by the 'shading' of death?"
The Shu monk Tai Liu, while living among the monastic community, often lamented that the Buddha-dharma was muddled and corrupted, with heterodox views arising like sharp blades.
He then said, "I shall study Chan; if I attain true and correct insight, I will not spare my verbal karma. He subsequently made a vow and paid homage at the stupa of Mazu.
He practiced without ceasing for many years. One day, the stupa suddenly emitted white light, and he was moved by this to attain awakening.
Later, he traveled extensively through the monastic communities to test and examine the veteran masters. Passing before Mount Xuedou, he remarked, "This old fellow has his mouth dripping with water.
When Xuedou heard these words, they met later; Xuedou said, "Do you not approve of me, Master? Taizhou replied, "This old fellow!"
As expected, his mouth was dripping with saliva. He then struck his sitting mat once and departed. The temple steward (zhísuì) was resentful and sent someone to waylay him on the road to beat him;
he broke Tàiyī’s foot. Later, when Tàiyī arrived in the capital, he behaved wantonly in the marketplace.
An official invited him to his home to provide for him, ordering his concubines to serve him. Tàiyī repeatedly requested to leave, but the official was insistent.
He kept her there, treating her with even greater reverence and respect. One day, while waiting for an official to arrive, he intentionally flirted with his concubine.
The official, because of this, changed his attitude toward him, which allowed [the monk] to take his leave. A few days later, in the midst of a bustling marketplace, he sat upright and passed away.

At that time, you should offer a memorial service for Dayang. When the time came to enter the stupa, the disciples feared that Ping would bring harm to their master.
He then fashioned two yellow and white ritual vessels, claiming they had been donated by the Commandery Marshal Li Hewen, and recorded this in the inscription on the stupa;

however, in reality, no such items existed. Later, when Daoying resided at Dayang Monastery, he indeed requested that the stupa be opened and its contents burned. The senior monks earnestly admonished him against it, but Daoying said, "It will cause me no harm.
He subsequently opened the stupa and discovered Ming'an, whose countenance appeared as if he were alive. He then set him ablaze; though the firewood was consumed, the body remained solemn and intact.
The assembly was all struck with wonder. Píng used an oil bowl as fuel for firewood, and it was instantly reduced to ashes. The assembly reported the matter to the authorities;
Píng was charged with plotting to steal items from the pagoda and for the unfilial act of returning to secular life. He then called himself Wang Xiùcái (Scholar Wang) and went to visit Lángyá.
Lángyá said, "The attendant Píng of old is today Scholar Wang. When I was at Dà'yáng, I already saw where you were acting. Thereupon [he did not [accept him]).

He visited Nan’an, and later visited Gong’an; both places responded in the same manner. Ping wandered aimlessly with no place to return, ultimately unable to escape the prediction of the "Yangya" (the forked path). How tragic!
The Elder Bai of Mount Emei often said: "Xuedou has over a hundred verses on ancient cases (songgu), yet their phrasing and meaning do not particularly stand out from others.
How is it that he has gained such a great reputation in the world? He then composed one thousand verses himself, believing that quantity was superior to quality.
Having compiled this collection myself, I harbored the vain hope that in the future my fame would rival that of Xuedou, and thus I traveled everywhere seeking someone to appreciate my work.

There was a master of Dahuashan who had visited all the eminent and realized elders of his time; he had received the Dharma from Chan Master Fachang Yu but did not enter the world, instead residing at Dahuashan as its "Mountain Master.
His spirit overwhelmed all quarters, and he never granted his approval lightly. I took these verses with me and went to pay him my respects.
He sought a single word of verification, wishing to gain the confidence of future students. When Daie saw it once, he spat upon it and said:
"This verse is like a person suffering from *kawa-ju* (crow-smell) who stands upwind; its odor cannot be smelled. From that time on, [Daie] did not dare to produce anything resembling human speech.
Later, Huang鲁直 (Huang Tingjian) visited that temple and inscribed on its wall: "The White Old Man of Mount Emei has composed a collection of a thousand verses himself.
In the Dàhé era there was once a saying: 'A crow with a foul odor stands against the wind.'"
Chan Master Guizong Kexuan was a native of Hanzhou and a successor of Langya Guangzhao. He was on close terms with Guo Gongfu.
When the Magistrate of Nanchang came to confront him with certain matters, Kexuan sent a messenger with a letter to Gongfu, instructing him not to let the Magistrate see it.
At that time, Gongfu was serving as the District Magistrate of Xingzi. Upon receiving the letter, he read: "I have six more years of worldly affinity remaining."
It is not yet finished. Today, I cannot bear this oppression; for now, I entrust myself to your family for six years, hoping that you will look upon me with compassion.
Gongfu received the letter; he was both startled and delighted. In the middle of the night, he had a vague vision of Xuan entering his bedchamber.
Unconsciously, he cried out, "This is not the place where the Master came from. When his wife asked the reason for this, Gongfu called for a lamp and showed her Xuan’s letter;
she found that she was indeed pregnant. When the child was born, they named him Xuanlao. Hardly a year old, he possessed the memory and speech of his former life. By the time he reached three...
In the year [blank], Master Baiyun Yuan passed by his home. When it was time for him to come out and pay his respects, Xuan called out, "Teacher-nephew!
as soon as he saw him. Baiyun asked, "How many years has it been since we parted from the Master? Xuan counted on his fingers and said, "Four years. Baiyun asked, "Where did we part?
Xuan replied, "At Bailian Zhuang, while eating oil-cakes. Baiyun asked, "What proof do you have? Xuan—
[Daokai] said, "Father and mother, tomorrow we shall invite the monk for a meal. Suddenly, a cart passed by outside the gate.
Daokai asked, "What sound is that outside the gate? Xuande made the gesture of pushing a cart. Daokai asked, "What happens after it has passed?
Xuande replied, "A single ditch across level ground. Six years later, he passed away without illness.
The Venerable Haiyin Xin was a native of Gui Prefecture and a successor of Langya. He resided at Dinghui Monastery in Suzhou and was over eighty years old at the time.
On ordinary days, he received offerings from the residence of Defense Commissioner Zhu and frequently visited his home.

One day, Zhu asked, "Will you be able to come to my house to take rebirth after your passing? Xin smiled and gave his assent. Upon returning to the monastery, he felt slightly unwell for several days.
She transformed herself day by day. As her transformation progressed, Zhu’s family gave birth to a daughter. When Chan Master Yuanzhao heard of this matter, he went to visit them.
Just as she emerged from the month [of pregnancy], she saw him and smiled. Yuanzhao called out, “Haiyin, you have made a mistake!
The girl then wept and immediately passed away.
The Elder Kaishōkaku of Wazhou went to attend upon Master Fu of Changlu. After a long time, he had gained nothing.
Hearing of the Dharma-way of Wuzu, he went directly to his seat. One day, in the meditation hall, Wuzu asked him: "Śākyamuni and Maitreya are still but his servants."
"Tell me, who is he? Jue said, "Hū Zhangsan and Hē Lisi. Zuzhao approved of these words. At that time, Yuanwu was the head of the assembly (zuoyuan).
Zuzhao recounted this to him, and Yuanwu said, "It is good, but I fear it is not yet real.
You must not let him go; search further beneath his words. The next day, when Jue entered the room for private instruction, Zuzhao questioned him as before. Jue said, "Yesterday I spoke toward..."
The Master finished speaking. Zhaozhou asked, "What did you say? Zhenjue replied, "Hū Zhangsan and Hē Lisi. Zhaozhou said, "Not so, not so.
Zhenjue asked, "Why was it 'so' yesterday, yet today you say it is 'not so'? Zhaozhou said, "Yesterday it was so; today it is not so.
At these words, Zhenjue attained great enlightenment. Later, he appeared in the world at Kaisheng Temple and visited Changlu.

The Dharma assembly flourished greatly. At that time, [Fufeng] did not investigate the source from which he had obtained [his realization]. While offering incense, he suddenly felt as if his chest were being pounded.

Consequently, an abscess broke out at the painful spot, forming an opening. He constantly used milk-incense (guggulu) to make cakes and stuff them into it, but it did not heal after a long time, and he eventually passed away.
The Elder Fú of Chánglú had been deeply involved in worldly affairs for some time, yet his insight into the Way remained unclear.

He frequently used the offerings he received to load onto boats and travel upriver to provide meals for monks. When Chan Master Xiù of Yuántōng heard of this, he went to verify whether it was true or false.

Just as he arrived, the Master encountered [Fú] giving a formal discourse (shàngtáng), which began: "Entering a field of weeds, one does not discriminate; it is fit to slaughter the dull-witted. Grasping at whatever grass comes to hand..."
After saying, "A mere trifle," he descended from his seat. Xiu was greatly astonished and said, "If this is how Chan is taught, who would say one does not understand?

He then remarked that [the teachings] everywhere were merely matters of arising and ceasing, and so he went in person to the abbot’s quarters to pay his respects. He recounted the previous events in detail and requested instruction on the words of the master's proclamation.
Fufeng explained the meaning according to the literal text. Xiu said, "If it is like this, then those in other places do not falsely claim that you do not understand."
Master Kai-xian Xian composed an inscription for the meditation seat of Chan Master Nanzheng of Gui-zong, saying: "A bright pearl is produced from an oyster;
a cool hare conceives within her womb. Behold this rope seat: it is the medium through which the Way is realized. Later, Nanzheng composed an inscription for Kai-xian, saying:
Once he had set foot on the ground, he was immediately at ease.
One day, Lord Jing visited Chan Master Yuan of Jiangshan. During their conversation, Yuan said, "Your Excellency’s breath is so forceful it overwhelms others;

you are constantly occupied with composing works and searching for knowledge, which exhausts your mental energy. Why not practice seated meditation to investigate this great matter? The Lord followed his advice.
One day, he said to Yuan, "Sitting in meditation truly does no harm to others. For several years I wished to compose the 'Eighteen Pairs of the Hu-pipa' (Hújiā shíbāpāi), but could not complete it.
Last night, while sitting in meditation, I finished it. Yuan laughed heartily.
One day, Lord Jing asked Lord Zhang Wen-ding: "A hundred years after the passing of Confucius, Mencius—the Sublime Sage—was born.
Why was there no one of such caliber thereafter? Lord Wen-ding replied: "How could there have been no one? I fear it was because there were those who surpassed even Confucius and Mencius.
Lord Jing asked: "Who were they? Lord Wen-ding said: "The Great Master Ma of Jiangxi, Chan Master Tanran, and Wuye of Fenyang."
The Chan masters Xuefeng, Yantou, Danxia, and Yunmen—when Lord Jing heard their names mentioned, he did not fully understand their significance and asked, "What does this mean?
Wen Ding replied, "The Confucian way is so austere that people cannot sustain it; they all turn toward the teachings of the Buddha."

Lord Jing sighed with joy and was deeply impressed. Later, he recounted this to Zhang Wujin, who struck his desk in admiration and remarked, "This is the ultimate discourse of a man of great attainment.
He took up his brush and recorded it on his desk.

He was left to his own observations. Internally esteemed as a man of integrity by the Emperor Taishang, he devoted his heart entirely to the teachings of Śākyamuni and traveled extensively to consult various spiritual teachers (*kalyāṇamitra*).
He would often sigh to himself, "I have fortunately attained human form, yet my physical body is incomplete and I do not even know who my biological parents are.
I suspect that in a previous life I treated others with contempt, which has brought about this retribution. Thereupon, he made a vow. When he encountered a day of rest...

Ren returned to his private residence and secluded himself from all worldly affairs. He lit incense to worship the Buddha and transcribed the *Avataṃsaka Sūtra* using his own blood, performing three prostrations for every single character.
He made a vow that in a future life he would recognize his parents. One day, a guest arrived to visit him;
Ren emerged somewhat late, whereupon the guest said angrily, "A visitor has reached your gate; why do you not come out? Ren smiled and replied, "I am at home writing."
There was a scroll of a royal pardon. A guest questioned him about its origin, and Ren answered truthfully.

He took out the scripture and showed it to him, saying, "This is the pardon for those who eat iron bars and swallow iron balls in the presence of Old Man Yan. The guest was struck with awe for a long time;
upon returning home, he also transcribed a copy for himself.
Chan Master Xintang of Xingjiao in Xuanchou was the son of the Niu family in Wenzhou. His family had been in the silver-smithing trade for generations.

While he was scrubbing and polishing a silver pitcher, he suddenly attained a profound realization. He subsequently left the household life, received full ordination, and traveled to study under various masters.

He became a dharma successor of Langya Guangzhao. When Chan Master Huai resided at Xingjiao, Xintang served as the First Seat. When Master Huai accepted an invitation elsewhere, he intended to appoint Xintang to succeed him as abbot.
At that time, Diao Jingchun was serving as the governor of Wanling. Fearing public criticism, he prayed before Guanyin, saying:
"If the Venerable Tan possesses clear insight into the Way and is worthy to succeed as abbot, I pray you grant me a dream, O Scholar Diao.
That night, Diao dreamed of an ox in the Hall of Flourishing Teaching. The next morning, Tan took his leave of the prefecture; Diao recounted his dream, and Tan was greatly [pleased].
He laughed. Diáo asked him the reason for this. Huái said, "The head seat Tǎn’s surname is Niú, and his birth year also falls under the Ox.
Diáo then took his seat and issued an invitation to him. Tǎn accepted the invitation and ascended the seat.

There was a master from Xuědòu named Shěngzōng, who came forward and asked, "Before the Buddhas appeared in the world, everyone’s nostrils reached the heavens; after they appeared in the world, why is there no news at all? Tǎn said:
Before Mount Kukkutapāda, the wind was still. Linji said, "Not yet; speak further. Xuantan said, "Great snow fills Chang'an.
Linji said, "Who understands this meaning? It makes me remember Nanquan. He then brushed his sleeves and returned to the assembly, refusing to prostrate.
Tanyun said, "The New Teaching has lost ground today," and he returned to his quarters.

He then sent someone to invite Zong, saying, "Just now, you gave an incorrect response to a turning phrase before the assembly of devas and humans. Why did you not prostrate yourself to cover it over? Zong replied:
"A great man has gold beneath his knees; how could he be willing to prostrate before a blind old monk? Tanyan said, "I have another saying.
Zong then resumed the previous conversation, arriving at the point where it ended with "Wait until later, I shall speak further. Tanyan said, "I have thirty blows to spare;
I send them to strike Xuedou. Zong then prostrated himself.
When Chan Master Zhenjing traveled to various places, his eloquent debates left the entire assembly awestruck; everyone regarded him as one who had reached the end of his studies.

While observing the summer retreat at Dayue, he heard a monk reciting Yunmen’s words: "Is it not that the Buddha-dharma is like the moon in the water? Yunmen replied, "In the clear waves, there is no path through. Upon hearing this, Zhenjing attained enlightenment.
Later, when he arrived at Deshan, he encountered Ying Damo’s informal sermon, which included the passage concerning the Sixth Patriarch.
He also cited the words of Yunmen, whereupon the assembly rebuked him. At dawn, he departed immediately, intending to visit Chan Master Yunfeng Yue.
Upon reaching Xiangxiang, he heard that Yue had passed away. He then proceeded to Yunju. At that time, the elder Shun had already constructed a funerary pagoda for himself.
Lingzhao said, "This worldly fellow does not stay overnight but leaves the mountain directly to go to Huangbo to see Chan Master Nan. Nan once asked about his studies.
A person asked: "When one is reciting praises atop the bell tower, how is it when planting vegetables beneath one's feet?
The assembly offered various responses, none of which were in accord with the truth. He then questioned the Head Seat, Sheng, who replied, "A fierce tiger sits blocking the road.

Nan Da praised this highly and subsequently retired to Jicui Hermitage, instructing Sheng to take his place. When Jing San arrived at the hermitage, their karmic conditions did not harmonize, so he said: "I..."
At the place of his own realization, he thought, "This old fellow is merely a monk of religious practice; he does not understand my words.
He then descended the mountain and went to Cuiyan, where he met Master Shun. Shun asked, "Where have you recently departed from? Jing replied, "Huangbo.
Shun asked, "Is the old master at the hermitage well? Jing said, "He is well. Shun asked, "Where are you from? Jing replied, "Guanxi."
Shun said, "Your way of speaking does not sound like that of a person from Guansi. Jing said, "I traveled abroad for my studies when I was young. Shun asked, "Where did you serve as a monk?
Jing replied, "I am a junior disciple of Master Guang at Beita. Shun continued, "Guang and Xiu both studied under Shuangquan Yu.
When I attended the late Master Nanquan, I could not understand the speech of those two great elders; yet now, when it comes to me... [Jing] wept.
Having attained some realization of Chan, she wished to see him, but he had already passed away. For this reason, she was called "Grandmother Shun.
She then asked, "How is the new Huangbo doing? Jing replied, "Very well. Shun said, "He has only managed one good turning of a phrase."
He then stayed at Huangbo, yet he had not even dreamed of Zen. Because of this, Jing suddenly attained enlightenment and perceived the point of Jicui’s application;
he subsequently composed several verses. He sent them ahead to Jicui while on a temporary visit, so that Nan would know of his arrival through these verses.
When Jing arrived, Nan asked him where he had come from. Jing said, "Cuiyan. Nan said, "It happens that I am not here. Jing said, "Where [have you gone]?"
Nanyue said, "Tiantai was performing communal labor; Nanyue went mountain-climbing. Jingzhou said, "If that is so, then I, your student, must also have attained mastery.
Nanyue asked, "Where did you get those shoes on your feet? Jingzhou replied, "I bought them for seven hundred coins at Mount Lu.
Nanyue said, "When did you ever attain mastery? Jingzhou pointed to his shoes and said, "When did I ever lack mastery? Nanyue—
Nan-chuan found this strange. One day, while the attendant was rolling up the curtain, Nan asked, "What is it like when the curtain is rolled up?
The attendant replied, "It illuminates all under heaven. This attendant was Chan Master Fotuo Xun. Nan then asked, "What is it like when the curtain is lowered?"
The Master said, "It is as impenetrable as water being unable to leak through. Nan asked, "What is it like when one neither rolls up nor lets go? The Master was speechless.
Nan reported this to Zhenjing, who said, "The Master must have his attendant enter the Nirvana Hall for you before it will do.

Nan spoke out with a stern voice, "People from Guansi have never had such a headache since they were born. Zhenjing then pointed to a monk standing nearby; this was Yunju You, who at that time was serving as...
The Abbot said, "This very abbot has not even dreamed of it. Nan laughed heartily.
When Master Zhantang Zun read the "Memorial on Sending Out the Army" by Zhuge Kongming, he suddenly attained realization regarding the composition of literary works.
There is a *luohan su* (Rohan Sutra) which says: "Arhat" is a Sanskrit term; in this [Chinese] language, it means 'non-arising' (*anutpāda*). It transcends the twenty realms of the three worlds.
Fifth, there is the presence of worldly afflictions. Having transcended the cycle of birth and death in its segmented form, he has received the Tathāgata’s entrustment;

as one worthy of offerings from devas and humans, he brings benefit and merit to all sentient beings. Donors should therefore arouse the intent to make offerings. Furthermore, the *Water Mill Record* states:
"Mount Letan is the Great Site for Selecting Buddhas where the Chan Master Mazu Daichi and his former disciples of the Chan school practiced. Although the years since have been many..."

It seems distant, yet the Buddha-dharma has never been distant. However, because the insights of those who serve as spiritual friends (*kalyāṇamitra*) within it differ, there are variations of superior and inferior;
thus, it appears distant. For example, when a monk asked Mazu, "What is the Buddha? Mazu replied, "This very mind is the Buddha.
By observing the reason for this, one knows that sentient beings are fundamentally already Buddhas, with no distinctions of high or low. As for those distinctions of high and low—
It lies in the person, not in the Dharma. How much more so in this degenerate age for those who claim to possess a self and preach the Dharma!

Therefore, when selecting a Buddha and seeking a teacher, one cannot but be thorough. In the Wuyin year of the Yuanfu era of the Great Song, there was a śramaṇa from Hanzhong named the Venerable Yizhong.

Seeking teachers and inquiring after the Way, he selected a Buddha and engaged in Zen meditation. Carrying his staff and wooden block wherever he went, he performed his art upon meeting the stage. Yet, as for that stage...
It was a jest for a single moment, yet by its merit, it has benefited a thousand ages. Thus, one reforms old systems;
though the people of Ying may still be lost in confusion, seizing the vessel and responding to the opportunity, the power of transformation and adaptation lies within oneself.

How could one allow the great design to be constrained by the line and square, or be limited by the rules and compasses of the ancients? This is what is meant by saying that a son cannot be taught; as for those who can be taught:
Words and language are but dregs; they do not constitute the ultimate subtlety of the mind. That ultimate, subtle mind resides within oneself and does not reside in written words or speech.
Even if one were to receive a secret transmission from an enlightened master, it would not equal the mind’s own self-attainment. Therefore it is said:
"Attaining it in the mind and responding with the hand" are both the wondrous functioning of the numinous mind-dharma. Thus, there are those who use it to thresh grain.
It becomes a millstone when one wishes to husk rice; it becomes a roller when one seeks flour; it becomes a sieve when one wishes to remove the bran; and it becomes a fan.
Its overall design and principles all possess the essential pivot. Once the mechanism is aligned, it turns of its own accord without being pushed, driven by the water.
As soon as a single wave stirs, the preceding wave and the following wave follow one after another, wave upon wave.
It responds without end because it is a millstone. Once a single wheel is raised, the great wheels and small wheels revolve one after another in an inexhaustible cycle.
Thus, the upper and lower parts correspond, and the high and low work together. This wondrous function emerges spontaneously.
Therefore, without relying on human effort or craftsmanship, it is wondrous and sublime to behold—mysterious within mystery.

Thereafter, it revolves left and right, moves vertically and horizontally, and as they strike and touch one another, they produce the great sound of the Dharma, proclaiming suffering, emptiness, impermanence, and non-self, as well as the various pāramitās.
Thus, those who hear it hear its mind; those who see it see its nature. By means of this—
Reaching the point where they perceive through smelling and tasting, they shall fully obtain the joy of the Dharma and the bliss of dhyāna. Furthermore,

why not provide rice, flour, and all necessary provisions to the Fragrant Accumulation Kitchen (Gandhavyūha-kūṭa) to serve as two meals for the assembly of meditators who come and go to select the Buddha?
When Chan Master Yuanwu was first at Mount Gui, one day Master Zhenru asked him, "How is it?
Yuanwu replied, "Arising and ceasing without ceasing. Zhenru said, "One can tell you are but an ordinary person of this world;
for thirty years I have practiced within this state and have only attained something similar. Later, he visited Huitang, who said, "I have been in charge of this monastery for twelve years..."
"I understand. Now I finally understand. Even from the tip of his toe, he kicks out a Buddha.

Later, while residing at Zhaojue, an elder asked him about the story of Liu Tiemo visiting Mount Guishan, as well as Xuedou’s verse on "The Imperial Street": "I do not know what the meaning of this is."
Wu said, "Even if this old monk were to practice for another forty years, I would still not reach the level of Xuedou.
The Elder sighed and said, "If even Zhaojue speaks in such a manner, what can be said of others?"
Liu Yi’ung once studied under Foyin and was quite conceited; he held Zhenjing in very low esteem.
One day, coming from Yunju to visit Guizong, he entered the Dharma Hall and saw Zhenjing, immediately asking, "How many years has it been since you began writing plays? Zhenjing replied:
[The monk] waits specifically for the musicians to arrive. The Old Man says, "I will not enter this 'protection society' of yours.
Jing says, "What can be done? Right now you are right here in this very arena. As the Old Man hesitates, Jing claps his hands and says, "Frog-meditation! You can only hop once."
The old man was greatly impressed. During another sitting, the old man pointed to his patched robe and asked, "What do you call this?
Jing said, "A Zen robe. The old man asked, "What is Zen? Jing shook it out and said, "It cannot be shaken out. The old man was speechless.
Jing struck him and said, "Your skill is such as this, yet you wish to test an old monk!"
The Magistrate Qian Yi visited Zhenjing for a long conversation and then wished to go to the toilet.
Zhenjing ordered an attendant to lead him away through the west side toward the Yanshou Hall. Qian immediately said, "Since this is the latrine (dōng-sī), why are you leading me toward the west?"
Zhengjue said, "How many people go eastward seeking [the truth]?
The various mountains of Nankang meet together. Later, Foyin arrived; Zhengjue asked, "Why have you come so late from Yunju?
Foyin replied, "Because I was wearing straw sandals while passing through the belly of Guizong, that is why I am late. Zhengjue said, "I was caught by Guizong..."
[Zhaozhou] swallowed it. Yinyuan said, "What can you do? You cannot spit it out. Zhenjing said, "If you cannot spit it out, then defecate it!
Master Zhenjing sometimes suddenly called to his attendant, "Bring the portrait of the Old Monk here.

When the attendant brought the portrait of National Teacher Nan to him, he spread it out and placed his hand upon his forehead, saying, "Were it not for this old monk, how could [the Dharma] have been so?"
Thus, he would immediately frown for half a meal’s duration and strictly order it to be put away; he did this every time.
When Master Yuan of Qian’an saw the portrait of Master Nan, his tears would flow.

When Zhenjing finished his period of study, he took leave of Master Nanshan. Nanshan cautioned him, saying, "You must still go to see Master Ying of Shaowu. Zhenjing followed these instructions and went to see Ying.
Upon entering the room for private instruction, they reached a state of mutual accord. Ying said to him, "You have truly mastered the Chan of Yunmen.

Nanshan often remarked with admiration, "Master Ying’s teaching approach is vast and expansive; I am not his equal. Such was the high regard in which he was held by Jicui. Nanshan then showed [him the way].
Ji was serving as acting abbot when Lengtán’s seat became vacant. Nánchāng issued an official document appointing Yīng to fill the position.
Yīng rose with a start and said, "As for the Way of Huánglóng, who but I could uphold it? He accepted the appointment without hesitation.
One day, while the administrators were disputing incessantly, Yīng said, "I have failed to maintain discipline among the assembly; I am ashamed before my late master. He then suddenly passed away.
Li Wenhe, the Commandant, requested Master Jue of Langya to provide a commentary on the *Xinxin Ming*.
Langya wrote one phrase in large characters and the following phrase in small characters. Upon seeing this, Li Wenhe was greatly impressed and expressed his profound admiration.
Xuedou was once in the assembly of Chan Master Lin of Lushan. One day, he and Lin were looking at a newly excavated pond.
Lin asked, "The excavation of the pond did not wait for the moon; once the pond was completed, the moon came of its own accord. Now that the pond is finished, why do we not see the moon?
Xuedou threw a tile into the pond. Lin was pleased with this. One day, as Lin ascended the hall to give a discourse, Xuedou stepped forward and asked: "Dharma..."
"It is not so; it is not so. "How can you point the way? Lin said, "It is precisely because it is naturally so.

Dou said, "Everyone, take note of the Master’s response," and he shook his sleeves and returned to the assembly. The administrative official was incensed that he did not prostrate and wished to humiliate him.
He then invited them to the storehouse office to ask about the reason for this. Dōu asked, "What did the Master say? One monk replied, "It is the nature of things;
it is not otherwise. Dōu said, "What you have said is incorrect. He then questioned the next monk, who likewise replied, "It is the nature of things; it is not otherwise."
Dong said, "This lacquer bucket! He then brushed out his sleeves and departed, leaving behind a poem for Mount Shizi Peak.
One day, Old Man Shun asked Xiu Yuanthong, "I have heard that you saw Master Hui; is this true? Xiu replied, "It is."
Shun said, "What words or phrases were there? Xiu said, "There was a verse on seizing the opportune moment which says: 'One, two, three, four, five, six, seven;
standing alone with one foot before the ten-thousand-fathom peak. Having snatched the pearl from the jaws of the black dragon, a single word exposes Vimalakīrti.
Shun said, 'Not good. What other words or phrases were there? Xiu said, 'One day an elder came to visit.'"
Huishai raised his whisk and said, "Do you understand? The Elder said, "I do not understand. Huishai said, "Two patches of skin for ears; a set of bones for teeth.
Shun sighed and said, "A truly excellent spiritual friend. From this point on, Xiu devoted himself to the service of the old man Shun.
Chan Master Dongshan Bao was a successor of the Venerable Wuzu Jie. A native of Luzhou, he was born into a house of prostitution and had no surname.

He was by nature upright and prudent. He once served as the administrator of the monastery under Wuzu. When Wuzu fell ill, he ordered an attendant to go to the storehouse to fetch ginger for decoction.
Bao scolded him. The attendant informed Wuzu, who told him to take money back to purchase it; only then did Bao retrieve it.
He gave him some ginger. Later, when there was a vacancy at Dongshan in Junzhou, the Prefect sent a letter entrusting Huaihai with the task of recommending someone to take charge of it.
Huaihai said, "A man who sells raw ginger can manage it. He was consequently appointed to the abbacy of Dongshan. Later, he moved to Guizong.
One day, as he was leaving the gate leaning on his staff, he saw a procession of horsemen approaching. He asked what kind of official they were, and they replied, "The County Magistrate."
He ordered the road to be cleared for him. Huibao stood to the left of the path to avoid him, when suddenly he saw the horse kneel down and refuse to move.
Huibao said, "Even an animal recognizes a man. The Commandant bowed twice and departed. Later, Huibao moved to Yunju; one night, a mountain deity carried his sedan chair and walked around the temple.
Baoyun said, "Lift up your father; lift up your mother; carry them to the Abbot’s quarters. The spirit then carried the sedan back to the quarters.
When Baoyun first traveled as a wandering monk, he once stayed at a guesthouse. One night, he was harassed by a courtesan, so he yielded his bed to her and slept elsewhere.
When Bao was practicing meditation at dawn, a courtesan came to demand payment for her lodging. Bao gave it to her; she then went out and burned his bedding before departing.
The courtesan told her parents the truth, and they subsequently invited him back to offer a vegetarian feast in apology, regarding him as a true son of the Buddha.
He once composed a eulogy for the Patriarch Bodhidharma, which was widely disseminated throughout the monastic communities. Master Langya Jue wrote a response to it.
Now, in the *Zhengfayan zang*, it is recorded that among the assembly of Master Dayu Zhi, there was a monk who recited the *Vajracchedikā Prajñāpāramitā Sūtra* two hundred times every day.

When Master Zhi heard of this, he ordered an attendant to invite the monk to him. He asked, "Is it true that you recite the *Vajracchedikā Prajñāpāramitā Sūtra* two hundred times every day? The monk replied, "Yes."

Dongzhai said, "Is that so? Zhi asked, "Have you ever investigated the meaning of the scriptures? The monk replied, "I have not. Zhi said, "Simply recite them once every day and investigate the Buddha’s intent.
If you attain awakening under even a single phrase, it will be like drinking the water of the ocean and thereby knowing the taste of all its hundred rivers.

The monk followed these instructions. After reciting them from beginning to end in a single breath, he reached the passage: "It should be known thus; it should be seen thus; it should be believed and understood thus."

While at the place where the Dharma-characteristics of non-arising are manifested, he suddenly attained realization. He then reported this to Bai Zhi. Zhi immediately pointed to the dog before the meditation seat and said, "The dog barks.

He arrived at the residence and sat upon the hall. When Minister Shen was about to go out to see him, he thought to himself:

While he was arranging documents, he suddenly saw those two characters before him; only then did he realize they were a prophecy.

[He] struck him. Yuanjin stepped forward and said, "We two have come from thousands of miles away specifically to study the Chan of the Master.

How can we leave after being splashed with a single ladle of water? Even if you were to strike us to death, we would not leave. Yunshan laughed and said, "If you two wish to study Chan, then go and register as monks.
Subsequently, he invited Yuanjin to serve as the head cook (dianzuo). The assembly suffered from the austerity of his diet. One day, Yunshan happened to—

When the meal was over, Huiyuan left the hall. Huisheng secretly took the keys and used the monastery’s oil and flour to make a five-flavor congee. When the congee was ready, Huisheng suddenly returned and went to the hall.

After the meal, he sat outside the hall and ordered the steward to be summoned. Huiyuan arrived and confessed, saying, "I indeed took the monastery’s oil and flour to cook this congee; I beg the Master to punish me.
Huisheng ordered that the value of the items be calculated and his robes and bowl assessed to be returned to him before he was struck.
[Xuefeng] was given thirty blows of the staff and expelled from the monastery. Yuan went to the marketplace to seek the mediation of a fellow practitioner, but Xuefeng refused to grant him leave.
Yuan said again, "If you will not allow me to return to the monastery, I simply beg to join the assembly for the evening zazen. This too was refused.

One day, as he was walking through the streets, he saw Yuan standing in front of a guesthouse and said, "This is the corridor of the monastery's quarters; why have you been staying here all this time?"

At that time, [Hui]yuan asked, "Have you ever returned the rent money? I shall now calculate what remains owed and collect it. Huiyuan showed no sign of distress; he took his alms bowl to the market and collected money to return it.
One day, while walking through the streets, [Hui]yuan saw him holding his bowl again. Upon returning, he said to the assembly, "Huiyuan truly has the heart for Zen practice.
He then had someone call for him and bring him back.
One day, Chan Master Wude of Fenyang said to the assembly: "Last night, I dreamed that my deceased parents were seeking wine, meat, and paper money.
I could not help but conform to worldly custom by preparing offerings for them. I had the items prepared in the storehouse and set up an altar according to secular rites.
After pouring the wine, serving the meat, and burning the paper money, I ordered the administrators and heads of the community to gather and distribute the remaining dishes."
The attendants turned him away. Wude sat alone at the center of the assembly; he ate and drank as usual, then departed, intoxicated and full.
The monks murmured among themselves, "A monk who devours wine and meat—how can he be fit for the Master’s Dharma?

They all wrapped their sashes and left, with only six or seven people remaining, including Ciming, Dayu, Quan Daowei, and Daoguo. On the following day, Wude ascended the hall and said, "How many idle spirits there were!"
"Wild ghosts require nothing more than a single platter of wine and meat, and two strings of paper money, and they are sent off to their rest.
Have you not seen it? The *Lotus Sūtra* says: 'This assembly has no branches or leaves; there are only those who are truly real. Then he descended from his seat."
When Lord Wen Zheng was governing Poyang, the Jianfu Monastery was short of personnel. He used all his influence to bring the Ancient Pagoda Master (Gu) to take charge of the abbotship.
One day, while they were eating together, the attendant Guang, a native of Xuanzhou, stood beside him. The Ancient Master took a piece of sugarcane from his plate and passed it to him.
As soon as Guang received it, he went to prop up a bed leg. The Ancient Master looked at Lord Wen Zheng and said with a smile: "This fellow has no sense of propriety."

He said, "This son must later attain Chan through formal study. This account ends there, as it was not further expanded upon. His worldly lifespan was eighty-four years; he passed away without illness.
When Master Zhenjing was traveling, he journeyed together with two monks to the place of Xue Datou at Guyin. Xue...
The question was asked: "When three people travel together, there must be one who possesses wisdom. What is this 'one who possesses wisdom'? Both monks remained silent.
Zhenjing stepped down from his shoulder and immediately let out a shout. Xue raised his fist and made a gesture as if to wrestle.
Zhenjing said, "There is no need for further examination. Xue dragged his staff and drove him out. Xue then went to see Shimen Cizhao.
Chang-chu Ching was a native of Shu, renowned throughout the monastic communities. He had extensively studied under various great masters, including Zhenru, Haitang, and Zhaojue.
Traveling from Mount Lu to the capital, he met Chan Master Fayun Yuancong. Accompanying him was Master Xiu;
upon arriving at Fayun, Xiu was granted access to the meditation hall. Someone then informed Yuancong of Chang-chu Ching’s name, whereupon Yuancong said: "For now..."
He was ordered to stay elsewhere until a unit became vacant in this monastery, at which point he was to be admitted to the hall. While Qing was staying with Zhihai, he happened to fall ill.
Xiu wished to go and inquire after his illness, but as there were no leave passes available from the mountain gate, he instead went out secretly to see Qing at Zhihai’s quarters.

Fengqing wrote a letter to Yuantong, stating that Xiu had transgressed the rules in his conduct. When Yuantong received the letter, he scolded him severely during the night assembly, saying: "This man is truly a petty person.
Because of the principles of the Way, he risked being expelled from the monastery to inquire after your illness;

instead, you report him in this manner. How could such an act be performed by an upright man or a gentleman? Upon hearing this, Fengqing died suddenly. The monastic community ultimately judged Fengqing to be... [the rest of the sentence is missing from the source].
He met with a single rebuke from Yuan Tong and passed away.
Chan Master Ming-shui Xun of Fu-zhou was serving as an attendant in the quarters at Fa-yun Temple.

At that time, Chan Master Lin-lin of Dao-lin arrived for temporary lodging, and the Abbot specifically prepared tea for this new arrival. Xun went personally to the quarters to invite him, but it happened that Lin-lin was not there. Xun...
A fellow monk was sitting at the same table as Lin. The monk said, "You go; wait for him to come, and I will request [the tea] for you.
Lin departed. The monk suddenly forgot about it. When the midday meal concluded and the drum was struck to assemble for tea, Lin had not arrived.

Yuantong asked, "Is the newly arrived one here? He sent someone to summon him. When Lin arrived, Yuantong ordered him to withdraw from his seat, stand before the assembly, and rebuked him, saying, "The mountain gate..."
This special tea was prepared to manifest the formal etiquette of the monastic community (*saṃghārāma*). Why did you arrive so late and with such negligence?
Lin said, "Just now I heard the sound of the drum and intended to go to the tea ceremony, but suddenly I was pressed by internal needs and went to use the toilet;
I could not make it back in time. Yuan Tong said, "My drum is no *bādara* (castor bean); as soon as it is struck, you would have to defecate. Xunbai replied, "It was I who forgot to invite you."
A certain monk was due to leave the monastery. At that time, a fellow practitioner stepped forward from the assembly and said, "This does not concern the attendant or the newly arrived monk;
it is I who am unfit to bear the responsibility, for I failed to remember when I made the request on their behalf. He continued, "I shall take the place of both men and leave the monastery.
Yuan Tong admired his integrity and magnanimity, and pardoned them both.
Chan Master Daomian of Daguang was serving as the Head Seat (Shouzuo) in the assembly of Master Weishan Lingyou.

The mountain gate had invited twenty people to serve as供养主 (offering masters), and on the day before their arrival, their names were submitted to the Hall Office so that they might be informed in advance.

On the following day, they were to receive instructions from the Abbot’s quarters; however, during the tea ceremony, one person suddenly went missing. When Weishan asked who he was, they replied, "Yong of Suizhou."
The Elder Tai requested leave before the assembly had even understood his intent, asking that another monk be appointed to fill his post. Daowei was greatly impressed by this.

Shortly thereafter, someone reported that Tai was actually present as the head seat (shouzuo) and had been hiding himself. Daowei immediately ordered him to be sought out; when Tai was indeed found, he was sent back to his quarters.
Thereupon, the bell was struck to assemble the community, and Daowei rebuked Xiu, saying: "You are the leader, setting an example for future generations. As for your state of mind—"
This was unjust. How could he encourage and inspire his students? Xiu’s tongue was large and parched; distressed and unable to respond, [the monk] eventually drove him away with a staff.
The monastic community thereafter stood in awe and submission.
When various venerable elders passed away, they obtained a great many *śarīra* relics upon cremation;
however, the *śarīra* of Master Zhenjing were as large as beans, five-colored, crystalline, and moreover, extremely hard and solid.

Chan Master Guzhuang Zu, a preeminent disciple of Zhenjing, collected a great many of them and kept them in a lapis lazuli bottle, carrying them with him for veneration. When Miaoxi visited Guzhuang, he once...
Suppose one were to place it upon an iron anvil and strike it with a hammer; both the anvil and the hammer would be dented, yet the śarīra would remain undamaged.
Is this not the result of having long practiced with clarity and attained a transcendent realization of the Way?
Xian Pengtou was a native of Jiangzhou. Among the eminent figures within the assembly at Weishan Zhenru’s monastery, he stood out as a peerless talent.

His realization of the ground of reality was clear and lucid, and his spiritual acuity was sharp and penetrating; his compositions surpassed even those of his master. However, because his conduct was not disciplined, the entire community held him in low esteem.

Zhenru built a small hermitage behind the abbot’s quarters and had Xian dwell there alone, allowing only a narrow path for him to pass directly in front of the abbot’s quarters, and forbidding all other access.

The brothers visited one another for two more years. [Changsha] was then elected as the head of the assembly and established as a monk; he held the whisk and preached the Dharma, possessing qualities that greatly surpassed those of ordinary men.

Because of this, people’s perceptions were transformed. He resided at Xingyang in Yingzhou for several years, and his Way flourished extensively. When he manifested his passing, his physical body remained incorruptible.
When Master Yuanwu was at Mount Gui, he witnessed these events firsthand. Even when Miaoxi traveled to Xingyang, he was still able to see them.
As for his physical remains:
Chan Master Huangbo Quan of Yunzhou initially studied the *Śata-dharma-śāstra* and gained renown in lecture halls.

Later, changing his robes to travel south in search of instruction, he met Master Zhenjing at Dongshan and composed a verse on his realization of the Way, of which the opening lines read: "A single blow breaks through the void..."
He possessed all treasures of the treasury. His spiritual sharpness was so swift that none could withstand its edge.
Zhenjing once sighed, saying, "What a pity that the former master will never see this again. Later, when he ascended the hall to preach the Dharma, he entered nirvana without rising from his seat;
thus, Zhenjing’s words were further proven true.
Venerable Zhantang Zhun was a native of Xingyuan Prefecture and the direct successor of Zhenjing.
When the position at Yunyan in Fenning was vacant, the Prefectural Governor instructed Huanglong Sishi Chan Master to recommend someone he knew who could fill the post. Sishi said:
"Zhunshan was able to maintain his position as abbot because I did not know him; I only saw that he had a fine verse on Zhaozhou washing his bowl.
The District Magistrate asked, "May I hear it? Sixin recited: "The particle 'zhi', the particle 'hu', the particle 'ye'—the nostrils of the patch-robed monk point their great heads downward.
If you practitioners do not understand this, go ask Old Woman Wang of the eastern village. The District Magistrate marveled at this and prepared [to offer him support].

Liu invited him with great courtesy, and Zhuan likewise did not decline. Throughout his life, he disciplined himself with austerity; even while leading disciples and propagating the Dharma, he was no different from when he was among the common assembly.
After rising in the morning, he would go to the rear shed and take only a small ladle of hot water to wash his face, using the remainder to wash his feet.

All other articles of use were generally of this same simple nature. As soon as the evening session concluded, the attendants and laborers of the abbot’s quarters would treat him as if he were a stranger on the road.
He personally swept the floors and brewed tea; he possessed the refined demeanor of the ancients and served as an excellent model for later generations.
Chan Master Foyun Foguo Zhaogao once retired to the Iron Arhats Hall at Jingde Temple.
In the hall were several wooden arhats, and during the bitter cold of the capital, Foguo took them to burn as fuel, sitting by the brazier until dawn. The following day, he washed [the ashes].
From within the ashes, countless *śarīra* relics were obtained. The various abbots all regarded him as a follower of non-Buddhist paths;
they did not realize that Fo-zhao was of the same lineage as Dan-xia, one who cannot be scrutinized by the eyes of the mundane.
Chan Master Yangshan Wei had served diligently in lecture halls, and his reputation was widespread. When he reached the age of fifty, he finally changed his attire and entered the monastic community.
He went directly to Huangbo in Junzhou to attend upon National Teacher Nan. With resolute intent, he engaged in questioning and inquiry for a long time, yet he had not yet attained awakening.
While drinking water from National Teacher Nan’s washing basin and walking along the corridors, he saw an elder of the mountain and immediately prostrated to him.
He bowed with tears falling and said, "I am old and infirm; please save me. [The Master] took him to a secluded room, where he set out a single couch for him to sit in solitude.
Whenever a guest arrived, he would immediately yield the couch and bid them take their seat. He would light incense and stand beside them with palms joined, offering no other words.
From then on, no one dared to cross his threshold. Nan knew of this and said to him, "You are far too austere in severing ties with others; it will not do."
Thus it was. Weï said, "I, Weï, am old; my spiritual practice is not yet complete. What leisure do I have to discuss human affairs? As the Venerable Zhaozhou said:
'For twenty years in the South, except for the two times of the midday meal and the evening gruel, these were all occasions where I employed my mind in a distracted manner.'"
Xing Wei was what kind of man? He dared to indulge in leisurely pleasures. Nan could not dissuade him from his resolve, and he grew all the more impressed by him.
Chen Liaoweng of Yanping, named Guan and styled Yingzhong, called himself the Huayan Layman; he was upright and incorruptible when serving at court.

He pointed out the sycophants and touched upon the depraved, possessing the heroic spirit of the ancients. He devoted himself to the Inner Canon (Buddhist scriptures), his discourses so compelling that they would have wrested the seats from others.
Yet, he alone had not yet achieved great enlightenment in Zen; regarding the causes and conditions of the Zen school, he relied mostly on intellectual interpretation.

He was deeply fond of the Recorded Sayings of Nan-chuan, having expounded them almost to the point of exhaustion. Only the *Vajracchedikā Prajñāpāramitā Sūtra* and the "Man Rubbing the Back of a Clay Figure" remained unannotated. He once said to people: "This..."
The mind has its origins and its destination, yet none have known them. As the proverb says, "Before the person of great wisdom, there are three deep red darknesses. Truly, this is not false.
Chan Master Fozhao Gaofeng retired from his duties at Fayun Monastery and resided at the Iron Arhat Hall of Jingde Monastery.
One day, while he was out drying wheat, he heard the Dharma Master Bai speaking with others, saying, "Zen practitioners are mostly fond of empty talk.
Fozhao went up to him and asked, "Dharma Master, is it true that you have mastered the lectures on the *Śata-dharma-śāstra*? The Dharma Master replied, "I dare not say so. Fozhao said:
"Yesterday it rained; today it is clear. In what dharma are these gathered? The Master of the Seat (Zezhu) had no reply.
Fozhao struck him with a rake in his hand and said, "Do not say that only Chan practitioners are good at speaking empty falsehoods.
The Master of the Seat said indignantly, "But tell me, Reverend, in what dharma are yesterday’s rain and today’s sun gathered? Fozhao replied, "The forty-second hour."
[The Master] said, "This is included among the non-associated dharmas. The Head Seat was thus humbled. While at Jingshan, Miaoxi ascended the hall and, citing the preceding circumstances, said:
"Yesterday it was sunny; today it rains. The timing does not correspond. Look for it three days from now."
Zen Master Cizhao Cong was a successor of Shoushan. During the Xianping era, he resided at Shimen in Xiangzhou.
One day, the local governor, acting on personal whims, flogged and humiliated him. Upon his return, the assembly of monks came out to meet him on the road.
The head monk stepped forward to pay his respects and said, "The governor has unjustly insulted and humiliated you, Master, to such an extent. Cizhao pointed to the ground and said, "Level ground."
He raised a heap of earth; the ground surged up a mound of soil at his finger. When the Prefect heard of this, he ordered someone to scrape it away, but it surged up again as before.
Later, unexpectedly in Xiangzhou, a monk asked, "Is there still Buddha-dharma within the deep mountains and rocky cliffs?
Zhao said, "There is. The monk pressed further, asking, "What is the Buddha-dharma within the deep mountains and rocky cliffs? Zhao—
It is said: "How strange! The shape of the stone resembles a tiger; when the fire burns the pines and cypresses, its momentum is like a dragon.
Master Mujin (Wujin Jushi) cherished these words, yet the *Shimen Lu* alone does not record these two matters. Both were personally related to me by Master Mujin.

Li Shanglao of Mount Lu was engaged in construction work when he offended the local earth spirits (*tǔ*). Consequently, his entire family contracted swelling; though they sought medical treatment, it was of no avail.

Thereupon, they thoroughly swept the halls and chambers and instructed each member of the family to purify their hearts. They burned incense and recited the *Chishengguang* (Blazing Light) Dhāraṇī to appease the offended spirits.
Before seven days had passed, he dreamed at night that an elderly man dressed in white was riding an ox at his house; suddenly the ground gave way, and they sank away, disappearing bit by bit.

The following day, everyone—both great and small—was unharmed. This was moved by the power of his utmost sincerity, as swift as a shadow or an echo. Could it be that such a thing is not possible through the power of the Buddha?
Yong was a successor of Chan Master Yuanzhao Ben. Initially, while climbing onto the toilet, he slipped and fell, smashing his water jar, which triggered a moment of awakening.
He composed a verse, saying: "This one fall, this one fall, Is worth ten thousand taels of gold. A hat upon my head, a bundle at my waist;
I carry the clear breeze and bright moon upon my staff. The Duke of Feng, Zheng Gong, once visited him to seek instruction. [End of excerpt.]
While looking around the left and right of the hall, he suddenly attained awakening. He sent a verse to Yuanzhao, saying: "A single glance at Master Yong, and my entry into realization was profound;

Through successive conditions, I have transmitted the heart-mind of the Elder Teacher. Who says that a thousand li of mountains and rivers are far? Before my very eyes, I face the numinous light and the wondrous sound.

When Lord Zheng retired from the相位 (prime minister) and resided in Luoyang, he longed for Yong’s instruction and requested him to reside at Zhaoti Monastery. Upon hearing that Yong had entered [nirvana]...

Zheng Jing personally went out to meet him. Just as they were about to mount the carriage, Sima Guang arrived. Zheng asked him, "Where are you going, Minister? Sima replied, "I am going to receive Master Yongyong of Zhaoti. Zheng said, "I shall go with you. They rode side by side out of the city and waited at a postal station. After a long while, they suddenly saw dozens of porters passing by. Sima asked, "Whose luggage is this? The porters replied: [The Master’s]. Sima said, "I have been waiting for him for a long time; why has he not yet arrived? The porters said, "He has already arrived. Sima said, "If he has already arrived, why do we still see these porters? The porters said, "That was the Master's baggage; these are the baggage of his disciples. Sima said, "How can it be that the Master has already arrived, yet his disciples are still carrying their belongings? The porters said, "The Master has already entered the monastery; these are the disciples returning from the marketplace. Sima said, "How extraordinary! How extraordinary! He then hurried back to the station to wait for the Master. When the Master finally arrived, Sima bowed deeply and said, "I have come to pay my respects. The Master said, "I have been expecting you for some time. Sima said, "I have been waiting for you for a long time; why did you not inform me when you arrived? The Master said, "I did not wish to trouble you. Sima said, "I have heard that the Dharma is difficult to encounter. I have come from afar to seek instruction. May I ask what the essentials of the Way are? The Master said, "The essential point is simply to be free from delusion. Sima said, "What is meant by 'being free from delusion'? The Master said, "To realize that the nature of mind is originally empty and tranquil, and that all phenomena are fundamentally non-arising—this is to be free from delusion. Sima was greatly enlightened. He then took leave and returned home. Later, he composed a poem to express his realization:

"Since ancient times, the Way has been vast and profound; How could I have known its essence was so simple? If one but realizes the mind is originally empty, Then all phenomena are naturally non-arising. From now on, I shall dwell in the realm of non-action; No longer will I be bound by the dust of the world. This account is recorded in the *Wudeng Huiyuan* (Compendium of the Five Lamps). It illustrates how even a high official like Sima Guang could attain sudden enlightenment through a brief encounter with a Chan master. It also demonstrates the Chan tradition’s emphasis on direct, personal transmission over formal ritual. Sima’s subsequent composition of a verse reflects the integration of his realization into his own life and the literary expression common among scholar-officials of the Song dynasty. This episode remains a classic example of the transformative power of Chan encounter dialogue.
Ying replied, "The Master of the new Zhaoti Monastery is traveling; I shall therefore seek a horse and return first. Zheng Gong said, "I wish to see Huayan;
for what reason do you return instead? Wen Gong said, "I have already seen him," and he ultimately returned ahead of time.
Miaoxi once heard Li Yizhong, the Vice Minister, speak of this.
Shun Laofu resided at Qixian on Mount Lu, while Huai Dugu served as the Magistrate of Nan’gang. Due to a private grievance, the people stripped him of his monastic robes.
Chan Master Lingquan Da’jue Lian had once entered Shun’s quarters; hearing that Shun had returned to secular life, he specifically dispatched someone to fetch him back to Jingyin Monastery.
He assigned Shun the main hall to dwell in, while occupying a side chamber himself. Emperor Renzong summoned Lian several times to the palace.
The Inner Quarters asked about this, but he ultimately did not mention the matter of Shun. One day, Prince Jia obtained an imperial edict to provide a meal for the monastics at Jingyin Monastery.

Seeing that Liai was standing by Shun’s side with great reverence, he returned and reported this to Emperor Renzong. The Emperor summoned him for an audience in the private hall. At that time, Lord Zheng of Fu was the Chancellor;

he submitted a memorial stating that Shun had been subjected to corporal punishment and thus should not be permitted to have an audience, allowing Liai to see the Emperor alone. Emperor Renzong granted this.
He sighed and remarked, "The resonance of his Way is extraordinary and sublime; he is truly a man of realization from the mountain forests.

He then wrote upon the surface of a fan: "I grant Xiao Shun permission to remain as a monk; furthermore, I bestow upon him purple robes and a silver alms bowl. By special imperial decree, he shall once again reside at Qixian.
On the day Shun departed from Qixian, two strong men carried his sedan chair on their shoulders to the front of Luohan Temple. As they walked, the two men said to one another:
Since he was not an elder of our monastery, he could not travel far; he abandoned his palanquin midway and returned.
When Shun arrived at the monastery again, he first sent someone to comfort the two village laborers, saying: "What you did at that time was correct. Just set your minds at ease;
there is no need for suspicion or fear. When Shun entered the hall to ascend the dais, he recited a verse: "Without cause, I was slandered; Unjustly, I met with misfortune. Half..."
Zaiyouru became a layperson. Today he returns once more to Sanxia Temple; how much joy, and how much anger?
Master Wujin, since leaving his post as Left Secretary to serve as Governor of Nanchang during a year of famine, opened up Donghu Lake to relieve the people.
The people were so distressed by forced labor that countless died. At that time, there was Master Jì, a descendant of the Qián clan of Wúyuè, who resided at Shànglán Monastery.

Wújìn ordered him to select a capable attendant to collect and bury the remains of the deceased until they reached a total of one thousand, after which he would grant him a *duòdì* (ordination certificate).
Jì dispatched the attendant Wénwēn, a native of Fúzhōu who spoke with a Mǐn accent. Wénwēn composed a poem for Wújìn, saying: "I know..."
The Left Assistant Director of the Prefecture is truly extraordinary. He has instructed me to collect corpses from the East, South, West, and North Gates.
I pray that the Left Assistant Director will soon enter the Zhongshu (Secretariat) and give birth to a great son, further realizing *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*.
I wish for stillness and would prune away [delusions]. Wujin knows this. Please have someone deliver these words to the Elder. The practitioner’s poem is excellent.
Do not strike him, Old Man Shun.

One day, Master Yanguan called to his attendant, saying, "Bring me the rhinoceros fan. The attendant replied, "The fan is broken. Yanguan said, "Since the fan is broken, bring me back the rhinoceros. Master Shun once raised this case:
"One day, Master Yanguan called to his attendant, 'Bring me the rhinoceros fan. The attendant said, 'The fan is broken. Yanguan said, 'Since the fan is broken, bring me back the rhinoceros.'"
The attendant was speechless. Shun said, "It is the height of the three summer heats; one truly needs a fan.
It is only because the attendant did not handle the matter properly. Although this was so, Yanguan was too wordy. Why not simply let go of it all?
Had the attendant seen Yanguan say, "Since the fan is broken, give me back my rhinoceros," he would have immediately replied to him, "It has already been blown away into the dust."
[The character for] "mound" (tǔ) has been omitted here. Li Kangjing was a native of Xuzhou.
During his humble years, he served as an attendant at the residence of a local magnate;

that magnate was skilled in geomancy and, appreciating Li’s loyalty, filiality, integrity, and candor, bequeathed a burial site to him so that he might inter his father there. Furthermore, he said to him: "If you wish for your own person..."

He served as one of the Three Ducal Ministers (*sān gōng*). [The tomb] was then lowered by several *chi*. Had he wished for his descendants to enjoy perpetual honor and distinction, it could have been raised by several *chi*;

yet although the burial was high, the Duke’s rank still reached the Two Palaces (*liǎng fǔ*). When he first passed the examinations, he received the post of County Magistrate Clerk (*xiàn zhǔbù*) under the Wenxī Duke.
Aside from using his salary to provide for his household, he spent it solely on teaching his son to read. The Duke of Handan, whose courtesy name was Shu, was then only seven years old.

When Emperor Zhenzong went on a tour of inspection to Yangzhou, Imperial Counselor Yi was prepared to serve as his advisor. A man from Handan, wearing a *fuhetou* head-wrap and a green robe, stood to the left of the bridge holding a letter.
When the Emperor saw him from afar, he ordered his attendants to carry the man to him and read the letter.

Still harboring doubts that it had been composed by proxy, he ordered another person to compose the "Fu on the Taiching Bridge" (Fu on the Great Clarity Bridge). [The author] immediately knelt before the Emperor and presented it for inspection.

The Emperor was greatly pleased. Yang Neihan memorialized, saying, "This is an auspicious omen for the state; we ought to offer congratulations to Your Majesty. It was then sent to the National Academy (Guozi Jianshi).
He was promoted three times to enter the Hanlin Academy, serving for a total of sixteen years. Emperor Renzong, who cherished his talent, once said to his attendants:
"Li Shu is like a single branch of a flower; I fear he cannot withstand the wind and frost. Were I to appoint him as Chancellor, it would only hasten his death.
His brilliance surpassed that of others by several degrees; when reading, he could take in five lines at once—a rarity throughout ancient and modern times.
His reputation was preeminent in his time; when eminent figures of the age passed away, it was considered unfilial for their sons not to have Kang Xing engrave the epitaphs for their tombs.
Indeed, Kang Xing subsequently entered the two government councils, and his descendants have enjoyed stipends from the imperial court for generations.
That his fame has not declined is truly due to the hidden virtue (*yin-de*) exercised by Kang Xing.
Cuiyan Zhen Dianxiong was constantly reviling Shun Laofu for preaching "Zen of Non-action. Master Shishuang Yong sent someone to deliver a message to Zhen, saying:
"Shun attained enlightenment at Dongshan through the 'Ancient Mirror' kōan. How could such a thing be called preaching 'Zen of Non-action'?
You revile him, and you have lost one of your own eyes yourself. Upon hearing this, Shun composed a verse, which begins: "Yunju did not..."
"Practicing Chan: Washing one's feet and going up to bed to sleep. The winter melon is straight and clumsy; the gourd is curved and winding. Master Yong composed a verse saying:
"Shishuang does not understand Chan; he washes his feet and goes up to bed to sleep. When the pillow falls to the floor, it breaks the monastery’s brick.
One day, Master Shun ascended the hall and said: "After dusk, I take off my socks and sleep; in the morning, I rise."

He was just tying up the entanglements of his practice when the wind blew and the fence collapsed during the night. He immediately called for his servants to split bamboo and bind it back up, then descended from the seat.
Among the assembly of Master Wuzu Yan was a monk named Fashan. On one occasion, as he entered the room for instruction, Wuzu asked him: "Not giving with the ten thousand..."
"Who is it that takes the Dharma as a companion? Shian replied, "The Dharma and I are not thus. The Patriarch pointed his finger and said, "Stop!
Stop! If the Dharma and you are not thus, how is it? At these words, Shian attained realization.
Later, he went into the quarters of Master Xuanmihu of Donglin, where he fully mastered the essence of the "plain and real" (pingshi) teaching. One day, holding a single flower, he circled...
He circumambulated the meditation seat once, then turned his back to it and thrust his hand into the incense burner, saying, "Master, tell me:
what is the meaning? Xuansu attempted several times to offer a reply, but Shian would not accept them. After two or three months had passed, he finally asked Shian, "Try to say something."
Fashan said, "Fashan merely placed the flowers on the incense burner; it was the Master himself who harbored doubts. What business is there in that?
Master Yuanwu had once studied under Chan Master Fang of Beiwuya, while Master Fojian had once studied under Chan Master Xuanmi Du of Donglin;
both attained the essence of illumination and practicality. Together they entered the quarters of Wuzu, where [Wuzu] was impartial...
"Attained through birth, not a single word was used. After a long time, there was no karmic affinity for realization;
everyone said that the Fifth Patriarch had forcibly changed him, and he spoke insolent words, departing in a fit of rage. The Patriarch said, "Go travel in Zhejiang;
when you are struck by a severe fever, you will finally think of me. When Yuanwu reached Jinshan, he suddenly contracted a case of typhoid and became exhausted.
He entered the chamber where he was gravely ill and attempted to test the Chan he had attained during his ordinary days; not a single word proved effective.
Recalling the words of the Fifth Patriarch, he made a vow to himself: "Once my illness has slightly abated, I shall go straight back to Wuzu.
While Fojian was at Dinghui, he too suffered from a severe case of smallpox that was extremely critical. After Yuanwu’s illness had recovered, he passed through Dinghui on his way.
He urged him to return with him to Huaisi, but Fojian remained stubbornly resolute and instead ordered him to travel on ahead. Yuanwu returned immediately to the ancestral mountain.

The Patriarch said with joy, "Have you come back? That very day, he entered the hall for formal practice and was assigned to the position of attendant in the *shizhe* quarters. After half a month had passed, [the Patriarch]...
Once, when Provincial Inspector Chen was returning to Shu after handing in his official seal, he passed through the mountains and went to inquire about the Way.

During their conversation, the Patriarch said, "Inspector, did you read any light erotic poetry in your youth? There are two lines in such poems that are quite similar: 'Frequently calling for Little Jade, yet there is no real business;
it is simply that the young husband wishes to recognize the voice. The Inspector responded with an affirmative "Yes. The Patriarch said, "But listen closely, Yuan."
Wuzu returned from outside and was standing in attendance when Yuanwu asked him, "I heard you recite a minor erotic poem;
did the Circuit Intendant understand it? Wuzu replied, "He only recognized the sound. Yuanwu said, "It was simply that he wanted the lover to recognize the sound.
Since he already recognized the sound, why was it not correct? Wuzu then asked, "What is the meaning of the Patriarch’s coming from the West? Yuanwu replied, "The courtyard."
Formerly, when Baizhang was a tree-spirit, Yuanwu suddenly attained a realization. He hurriedly went outside and saw a chicken fly onto the railing, flapping its wings and crowing.
