He said to himself, "This, too, is not sound. He then tucked incense in his sleeve, entered the room, and communicated what he had realized.
The Patriarch said, "This is the great matter of the Buddhas and Patriarchs; it is not something that those of inferior capacity or small roots can reach. I shall assist you."
Erxi then led him away and told all the senior monks throughout the mountains, "My attendant has attained Zen.
When Master Foyan was at Wuzu’s place, Yuanwu cited Linji, saying: "If one realizes the first phrase, one is fit to be a teacher to Buddhas and patriarchs.
If one realizes the second phrase, one is fit to be a teacher to humans and devas. If one realizes the third phrase..."

"I have attained it, yet I am not yet able to save myself. One day, Foyan suddenly said to Yuanwu, "I shall present three phrases to you," and pointing with his finger, he said, "This is the second phrase; the third has already been spoken," and then he departed.
Yuanwu related this to Wuzu, who remarked, "That is quite good. Thereupon, Yuanwu took leave of Wuzu and went to study under Master Zhenjing of Guizong. He departed.
Later, the Patriarch said to Yuanwu, "Guizong’s waves are vast; you may go there, but it is uncertain that you will find mutual accord.
Not many months later, a letter arrived for Yuanwu stating: "When I recently went to Guizong, I happened to escape his net.

However, I heard that the Head Seat Qing of Yunju had composed a eulogy for Huitang, which says: 'Rich and noble when heard, poor and destitute when seen. I have been somewhat suspicious of this. And so on.

They met and their realization was in perfect accord, as the records relate. After more than a year had passed, he returned once more to the Patriarchal Mountain. The assembly requested that he hold the whisk, but he instead spoke on the Chan of the nature and mind.
The Patriarch said, "Even if Yuan speaks of Chan in such a manner, do not concern yourselves with it."
Huian Monastery in Fengxin County, Hongzhou, is situated on the left side of the main road. Monks traveling between Ledu, Huanglong, Dongshan, and Huangbo invariably pass through it.
As the seat of the Dharma had long remained vacant, the Prefect sent a letter to Chan Master Bao-feng Zhen-jing, requesting him to select a person to preside over it.
At that time, the head monks, administrators, and senior elders were all reluctant to undertake the journey. It was then...
There was the Senior Seat (Zhousuo) Yuan, a man from the north who was solitary and firm in his self-reliance.
Having studied under Huìtáng and Zhènjìng, he had attained genuine realization. He lived inconspicuously among the assembly, and no one knew of it.

When the Head Officers and Administrators sought to appoint him to a position but he refused to accept, Yuan said to Zhènjìng, "May Huiyuan go [to serve]? Zhènjìng replied, "You may go. Thereupon, he returned [to his duties].

The letter recommended Yuan. Upon receiving the official document, Yuan took his leave immediately. At that time, Zhantang was the Seat-Head (Zuoyuan). He asked Yuan, "How will you manage the abbotship after you depart? Yuan replied, "I have no merit;
I shall instead cultivate karmic connections with all people by carrying a wicker basket on my shoulder and begging through the streets for the sake of the assembly.
Zhantang said, "This must indeed be done by an elder brother like you. He then composed a verse to see him off: [Verse omitted as per instructions]
The Master entered Xinwu, leading and carrying forth all sentient beings. He first gathered in the "donkey's feet" and then unfolded the "Buddha's hand.

Pointing out right and wrong, distinguishing the beautiful from the ugly, he wielded the sword of killing and giving life and let out the lion’s roar. Responding to the capacities of all living beings, he opened the mouth of the dharma-bag.
Scattered toward the south, north, east, and west, causing the pearls to turn and the jade to roll. May all those who are ignorant of themselves suddenly emerge from the trap of ignorance.
A-he-he! Seeing three times three—three times three is nine. Transmitted from patriarch to patriarch, handed down from Buddha to Buddha.
Yuanzhu stayed at Hui’an, begging for alms every day; whenever he encountered a transient visitor, he would immediately invite them back to the monastery to rest.
Dongpo said, "I shall wait for Master Rong to return so that we may prepare offerings. In this manner, thirty-five years passed without change, even amidst wind and rain.
He renovated and newly constructed the Buddha Hall, the Wheel Repository (Lunzang), and the Arhat Hall; everything appropriate for a monastic community was fully provided therein.
When Chan Master Sishin of Huanglong visited him, Yuan said, "New Abbot, you have always loved to employ those who lack clever intellect."
Zhuozi said, "This man is truly one who understands. Tonight, let him stay here for a while, so that we may discuss some subtle and great Dharma gates together.
Xindan was alarmed by this and said to his attendant, "This fellow is truly one who has realized it; I cannot 'tear his teeth apart' or 'split his jaw' with him.
It is better to leave and stop here. He did not stay the night but departed. Yuan (Zhuozi) eventually passed away at Huian. Six years after his cremation...
There were three instances where the foundations did not decay; countless relics were obtained, and a wondrous fragrance filled the chamber for many months without ceasing.
Although the new army’s weapons left nothing behind but ruins, the various halls of Hui’an alone remained towering and intact.

Is this not because his power of aspiration was fulfilled and divine beings provided protection, ensuring they did not decay? Today, those in all quarters fold their hands and enjoy these perfected, ready-made benefits.
As for this, having heard the reputation of Master Yuan, would one not feel shame in one’s heart?

Lü Juren, when first beginning his official career, was appointed as the Assistant Magistrate of the Salt Administration in Chu Prefecture. There was a scholar named Xie who examined his pulse and said, "In twenty years, the Assistant Magistrate will suffer from a sudden illness of hunger.
Later, it indeed came to pass exactly as he had said. When Lü sought him out again, the physician— (Note: The provided text ends abruptly; the translation reflects the available portion.)
Xie said, "Although it does not harm me, my physician has prescribed that I must not take warming medicines. I always carry some cakes, snacks, and a cup of wine with me.

When he was appointed as Director of the Bureau of Ceremonial (Qi ju shi ren), one day during an audience, he suddenly felt hungry. He immediately memorialized the Emperor, saying, "Your servant suffers from an urgent hunger;
please permit me to withdraw to a private place to take medicine. The Emperor smiled and granted his request.
Duke Wang Jinggong asked Master Zhenjing, "All the sutras begin by specifying the time and place; why is it that the *Sūtra of Perfect Enlightenment* alone does not do so?

Zhenjing replied, "That which is expounded in the Sudden Vehicle directly points to the daily activities of sentient beings. Since these daily activities are manifest before us, they do not belong to the past or the present.
Right now, I, this mountain monk, and you, Excellency, have entered together into the Great Luminous Treasury (*Mahā-ābhāsvara-garbha*) and are playing within the three realms."
[They] are obscure. They act as host and guest to one another; it does not depend on time or place. Again, [a question was asked]:

"All sentient beings realize Perfect Enlightenment (Yuanjue), yet Guifeng changed 'realize' (zheng) to 'possess' (ju). Is this a scribal error by the translator? Is its meaning correct? Zhenjing said:
"If the *Sūtra of Perfect Enlightenment* could be changed, the *Vimalakīrti Sūtra* could also be changed. Does Vimalakīrti not say: 'Nor do I extinguish sensation...'"?
One attains realization without extinguishing the aggregate of sensation (vedanā-skandha). How does this differ from the meaning of "realizing them all"?
For the ignorance manifested in the conduct of sentient beings is precisely the fundamental great wisdom of the Tathāgata; thus, Guifeng’s explanation is incorrect.
When Lord Jing (Wang Anshi) had removed his official robes, Master Fojian returned from Zhejiang to the ancestral mountain. He hesitated and was unwilling to register as a resident monk.
Yuanwu said, "It has been barely a month since we parted; how are you now compared to when we last met? Fojian replied, "I am merely in doubt."
"You have done enough for now," he said, and then proceeded to attend the hall. During a conversation with Yuanwu, Dongshan cited the story of how Master Dongsi asked Yangshan, "Where are you from?
Yangshan replied, "I am from Guangnan. Dongsi continued, "I have heard that Guangnan possesses the 'Taming Pearl' (Zhènghǎi míngzhū)."
"Have you ever received it? The Mountain said, "I have received it. The Abbot said, "Why do you not present it to this old monk?
Yangshan bowed with his hands joined and stepped forward, saying, "When Huiji went to Mount Mushi recently, he too was asked for this pearl, and I was left with nothing to say in response."
There is room for further elaboration. Dongsi said, "It is like a gnat making its nest upon the eyelashes of a mosquito, then shouting at a crossroads:
'The land is vast and the people are few; those who encounter one another are scarce. He then spoke to Fojian as follows:
Since it was said that he had "recovered" [the pearl], when he was asked for this very pearl, he again had no words with which to respond and no principle by which to argue.
How could this be? One day, he suddenly said to Yuanwu, "I have a statement regarding the causal connection concerning Yangshan’s meeting with Dongsi."
At that time, Tōji requested only a single *koku*. Yangshan immediately poured out an entire load-basket. Yuanwu deeply approved of this.
Master Fayan Wuxin Guangzhao traveled extensively through the various lineages until he arrived at the assembly of the Chan practitioner Yuantong Zhi. He entered...
In the private quarters, [Ji] raised the case of Zhaozhou asking Touzi, "When a person who has died the great death returns to life, what then?
Touzi replied, "Night travel is not permitted; you must arrive by dawn. Ji asked, "What is the meaning of this? Gaofeng said, "The kindness is too great to be repaid. Ji highly praised this.

A few days later, he raised the matter of Gaofeng presiding over the whisk (the *bifan*) during the ordination ceremony. [Gaofeng’s] mental faculties were slow and dull, and the entire hall burst into laughter. Gaofeng...
He appeared abashed. On the following day, tea was specially prepared for the assembly in the hall. The tea service implements were placed upon the table in the head seat’s quarters (*shouzuo liao*).

By chance, the tea ladle fell to the ground and bounced several times; suddenly, he attained awakening and his verbal responses became as swift as a sharp point (*jifeng*), such that none dared to confront him.
He then went to Zhenjing’s place, where, while contemplating a verse by the Patriarchs, he read: "The mind is identical to the realm of empty space... and so forth.
The dharmas are equal to space. When one realizes space, there is neither "is" nor "is not. He attained a sudden, great enlightenment.

Later, when he appeared in the world and ascended the hall for a small *sǎn* (informal discourse), he often said to people: "In the third year of the Shaoxing era, on the twenty-first day of the eleventh month, I realized the Chan of the 'square inch' (the mind).
By imperial decree, he was appointed to reside at Fayun Monastery. On the day he ascended the hall, an imperial messenger presented [him with the throne].

When the imperial incense arrived, it was required that the recorded sayings (*yulu*) be presented for inspection. At that time, Hong Juefan was among the assembly; he ordered an attendant to invite [the Master] to compile the records.
[The Master] said, "Let us first look upon the face of the old monk. Juefan compiled and arranged them, presenting them for review. Upon finishing the reading, [the Master] said:
If you seek the Chan that brings an end to birth and death, you must look to our Master.

As for those who compose ornate prose like gathered flowers and clustered brocade, or indulge in idle talk and long-winded speech—this is something my elder brother Hong alone is capable of. Throughout his life, Fayun has sought to swallow all quarters with his vital energy.
That he could thus comfort his contemporaries was surely due to the fact that he possessed qualities far exceeding those of ordinary men.
Master Fuyan Zhen, a native of Dongchuan, first traveled to study under Chan Master Zhenru, through whom he realized and clarified the correct view.

While serving as the guest prefect at Mount Gui, he was established as a *sheng* (monastic official). Due to a lapse in his speech, he requested to retire to serve as the garden head (*yuantou*) to atone for his offense.
Zhenru said, "You have little merit; tending the gardens to provide for the assembly is what is appropriate for you.

After two years had passed, he sought a replacement and took leave of Zhenru, intending to go to visit Zhenjing Wuzu. Zhenru said, "When traveling throughout all quarters, first seek out the ancient sages..."

"Yifan, do not delay in your journey; go straight to Dongshan. There you will find mutual accord within his quarters. Zhenjing took over the leadership of the assembly and established the monastic order.
After some time, he went to the assembly of the Fourth Patriarch, Master Xuan. From time to time, he visited the Fifth Patriarch for audiences, where they engaged in formal examination and debate.
It was evident that he possessed qualities surpassing those of ordinary men. The Fifth Patriarch said to the Fourth Patriarch, "The Head Seat Zhen is a man of realization in the monastic community."
"Why not recommend him to lead the assembly? The Fourth Patriarch acted according to these words. Later, when the Fifth Patriarch ascended the hall, he praised his insight and strategic conduct.

At that time, Li Xiuzhuan was the Prefect of Changsha; the Fourth Patriarch wrote a letter of recommendation for him. Not long after, the seat at Fuyan Monastery became vacant, and Ping Puyong again recommended him.
Li said, "I ought to give priority to the Fourth Patriarch's request," yet though he searched for the letter, it could not be found.
While they were seated as guests, a mouse dragged down a scroll from a shelf and placed it before them.

Upon taking it up and examining it, they found it to be the letter by the Fourth Patriarch appointing [the Master] as the Head Seat (shouzuo). Li was struck with wonder and immediately ordered a formal invitation to be issued.

The Venerable Létán Shēn was a native of Hédōng and a successor of Zhēnjìng. He had an attendant named Wù who, while incidentally in the guest prefect’s quarters, suddenly attained realization upon seeing a falling ember.
Wù went directly to the abbot’s quarters to communicate his realization, but Shēn shouted at him to leave.
Thereafter, Wù lost his mind and hanged himself with a rope in the eastern latrine of Yǎnshòu. After midnight, he was frequently seen in the sutra repository.
The three locations—the Hall, the Guest Office, and the Latrine—were all sites of misconduct. Sometimes they struck the *qing* gong; sometimes they moved people's shoes and sandals;

and sometimes they diverted the water from the purification jars. The entire assembly suffered from these abuses. When Master Zhantang returned from traveling through Zhejiang, he was appointed as the Head Seat (*shouzuo*). Upon hearing of these matters, he took action.
In the middle of the night, Wuzu entered the Hall of Extended Life (*yǎnshòu táng*) and went to the privy to undress. A small lamp on the wall was dimly lit when it suddenly went out.
Just as he was removing his clothes, Wuzhu arrived carrying a water pitcher. Zhandang said, "There is no need; wait until I have finished undressing.

Once he had finished undressing, Zhandang took the pitcher and left. At that time, while Wuzu was in the midst of undressing after having hanged himself, a tally (*chóuzi*) was brought to him shortly thereafter.
Having washed it clean, he called out, "Take the bottle. As soon as Wuzhuo took it, [Zhaozhou] seized him and felt his hand; it was sometimes soft and sometimes hard.
He asked, "Are you Wuzhuo, the attendant? Are you the one who was in the Guest Prefect’s quarters at that time?"
"I see you dropped a matchhead. Is there a point of awakening for you? In Zen practice and the study of the Way, one must simply know where one’s own primal source (the *benming yuanchen*) falls.
When you were in the Scripture Hall, did you not awaken at that time when you moved the shoes of the Head Seat?
And when you were in the Guest Prefect’s quarters, did you not awaken at that time when you moved the pillow?"
"Every night you stand here carrying pitchers and drawing water for others; is this not what you realized at that time?
Why then do you not know its true place? You remain right here, disturbing the great assembly. Tomorrow I shall urge the assembly [to expel you]."
"I shall look after your collection of the Tripitaka for you. I will gather funds to provide gruel offerings in your memory. You should seek liberation elsewhere;

study Chan and cultivate the Way to propagate the Buddha-dharma. Do not remain attached here. Having finished speaking, he gave a shove, and the pagoda collapsed like a pile of tiles and rubble with a hollow sound.
From that moment on, he vanished without a trace. Zantang’s arm remained as cold as ice for over a year.
The moon soon returned to its normal state. This was because a non-human being had attached itself to the moon’s shadow; thus, the cold vapor invaded people in such a manner.
Xu Zhike was a native of Piling who had previously passed the local examination but returned home after failing the provincial examination.

While his boat was moored at Pingwang on Wujiang, he dreamed one night of a person in white robes who said to him, "You have no merit of the shadow (no hidden virtue), which is why you did not pass the examinations. Zhike understood this.
He said, "My family is poor and has no means to give to others. The layman (baiyi) said, "Why do you not study medicine?
I will assist you with wisdom so that you may understand it and awaken to it immediately upon reflection. He followed these words and indeed attained the subtle mastery of Lu and Bian.

Whenever there was a sick person, regardless of their status as noble or humble, he would examine their condition and prescribe medicine without accepting any payment. Sick people came to his door every day; there were none who did not [recover].

Yu was subsequently recommended and again passed the local examination. As he was embarking for the Ministry of Personnel, his boat moored at Pingwang, where he dreamed of meeting the same man in white robes from before.
The man presented him with a poem that said: "The merit of your medical practice is universal, yet Chen and Lou lie between you and the goal.

In the palace hall, as names are called in succession, you will hear 'Six' called out as 'Five. Yu could not understand its meaning. Later, when he ascended to the rank of jinshi and his name was called, he was originally the sixth person; however, because [the Emperor]... (the text ends here).

His name was Dian; having failed the imperial examination, he did not receive an official stipend. He subsequently rose to fifth place, which fell between Chen and Lou, thereby finally realizing the prophetic meaning of his earlier poem.
Chan Master Foguang Wugai went from Cheng’an in Suzhou to reside at Huiri Hall of the Great Xiangguo Monastery in response to the imperial summons.
At Lín Chányuàn, Empress Huìgōng once observed from beneath the palace curtains that, after his audience with the Emperor was concluded, the Chan Master ascended into the air and departed.

Consequently, she ordered that the imperial meals provided by the Grand Cook be offered as sustenance for him. She further commanded that the leftovers from the Master’s own meal be brought back to the palace.
Moreover, she had a dharma robe fashioned from patterned brocade and personally inscribed a meditation plaque to bestow upon him, thereby manifesting her devotion to the Dharma.
In the winter months, he was granted a red brocade canopy; furthermore, his clothing and utensils were all bestowed by the Imperial Palace.
He bestowed his Dharma robes upon Chan Master Fayun Fozhao. Fozhao, in turn, sent a letter to Master Zantang of Baofeng in Hongzhou, which stated:
"I have given this 'earth-patterned brocade' Dharma robe to my junior brother Zhun, so that he may carry on the Way of our late Master. When Zantang passed away, [the robe remained with him].
He remained to preside over the mountain gate and hand over its administration; it remains intact to this day.
Chan Master Zhaojue moved from Letan to Huxi, where he accepted the invitation of Wang Zichen, the Guanchen, to open the hall.
Subsequently, all neglected affairs were restored. He ascended the hall for formal sermons and held private interviews with students every day without fail. He often remarked, "Huitang was truly..."
The various elders of the Pure School lineage have only been able to study the Chan of their former master; they have not attained the Way of the former master.
This is because they take mere ordinary, non-action as their practice, establishing neither knowledge nor views, and taking intellectual understanding to be the Way.

Furthermore, they do not seek wondrous enlightenment, yet they take the true, sudden realization of seeing the nature of dharmas—the teaching of all Buddhas and patriarchs, as well as Deshan, Linji, Caodong, and Yunmen—as [merely conventional].

To establish [this principle]: that which is taught in the *Śūraṅgama Sūtra*—that the mountains, rivers, and the great earth are all objects manifested within the wondrously luminous mind—is itself an establishment.
This is because those who take the ancients’ talk of the profound and discourse on the wondrous as "Chan" are deceiving the former sages and blinding future generations;
they are a breed of people with no sinews in their eyes and no blood under their skin, who follow the crowd in their delusions.
Inverted and unaware of it—truly pitiable. The *Nirvāṇa Sūtra* (Complete Enlightenment Sūtra) says:
"Sentient beings of the final age who hope to achieve the Way must not be allowed to seek awakening; this will only increase their learning and grow their views of self. It further says:

"Sentient beings of the final age may seek virtuous friends, yet encounter those with false views and fail to attain correct awakening; such individuals are termed of the lineage of external paths (*tīrthika*). False...
"The Master’s error is not the fault of sentient beings; how could it be empty talk?
Master Zhenjing gave a small lecture (*xiaocan*), saying: "In these times, there is a certain class of people who cling to the notion that 'the ordinary mind is the Way.'"
They take this to be the ultimate: heaven is heaven, earth is earth, mountains are mountains, waters are waters, monks are monks, and laypeople are laypeople.
They follow the rule that a large month has thirty days and a small month has twenty-nine; all such things are merely clinging to grass and leaning on wood.
Unaware and unconscious, they are led straight into delusion. Suddenly asked, "Why is my hand the Buddha-hand? they immediately say it is so.
"The Master’s hand; my feet—how are they like a donkey’s? Then one says, "These are the Master’s feet.
Everyone has their own karmic affinity (*jōen*). "What is the senior monk's karmic affinity? Then one says, "I am a person from such-and-such a province.
What kind of talk is that? Do not misunderstand. In all actions and endeavors, one must simply follow the ordinary path, regarding it as stable and settled. Resolve this firmly.
"Go along with it; do not dare to move another step further. Fearing you might fall into a pit or a ditch, for a long time you must be like a person born blind walking a path.
This single staff—do not let go of it for even an inch’s worth of distance. Grip it firmly and rely upon it as you go.
Master Heitang said to his students: "You go to Mount Lu to sit within the 'Armor of Nothingness' (*wushijia*)."

Gone! Now that those who attained the Way have passed, their descendants have melted away like ice and crumbled like tiles. Among them, there are but a few lingering remnants of the later stream, and even their schools are like extinguished ashes.
As the proverb says, "That which is true is difficult to extinguish; that which is false is easy to remove. How true this is!
Chan Master Fozhao Gaofeng initially resided at Guizong Temple, where he applied himself with singular devotion to the practice of the Way, never for a moment showing the slightest laxity.
One deep night, after finishing his devotions, he sat by the charcoal brazier in the monks' hall. Suddenly, he saw two monks enter the hall;
one had bushy eyebrows and hair as white as snow, while the other was young, both possessing a dignified and elegant bearing. Delighted, Gaofeng said to himself: "There are [sages] beneath my seat."
When the two monks had left the hall, Dao Gao followed after them and saw them enter the Buddha Hall. Dao Gao also entered with them;
the lamp light flickered brightly, and there was still fire remaining in the incense burner. Dao Gao offered incense and prostrated before the Buddha. The two monks then emerged once more.
He followed after them as well until he reached the front of the Buddha hall, where he suddenly lost his way. He thought to himself that he had forgotten the incense case inside the hall;
as he turned back to retrieve it, he saw that the hall door was locked. He then called for the attendant who served the hall, Shoushun, to open the gate.
Shun took the key and opened the door; he saw that the incense smoke in the burner had not yet dissipated and the incense casket was upon the jeweled steps.
He could not fathom the reason for this. Miaoxi personally heard Fozhao recount this, at which time Shun was standing by his side and pointed to him as a witness.
The Grand Chancellor, Duke Lü Mengzheng, was a native of Luoyang. During his humble years, his livelihood was precarious and his circumstances were dire.

For an entire month of heavy snow, he visited every prominent and wealthy household, yet few showed him any compassion for his urgent need. He composed a poem, the gist of which runs: "Ten times I have knocked at crimson gates, nine times they did not open;
covered all over in wind and snow, I return home. One can well imagine his state. On the road, he encountered a monk who took pity on him.

Falling into extreme poverty, he invited Huian back to the monastery. Huian provided him with grain and clothing, and gave him some cash before sending him on his way. Yet, barely a month later, these resources were exhausted once more.

He visited the monk again, who said, "This is not a long-term solution. You should move your family into the corridors of the monastery; at meal times, they may receive their food along with the rest of the community.
In this way, you may perhaps endure for a long time. Lü followed these instructions. Since he no longer had to worry about clothing, [he was able to remain].
Distressed by his lack of sustenance, he resolved to apply himself with vigor to his studies. That year, he took the provincial examination and was recommended.

A monk purchased a horse, hired a servant, and provided him with clothing and travel provisions to escort him to the capital. There, he passed the palace examination and was proclaimed the grand champion (the *daikui*).

When first appointed as a Vice Prefect of the Western Capital (Xijing), he met with monks as he would in ordinary times. He took his family with him when proceeding to his official post, and upon completing his term, he entered the Imperial Library.
After ten years, he eventually rose to hold the highest offices of state. Whenever there was a suburban sacrifice (*jiaosi*), he would deposit all his stipends in the treasury.
One day, Emperor Taizong asked him, "You have participated in several suburban sacrifices; why is it that you have not requested your stipends? He replied, "Your servant has private [obligations]."
The Emperor questioned him regarding his failure to repay this kindness. He then answered with the facts as they were. The Emperor sighed and remarked, "There are such persons among the monks.
He ordered that the man's name be recorded and submitted to the throne, granting him a purple robe and a posthumous title to honor his extraordinary merit.

Lü Ji’s accumulated stipends amounted to tens of thousands of strings of cash; an official decree was issued to the Western Capital ordering the monks to request these funds for the restoration of the temple buildings and for offerings.
The monk. That temple was originally the Iron Horse Camp, the birthplace of the two sagacious emperors Taizu and Taizong.
During the reign of Taizu, a temple had already been established there, and this monk was its abbot. Taizong separately granted him funds to rebuild the triple-gate (sanmen).
He was granted an imperial decree for the ordination of monks. Every morning upon rising, Mr. Lü would prostrate before the Buddha and offer this prayer:

"May those who do not believe in the Triple Gem never be born into my family. May my descendants, generation after generation, receive stipends at court and provide external protection for the Buddha-Dharma."
Shen Guogong, Yu's adopted son, would always, upon the arrival of the New Year’s Day, burn incense immediately after performing his prostrations at the family shrine.

He would then dispatch a letter to Chan Master Guanghui Liao. Shen Guogong’s son, Gongzhu, who was also enfeoffed as Duke of Shen, would likewise dispatch a letter to Chan Master Tianyi Huai on New Year’s Day.
Youcheng Hao Wen would dispatch a letter to Chan Master Yuanzhao Ben on New Year’s Day. Right.
Zhong, the son of the Grand Secretary, sent a letter on the first day of the New Year to Chan Master Foguo Gaofeng Yuanmiao.
His family had long possessed sincere faith and profound reverence; indeed, this has been so for generations. Therefore, I have recorded this to serve as a warning for future generations.
Chan Master Baoning Yong had two senior disciples, Chuqing and Chuning, who were fellow students of Chan Master Baiyun Yuan. Chuning served in the attendant’s quarters for the longest period.
Baiyun suffered from a chronic ailment of the upper abdomen; consequently, Chuning would constantly roast radishes to provide for his needs at any time.

When Baiyun composed a verse on the circumstances of the Great Master (Bodhisattva) lecturing on the *Vajracchedikā Prajñāpāramitā Sūtra*, he wrote: "How could the Great Master have ever understood it?"

While the sutra was being lectured, Master Zhigong used skillful means to assist him; with a single stroke of his hand, he rendered everything on the lectern useless. He went so far as to make King Liang squint his eyes.
[Zhigong] raised this and said to Yongning, "What is it that you are squinting at? This single phrase was the "old woman’s Chan" (pó chán) spoken for Yongning’s sake.
Because Yongning considered himself to have heard it directly from the master, he composed a verse based upon it. Later, Yongning resided at Mount Tianzhu in Shuzhou.
Qingzhu resided at Taiping in Shuzhou and possessed great eloquence and discernment; Master Wuzu Faian revered him.
Qing once said to Ning, "My brother’s Chan was obtained by exchanging it for a turnip braised by the Old Monk."
At the beginning of the Zhenghe era, there was a scholar named Xiong, a native of Poyang, who was traveling through the Western Mountains of Hongzhou when he passed by Cuiyan.
At that time, the Elder named Simen—a successor of Chan Master Yuan of Foyin and also a native of Poyang—sent two men to carry him.

The sedan chair arrived at Jingxiang Temple. As they passed through the forested ravines, which were shrouded in deep shade, he happened to see a monk whose appearance was ancient yet whose spirit was pure.
With bushy eyebrows and a snow-white head, he wore a garment woven from leaves and sat upon a flat rock, resembling the image of the Buddha-drawing monk Fotucheng.
Xiong said to himself, "In these times, there are no such monks as this. I have often heard that Master Liang is hidden in the Western Mountains; I suspect it must be him."
He was still there. Xiong stepped down from the sedan chair and, with an air of trepidation, stepped forward and asked, "Could this be Master Liang? The monk pointed his hand toward the east.
Xiong and his two attendants followed the direction of the hand to look, but when they turned their heads, the monk had vanished. At that moment, the light rain had just ceased.

The bear climbed the rock himself to look; the place where he had sat was still dry. Pausing and looking about in all directions, he sighed and said, "My karmic affinity from former lives is not deep."
"Meeting is like not meeting.
Chan Master Yue of Letan and Chan Master Nan of Huanglong were renowned as equals; the monastic community said, "Nan possesses meditative power (*samādhi*);
Yue possesses eloquence (*pratibhāna*). They often ate together, yet Yue was impatient and would finish his meal in a single gulp. He would then rinse his mouth and depart without looking back.
Nan was distressed by the slow pace of others. Chan Master Jin of Shanglan was Nan’s nephew. While attending him, he personally witnessed this and told Nan:
"If you wish for your uncle to wait a short while, simply raise one or two points from the *Śūraṅgama Sūtra* to question him; he will surely forget what he is eating.
Nan tried this, and it was indeed just as Jin had said. The questioning continued incessantly until Nan’s meal was forgotten.

Jiashan Ling and Shishuang Lin had long relied upon Chan Master Furi Cui. After they ceased their formal study, they traveled together along the Upper Yangtze River until they reached Huangbo, where they met Chan Master Nan.
When Nan ascended the hall for a small session of instruction (*xiaocan*), Lin did not understand its meaning; he therefore requested to enter the master’s room for private guidance.
Yuanling was enraged by this and spat out a mouthful of food, departing in a single stroke. Later, Lin attained great enlightenment;

his spiritual acumen was sharp and unrestrained, and his preaching of the Dharma was largely similar to that of Zhenjing, though he did not know him personally. While residing at Shishuang, he sent a monk to visit Zhenjing with a verse, the final line of which read:
"The travelers from all quarters who come to study Chan—if they do not reach Xinfeng, they are merely fools."
Daosheng, Sengzhao, Daorong, and Daoyi were the eminent disciples of Dharma Master Kumārajīva, renowned as the "Four Relying Bodhisattvas.

Once, when they questioned Kumārajīva regarding his commentary on the *Vimalakīrtinirdeśa-sūtra*, they all set down their pens upon reaching the "Inconceivable Chapter" (*Acintya-parivarta*). This was because such a realm transcends the reach of thought and verbal deliberation;

thus, they were unable to utter a single word. It is like the discourse of the Elder Li (Li Tongxuan) on entering the Dharmadhātu of the *Avataṃsaka-sūtra*, where the words are divided [into distinct categories].
The word-by-word commentary is as clear as the sun and stars; it is resolved and free from doubt. Were it not for having personally encountered one with complete realization, how could it be thus?
Chan Master Baoning Yong was a native of Siming. At the beginning of his monastic career, he changed his robes and relied upon Chan Master Xuedou Mingjue to inquire about the Way.
Xuedou rebuked him as the seat-preceptor Yangxiang. Yong was taken aback; before his term in the hall had even concluded, he immediately packed his bedding and set out.
He vowed while prostrating toward Mount Xuedou: "I am traveling on pilgrimage to study Chan; if my reputation for the Way does not surpass that of Xuedou, I shall certainly not return home.
He subsequently traveled to Yungai in Changsha to visit Master Yangqi Huaihui and Baiyun Wenzhun.

He was still the elder brother of his younger siblings. Later, he appeared in the world and resided at Baoning Monastery in Jiangning Prefecture, where his Way spread throughout the monastic communities, exactly as he had predicted.
On the day Chan Master Fuchan of Yunzhong Mountain opened the hall for formal discourse, a military officer from the music corps stepped forward and asked: "To swallow it all in one gulp—"

Regarding the waters of the West River, he did not ask further. He then turned his head toward the mounting platform before the steps and said, "I request that the Master swallow this mounting platform.
Spreading out both hands, he said, "Grind it into fine powder and bring it here. At these words, Yue Yingzhu attained realization.
Master Huai once said to Xiu Yuanthong: "Only you, Qingfeng, Jian, and Ru—these three of you—will fully realize my school.
All others have merely received the Way according to their individual capacities."
Subhūti was foremost among those who understood emptiness (*śūnyatā*). At the time of his birth, his entire household became empty.
As soon as the World-Honored One ascended the seat, Subhūti stepped forth from the assembly and said, "How rare, World-Honored One! Tell me, what principle did he perceive that he spoke thus?
The Bodhisattva Vasubandhu composed immeasurable verses, yet they merely praised those two words, "How rare. Zen Master Yuanwu said:
"Each phrase is an iron stake. Thus, when the Sixth Patriarch heard the words, "One should give rise to the mind by dwelling nowhere," he immediately attained enlightenment.
One day, Master Zhenjing said to Master Nan: "Master Duan has composed a verse on Linji’s three blows of the staff."
"Causes and conditions are just like one's own point of view. Nan said, "How do you understand his meaning?
As soon as Jing raised his voice, Nan shouted, "I see clearly! You do not understand!"
When the Fifth Patriarch, the Venerable Master, first studied under Chan Master Yuanzhao, he mastered all the causes and conditions of the past and present;

yet, he alone could not understand the case where a monk asked Xinghua, "What is it like when [the opponent] comes from the four directions and the eight quarters? Xinghua said, "Strike the one in the center. The monk bowed.
Huayan said: "Yesterday, Xinghua went to a village vegetarian feast. On the way, he encountered a sudden storm of wind and rain, so he took refuge in a shrine and was able to pass through it safely.
He then requested further instruction from Yuanzhao, who said, "This is the lineage style of Linji;
you must ask one of his descendants before you can understand it. Thereupon, Huayan went to study under Master Fushan Yuan and requested his guidance.

Regarding this koan, Yuan said, "I have a metaphor for you: it is like a woodcutter from a village of three households who, having hauled a load onto his shoulder-pole, asks people, 'What matters are they discussing today in the Hall of Secretariat?
Zuzhao said, 'At such a time as that, you are still far from the mark. Yuan then said to Zuzhao, 'You arrived too late; I am an old monk [who has already reached the goal].'"
"I am old and my hearing is failing. You should go and consult a junior elder, namely Master Baiyun Cunduan.

Although I do not know him personally, having seen his verse on the karmic conditions of Linji’s three blows of the staff, I see that he is pure and clean. Thereupon, the Patriarch went to consult Baiyun.
The Fifth Patriarch once asked Baiyun, "The mani-jewel no one recognizes; it is personally held within the Tathāgatagarbha.
What is this jewel? Baiyun then gave a shout, whereupon the Patriarch attained great enlightenment.
Once the Fifth Patriarch entered the quarters of Baiyun, Baiyun appointed him as the miller at the front of the mountain.

Each year, the Patriarch collected money for the bran and chaff from the mill; he invested these funds to earn interest and hired laborers. Beyond what was required for the daily offerings, any surplus money was deposited into the monastery’s common treasury (*changzhu*).
However, people frequently spread rumors and slandered him in the abbot’s quarters, saying, "The miller drinks by the mill every day."
Wine, meat, and grain husks were being consumed until they were nearly exhausted. In one courtyard, there was great commotion.

When Nanyue heard of this, he intentionally bought meat and brewed wine, hanging them in the mill courtyard. He would mock them with his hands, chatting and laughing with the women without any sense of restraint.
One day, Baiyun summoned him to the abbot’s quarters and asked for the reason. Nanyue simply responded "Yes, yes" and said nothing more. Baiyun—
Yun struck him with his palm and said, "Go away and withdraw! Yun’s expression remained untroubled, and he said, "Wait until the accounts are settled, then please have someone hand over the property.

He then paid his respects and departed. On the following day, Yun went to the Abbot's quarters and said, "While I was at the mill, after purchasing wine and meat, there were three hundred thousand coins remaining;
I have offered them to the monastery. Baiyun was greatly astonished, for only then did he realize that Yun had been jealous of him.
In the [X] year, when Fushou Yuan-tong was serving as the Head Seat (shouzuo) and had accepted an invitation to reside at Si-mian, he immediately requested Chanju to serve as the First Seat.
When Fushou subsequently moved to take up residence at Xi-xian, Chanju again succeeded him by taking up residence at Si-mian.
Baiyun once asked Wuzu about a monk’s question to Dongshan: “What is the eye of a good spiritual friend? Dongshan replied, “A paper wick without oil.
What was the meaning? Wuzu said, “There is no place to grasp it. Later, when Wuzu emerged from seclusion to reside at Sishian, Baiyun sent him off with this verse:
“The illness of having no place to grasp is difficult to remove; One must let go of the snake’s head to stroke the tiger’s whiskers.”
Today the two springs have merged into a single stream; behold the moon rising over the long coral.
Master Wuzu said: "What is this Chan of mine like? It is like a family skilled at thievery who has a son who has grown up.
He suddenly thinks to himself: 'When my father was alive, he supported the family. My father has grown old...'"
Later, [the son] said, "But how shall I support my family? I must learn a trade. He then informed his father, who said, "Very well.

One night, he led him to a wealthy household; they broke through the wall and entered the residence, opened a cabinet containing goods and silks, and said to the son, "Go ahead and enter the cabinet to take what you want. As soon as the son had entered, the father closed the cabinet door and...
The locks were fastened, so he struck upon the floorboards to startle the household into awakening. He then first sought out an old drain and escaped.
When the family rose and lit a fire to inspect the interior, they indeed found a thief; however, he had already gone.
While the young thief was inside the cupboard, lamenting, "Father, why did you act like this? he suddenly hit upon a plan while in his state of distress.
He then made the sound of a rat gnawing. The man’s servant girl lit a lamp and opened the chest;
as soon as the chest was opened, the thief’s son sprang out, extinguished the light with his breath, threw the girl down, and fled in haste. The man’s family pursued him to the middle of the road.
The thief’s son suddenly saw a well and pushed a large stone into it.
When the man of the house went down into the well to search for the thief, the boy ran straight home and asked his father, "Why did you lock me up in here?
His father said, "Do not speak of this yet; how could you possibly have gotten out? The boy recounted everything that had happened. His father said, "If you were like that..."
"Dongshan was indeed capable.
One day, Wuzu said to Yuanwu, 'You are also quite good, but you have some ailments. Yuanwu replied:"
[The monk] did not know what illness he had. The Patriarch said, "Zen is far too much. Wuzu said, "I came here precisely for the sake of studying Zen;
why then do you disdain people speaking of Zen? The Patriarch said, "It would be much better if one simply spoke of ordinary matters. Subsequently, another monk asked:
For what reason did he resent people speaking of Chan? The Patriarch said, "A malicious disposition is precisely that.
Yuanwu, Fojian, and Foyan were all at Wuzu’s monastery. One day they said to one another, "The old monk’s Chan is merely dry and withered;
he often speaks of mind and nature, which is not acceptable. Thereupon, they requested instruction on the Buddha-body being unconditioned (*asaṃskṛta*).
"It does not fall into any categories. The Patriarch said, "It is like a pure maṇi jewel reflecting five colors;
the colors are the categories, while the maṇi jewel is the Buddha-body. Yuanwu said to these two elders, "He understands and speaks with great ease.
When we speak, we expend great effort, whereas he settles it with just one or two sentences. He is clearly a great beast."
The Fifth Patriarch once said: "To speak of mind or to speak of nature is itself evil speech. He further said: "A cat has the merit of drinking blood;
a tiger has the virtue of raising the dead. This is what is meant by driving the plowman’s ox and seizing the hungry man’s food.
Were it not for this, all would be nothing but fellows playing with lumps of mud."
Master Fojian said: "When the Patriarch came from the West, he directly pointed to the human mind, so that by seeing one's nature one would become a Buddha.
Nowadays, in many quarters, people mostly point circuitously to the human mind and speak of attaining Buddhahood through the nature."
When Master Yuanwu had not yet left Sichuan, he had already heard the names of the Chan masters Dinghui Xin, Dongshan Wen, and Shishuang Lin.
After leaving Sichuan, he learned that Lin had already passed away; consequently, he remained within the assembly of Zhennu at Mount Gui for six or seven years.
Thus, he missed the opportunity to meet these three great elders, which became a lifelong regret.

When the Master first traveled abroad, he visited Chan Master Mingji Shaocheng of Xuanzhou. Cheng had extensively studied under senior predecessors such as Langya, Xuedou, and Tianyi, all of whom he had served and from whom he had requested the Dharma.
He later emerged from seclusion to succeed Master Jiaotan and subsequently moved to Ruizhu in Taiping Prefecture, where he retired to the West Hall.
The Master followed him there to seek further instruction on Xuedou’s *Niangu* (Verses on Ancient Cases) and *Songgu* (Verses on Ancient Cases).

Fazheng instructed Cheng to observe the conditions of dependent origination (*pratītyasamutpāda*), emphasizing that one must see for oneself and speak for oneself, without relying even slightly on the words of others.
Master [Dongshan] was profoundly versed in the subtle purport of the ancient sages. Fazheng once remarked to the assembly, "Guangmo is surely a person who has returned from a previous life.
He later traveled to Dayang in Yingzhou, where he met the head seat Yuan, the Venerable Dongshan Wei, and the head seat Jian; at that time, Wei was serving in the assembly at Furong.

He was the leader of the assembly, and Jian served as his attendant for over ten years. The Master spent a very long time attending upon the three successive patriarchs, and he fully grasped the essential spirit of the Cao-Dong school.
At the time of each transmission, they would burn incense on their arms to signify that the dharma had not been bestowed in vain.
The Master said to himself: "If Zen has formal transmission, how can it be the Dharma of self-realization and self-awakening realized by the Buddhas and Patriarchs? To discard [such a view]..."
He relied upon Master Zantang. One day, Zantang asked him, "Why is one side of your nostrils missing today?
He replied, "Under the gate of Baofeng. Zantang said, "A fabricated Chan monk!

On another day, while they were at the place where the Ten Kings were being adorned, Zantang asked, "What is the surname of this official? He replied, "His surname is Liang. Zantang then [struck him] with his hand...

Zhimeng stroked his own head and said, "What can one do about having the surname Liang? One simply lacks a *fukou* (head-wrap). Zhanrang replied, "Though you lack the *fukou*, your nostrils are the same.
Zhanrang said, "You are a fabricated Chan practitioner. Later, while reading a sutra, he asked, "What sutra are you reading?"
The monk replied, "The Diamond Sūtra. Zhandang said, "'This Dharma is equal; there is no high or low.
Why then is Mount Yunju high and Mount Baofeng low? The monk replied, "'This Dharma is equal; there is no high or low. Zhandang said:
Yet you have served as a presiding master (zuozhu) and directed those below you.
One day, Zhantang said to the Master, "Upādhyāya Gaofeng, you have grasped the Chan of this place all at once. If I were to ask you to speak, you could speak;
if I were to ask you to compose *niangu*, *songgu*, small sermons (*xiaocan*), or general discourses (*pushe*), you could do those as well. However, there is one thing—do you know it?"
He replied, "I do not know what matter. Zantang said, "You lack a single turning word; it is because you have not attained this turning word that [the teaching] exists.
When I, the abbot, speak it for you, there is Chan; the moment you leave the abbot's quarters, it is gone."
"When one is alert and deliberating, there is Chan; as soon as one falls asleep, it is gone. If this is the case, how can one withstand birth and death?
He replied, "This is precisely where I have my doubts. Later, because Tanzang was critically ill, the Master asked him:
"Master, if you do not recover from this illness, whom should I rely upon to bring this great matter to completion?
Danzhang said, "There is a diligent seeker whom even I do not know. If you meet him, you will surely be able to accomplish this matter.
However, once you have met him, do not immediately go off to practice; instead, come out in future generations to study Chan."
When the Master was at Baofeng, Yuan the Head Seat was extremely fond of him and invited him to visit Li Shanglao.
They had agreed that he would return within one month, but he did not return until forty days later. Upon seeing him, Yuan suddenly said, "Alas! It is finished; impermanence is swift.
The Master was so startled that he broke into a cold sweat.
The Master was reading Dongshan’s “Verse on Awakening to the Way” and became suspicious, thinking: "There is 'that one' and there is 'this one'; what kind of Chan is this?

He then requested instruction from Zantang. Zantang said, "Recite it again for me. When the Master recited it once more, Zantang said, "You have not even understood what you have recited," and he pushed him out of the room.

Because Master [Dahui] had requested Hong Juefan to compose a formal record of the life and deeds of Master Zantang upon his passing, and having further obtained a letter of introduction from Chan Master Daoshao of Doushuai, he traveled specifically to Jingnan to visit the Layman Wujin and request a stele inscription for the master’s tomb.
Upon first meeting Wujin, he stood and asked: "Sir, you have come such a great distance wearing these straw sandals just for this? He replied: "I have been counting..."
"Having traveled a thousand *li* to beg for alms, I have come to see you, Minister," he said. The Minister asked again, "How old are you? He replied, "Twenty-four.
The Minister asked again, "How old is the water buffalo? He replied, "Two. The Minister asked again, "Where did you learn this deception?
He replied, "I have seen you, Minister, face-to-face today. Wujin laughed and said, "Since you have come from afar, sit down and eat."
Tea was served. As soon as he was seated, [the official] asked again, "What brings you here from so far away? The Master replied, "The Venerable of Lestam has passed away.
During his cremation, his eyes, teeth, and rosary remained unburnt, and countless *śarīra* relics were obtained.

The senior monks of the mountain all wish to have Your Excellency compose a grand inscription for his stupa, to inspire future students; thus I have come from afar specifically for this purpose, daring to trouble your esteemed office."
Ting Wujin said, "I am here serving my sentence for a crime. I have never composed writings for others. Now I have a question to ask you, sir.
If you can answer it, I will write the inscription for your stupa; if you cannot, I shall give you five thousand cash and return to Doushuai to practice Zen.
The Master said, "Please, Excellency, ask the question. Wujin said, "I have heard that Old Man Zhun’s eyes..."
Wujin asked, "Is it indestructible? The Master said, "It is. Wujin said, "I am not asking about this eye.
The Master said, "What eye are you asking about, Excellency? Wujin said, "The Vajra Eye.
The Master said, "If it is the Vajra Eye, it is upon your writing brush, Excellency. Wujin said, "In that case, I shall light it for him."
"Clear! Let it illuminate both heaven and earth! The Master said, "The former master was most fortunate to have the Minister compose this stele inscription.
Wujin responded with a series of "yeses" and smiled.
Yuánwù asked the Master, "When Bodhidharma came from the West, what did he transmit? The Master replied, "One must not entirely view this through the perspective of a wild fox spirit.
Yuánwù asked again, "Regarding 'seizing the tiger's head and catching the tiger's tail,' the primary phrase reveals the fundamental tenet.
What is the first phrase? The Master said, "That is the second phrase."
Yuánwù asked the Master, "When a deceased monk passes away, where does he go? The Master replied, "He opens the precious stupa.
Yuánwù asked the Master, "As soon as Yántóu stepped across the gate of Dēshān, he asked, 'Is this the ordinary or the holy? At which Dēshān gave a shout. What was his intention?
The Master replied, "To kill a person, one must have the sword that kills; to bring a person to life, one must have the sword that brings to life."
A sword. A monk requested further instruction from Yuanwu. The monk asked Touzi, "What is the Ten-Body Tamer? Touzi descended from his meditation seat and stood there.

The monk asked again, "How far apart are the ordinary and the sage? Touzi descended from his meditation seat and stood there. [The monk] asked, "What is the underlying meaning of this? Touzi descended from his meditation seat and stood there.
Yuánwù said, "By all means avoid it. He then requested further instruction from the Master, who replied, "It is exactly so.
The Master said to Zhào Jùjì, "After the Old Monk has suddenly departed, there will be others who come to teach you Chan."
"How can this turning of conditions be understood? How can that turning be understood? Simply take note of this: 'I shall pour hot excrement upon you.
When the Master was serving as the Head Seat at Yunju, he once went to Xiji Village and encountered a temporary visitor from Yuancong Temple.
The monk approached and said, "I have attained a point of realization while contemplating the Head Seat’s verse on the story of the woman emerging from samādhi.
I have come specifically to seek the Head Seat’s certification. The Master said, "Go away! Go away! It is not so! The monk asked, "I have not yet spoken of my realization;
why do you say it is not so? The Master shook his head repeatedly and said, "Go away! Not so! Not so! The monk was crestfallen.
He smiled and withdrew. One day, Yuanwu went to the Head Seat’s quarters and spoke of Elder Mijin’s ascent of the Dharma seat at Jingshan, saying:
"Four years ago, when I saw him, he was just like this; yet when he ascended the seat at Jingshan, he was also just like this."
Di went through one round, then another, continuing on without ever bringing the fight to a conclusion. How could he possibly overcome the man?
It was as if he were carrying a cartload of precious swords; he drew one, then drew another, simply wanting to exhaust them all.
If he had possessed the true means, he would have taken up a single sword and killed the man on the spot.

There, he simply continued to bring it out and play with it. At that time, a monk who had heard of this said to the Master, "The other day, because I read his *xiaocan* (informal sermon) records, I knew that this man has always practiced subtle and refined work.
That is why, before the assembly, he insists on exhausting one segment after another and refuses to stop. The Master said, "The matter is not as you say."
This dragon king, having obtained but half a cup of water, is able to raise clouds, emit mist, and pour down heavy rain.
Yet he merely rolls about in the great ocean, thinking, "I have so much water. It is like people who are about to kill one another.
Holding a single spear, as soon as he sees the enemy cavalry, he knows for certain which one is his own.
He advances, strikes down the enemy with a spear, leaps onto the horse's back, and proceeds to kill the men. One must act in this manner to benefit others; only then will it suffice.
The Master once set fire to his curtains. The following day, he offered incense and raised the koan of the dog having no Buddha-nature, saying:
"If you wish to understand the meaning of Buddha-nature, you should observe the conditions of time and season. As the Great Master Yunmen said: "If one is a person who has attained it..."
When has the fire of the Way ever burned one’s mouth? Thus, he composed a verse: Zhaozhou says the dog has no Buddha-nature;
When has the fire of the Way ever burned his mouth? Last night it suddenly flared up above the curtain; The Persian from the South Sea had his nostrils singed.
The Master then raised the following case: Zhaozhou asked a monk, "Where have you recently come from?
The monk replied, "Xuefeng. Zhaozhou asked, "What words or phrases did Xuefeng speak? The monk said, "Xuefeng said, 'The entire earth is the single eye of a śramaṇa;
where do you all usually defecate? Zhaozhou asked, "Will you go back again? The monk replied, "This very day."

He then departed. Zhaozhou said, "I am sending you a spade. The Master said, "Nowadays, people everywhere discuss this, saying that Zhaozhou sent a spade to Xuefeng to have him 'weed out' that ailment.
Had he said at the time, 'I am sending you a bowl,' I do not know how they would have discussed it."
The Master then cited this: Dharma Master Zhao said, "Śākyamuni closed his chamber in Magadha;
Vimalakīrti sealed his mouth in Vaiśālī; Subhūti proclaimed 'non-speaking' to manifest the Way; and Śakra and Brahmā ceased listening as flowers rained down.

All of these instances were because the Principle was governed by the Divine, such that the mouth remained silent on its account. How could one say they lacked eloquence? It is simply that there is that which eloquence cannot speak. The Master [said].
It is said: Since principle is that which the spirit governs, it is not a matter of silence. Yet most people depart from this point;

they die there and cannot come back to life, leaving them with nothing but their mouths hanging on the wall. An ancient said: "Relying upon the foundation of non-abiding, all dharmas are established."
When Master Yunmen was alive, he would say: "The fan leaps up to the thirty-third heaven, striking the nostrils of Śakra.
A carp from the Eastern Sea receives a blow of the staff, and the rain pours down like an overturned basin.
Ying Péntóu once offered four turning words on this, saying: "Śākyamuni shut his room in Magadha—this is the Buddhas' speaking without speaking. Vimalakīrti..."
"Mañjuśrī remained silent at Vaiśālī; this is the Bodhisattva’s speaking without speaking. Subhūti proclaimed 'no speaking' to manifest the Way;
this is the Śrāvaka’s speaking without speaking. Śakra and Brahmā ceased listening while raining flowers; this is the ordinary person’s speaking without speaking.
These four turns of speech are quite excellent when applied to external objects, but they do not suffice for the purpose of guiding others."
Lī Dàoshān shaved his head and requested a small-scale discourse (*xiǎocān*). This mountain monk also has four turning phrases:
Śākyamuni shut his room in Magadha and exhausted his family’s wealth; Vimalakīrti remained silent in Vaiśālī and guarded the hitching post for his donkey;

Subhūti proclaimed "no speech" to manifest the Way and threw his hair-tuft into the magistrate’s office; and when Śakra and Brahmā ceased their listening, flowers rained down from the void. Looking toward the sky...
The Master said, "I once met an old master who, upon ascending the hall, declared: 'In the assembly of my former teacher, I attained the final word.
I cannot help but bestow it upon the great assembly. After a long silence, he asked: 'That which does not act as a companion to the myriad dharmas—what is it?'"
“Wait until you can swallow up all the waters of the West River in a single draught, and then I shall tell you. He then descended from his seat. The Master said, “I am not like that.
While I was in my teacher’s assembly, I obtained the ‘final phrase. I cannot help but bestow it upon the great assembly.
He then descended from his seat.
The Master entered the room for private instruction. Upon emerging, he said to the assembly: "In these times, many of you brothers rely on intellectual views and conceptual understanding;
you insist on answering questions here with idle talk and lengthy discourse.
This is very much like someone holding a priceless *maṇi* jewel in their hand, yet when asked what they have in their hand, they instead drop it and pick up a clod of earth."
"How utterly foolish! If you proceed like this, you will not attain realization even after as many years as it takes for a donkey to grow horns.
The Master said, "Nowadays, there are certain masters who, after three or five rounds of private instruction with a student, fail to discern the student's understanding.
Instead, they ask the student to state their realization, asking, 'What is your realization? The student then says, 'My realization is..."* *(Note: The source text ends abruptly at this point.)*
It cannot be spoken of. Yet he says, "You cannot speak of it; how can I see you go? If it is like this, how can one act for the sake of others?
Have you not seen when Great Master Quan arrived at the place of Ciming and said, "A single cloud spans the mouth of the valley"?
A traveler asked, "Where have you come from? Yunquan said, "Last night, where was the fire that burned out the ancient tomb?
Ming said, "Not yet; speak further. Yunquan made the sound of a tiger. Ming then struck him with his meditation mat (zuoju). Yunquan pushed Ming onto the meditation platform.
Having clarified this, he then made a tiger’s sound. Quan said, "Of the eighty-four *kalyāṇamitras* I have encountered, only you have succeeded in carrying on the Linji school's tradition.
Look at these few lines of question and answer; where is the point of seeing him?
"It must be like this before it can be attained.
The Master said, "I have no dharma to give people here; I simply settle the case according to the facts.
It is as if you were carrying a precious lapis lazuli bottle and cherishing it. What is it like? As soon as I see it, I smash it for you."
"You will soon obtain a mani-jewel; I shall snatch it from you. You will come along in due course like this, and I shall cut off both your hands as well.
Therefore, Master Linji said: 'When encountering a Buddha, kill the Buddha;
when encountering a Patriarch, kill the Patriarch; when encountering an Arhat, kill the Arhat. You say that one who is called a 'good spiritual friend' (kalyāṇamitra)..."
"How could one possibly wish to kill people? Tell me, what is the principle here?
The Master said, "Nowadays, when brothers practice the Way and do not attain realization, where does the fault lie?
It is simply because they seek to 'clarify' it. It is just as when it is said: 'It is not so,' nor is it 'not so. It is both so and not so..."
"No. You cannot grasp it at all. But how then do you clarify it? Can you take a single turning word to clarify it?
You can never clarify it. The ancients were exceedingly direct; it is simply that you are unwilling to practice in that place of directness.
It could be said: 'Precisely because it is so utterly clear, it causes what is attained to be delayed.'"
The Master said: "This mountain monk treats people with utmost sincerity; it must be that your own fundamental nature is such that you may attain it.
This is the 'one leap directly entering the stage of the Tathāgata. In practicing Zen, one must have a direct mind, a direct path, direct thoughts, and direct speech.

Because the mind and speech are direct, from beginning to end there are no stages, and throughout the middle there are never any signs of crookedness. When the Patriarch came from the West, he spoke only of the direct."
This points directly to the human mind. A monk asked Yunmen, "What is the Buddha? Yunmen replied, "A dried-up shit-stick.
To hesitate or engage in deliberation is already to have gone astray; how much more so to utter empty fabrications!
The Master said: "A student of the Way is like someone whose bright pearl has been stolen. One must first catch the thief before anything can be done.
Once the thief is caught, one may then interrogate him slowly; the pearl will naturally be recovered."
The Master said, "If you understand, you will go to one world, then another world, and yet another world.
The Master said, "In my place, I am empty-handed; I simply use what is yours."

The Master said: "In general, when investigating Chan, one need not claim that something is correct simply because it involves a sharp exchange of words. Formerly, the Venerable Yungai Zhi possessed clear insight into the Way.
Once, when the Prefect entered the mountains and rested at the 'Discourse on Emptiness' Pavilion, he asked him, 'What is the Discourse on Emptiness Pavilion?'"

Zhìyún remarked, "This is merely a pavilion for discoursing on emptiness. The Prefect was displeased and subsequently questioned Běn Mù. Běn said, "One simply preaches the Dharma from within the courtyard;
what need is there to discourse on emptiness with the mouth? The Prefect was delighted and transferred Běn to the abbacy of Yúngài. Comparing Běn with Zhì, the difference is vast.
Thus one knows that in matters of ultimate truth, a person cannot be judged by their sharp wit alone. —Bǎofēng.
As for Yuanzuo (Seat of the Primordial Head), there was a man of the Way whose response to the sharp thrusts of dialogue was dull. Juefan called him "Yuan Wudou" (Yuan’s Five Pecks);
this was because he had to open his mouth to draw breath and wait until five pecks of rice were cooked before he could deliver a single turn of phrase.
The Master said: "When Zhang Wujin met Dou-shuai Yue, he instead criticized Hei-tang, composing a verse that says:

'Long have I heard of the Dragon within Huanglong Mountain; Upon arriving, I find only an old mountain-dweller. One must know that beyond the 'backing' and 'touching' of the fist, There is another point of spiritual penetration.
At that time, there was no one among the various quarters who did not sigh in admiration. Later, when this mountain monk saw it, I regretted [it]."
Wujin had already passed away. He said: "One must know that apart from the touch or the strike of the fist, there is another 'single point of spiritual penetration'.
If one relies on this verse to seek out Huitang, is it not far removed from the mark?
The Master said: "When I was at Letan, I had not yet attained realization through Zen practice, but I first understood Fenyang’s 'Ten Wisdoms Identical with Reality.

I loved his saying, 'The face and features are present now,' and so I composed this verse: 'Rabbit horns and tortoise hair grow within the eyes; An iron mountain stands before me, its form towering and steep.
East, west, south, and north—there is no gate through which to enter; Eons of ignorance are instantly reduced to ashes.'"
Once I mentioned this to Hong Juefan. Juefan sighed and said, "How strange! I have been practicing my craft for twenty years, and I thought I had only reached this point."
One day, State Councilor Yi Han-ro, Gentleman Official Cai Ji-yeong, Grand Master Ch’o Yon-rin, and Professor Yi Don-yu gathered together at Unmun Hermitage.
On that occasion, the Master gave a small-scale discourse (sōparam) on the story of Zhaozhou’s “Cypress Tree,” offering this verse:
The cypress tree in the courtyard— Today it is raised anew. Breaking through Zhaozhou’s barrier, One needlessly seeks words.
[The Master] spoke. "I venture to ask the assembly: since you have already broken through Zhaozhou’s barrier, why do you still seek words?
After a long silence, he said, "At first I thought the thatch was uneven; having burned it, I find the ground is not level.
When Minister Li heard this, he attained sudden enlightenment and said to the Master, "Had there not been these final words, I would not have understood either. Li Duanyou [recorded this] privately.
Cai Ziying said to Chu Yulun, "It is not that Li Hanlao has attained Chan; rather, it is that Li the State Councilor has attained Chan.
Ziying replied, "Not so. The State Councilor is no rustic from a village of three households;
he must have attained it through his own self-acceptance. Yulun said, "What Ziying says is correct."
The Elder Wulong was visiting with Feng Jichuan during a conversation. Jichuan said, "In the past, someone asked the Great Sage of Sizhou, 'What is your surname?
Sizhou replied, 'My surname is He. When asked again, 'In what land do you dwell? Sizhou replied, 'I dwell in the land of He. What is the meaning of this?
Wulong said, "The Great Sage originally did not have the surname He, nor did he have a land to dwell in; he simply manifested according to conditions to transform and deliver beings."
Chuansu laughed and said, "What is the Great Sage’s surname? In which country does he reside?
He asked this back and forth several times, until he finally sent a letter to the Master requesting that he resolve this kōan for him. The Master replied, "I have sixty blows of the staff to send;
thirty blows shall strike the Great Sage for initially asking his surname, and thirty blows shall strike Layman Feng for saying 'Great'."
"What is the noble lineage of certainty? If it was the Elder Wolong, he was instructed to lead him out himself.
The Master went to the Hall of the Bright Moon and saw a painting of withered bones on the wall. Feng Jichuan offered this verse: "The physical frame remains here; where is this person?
Thus one knows that the single spirit does not belong to the skin-bag. The Master followed this with his own verse: "Right here are these very bones..."
"He is indeed that person: a single spiritual soul within a skin-bag, and a single spiritual soul within a skin-bag.
Because Wugai requested him to praise Fahai Zhen, he said: "The old master from Jiangxi laughs heartily at those under Yunmen in Jiangnan, yet he does not laugh at Jueyin.
This is because he once studied under Baoning Yong and the likes of Zhengjing; moreover—"
Xiu Yuan-tong once met Shun Lao-fu and Fu-shan Yuan; for this reason, he was distinct from the rest, who are all laughable.
This is because Fa-hai succeeded Jue-yin, and Jue-yin succeeded Yuan-tong. His words say: "Broaden the gate of Yuan-tong."

Continuing the Yunmen lineage, he sat cross-legged upon a huchang chair, surveying all manner of strange phenomena with the gaze of a tiger. Wearing the seal of Vairocana, he crushed and subdued demons and heretics.

With a single phrase facing the sun, even a flash of lightning was not swift enough. Entering samādhi within the unmoving realm of practice, both those who praise and those who revile him suffer from leprosy.
This is what is called the Elder of the Dharma Ocean; able to sport within the infinite at the tip of a single hair.
The Dharma-realm.

Postscript by Vice Minister Li (Hanlao):

The Elder Miaoxi, while recently instructing his disciples, invariably cited extraordinary events from antiquity whenever he raised a point for exposition, desiring that later students hear what they had not yet heard.
His disciples vied with one another to transcribe these onto scrolls of draft paper as records; some who were fond of such things have even passed them down.
These were not all written by the old man [Dongshan] himself; for this reason, the matters lack systematic order and the prose is unadorned.
They merely record facts as they occurred at the time, directly and straightforwardly clarifying the Way. Those within the monastic community who do not know these details in full—
Frequently, they judge right and wrong by these [external criteria]—treating ice and charcoal as gains and losses. Alas!

The scholars of today, who hold a bamboo tube to measure the heavens and a ladle to gauge the ocean, all arrive at this same conclusion: they lose the truth while following the counterfeit; they reject the root while rushing toward the branches.
Truly, there is much here. Yet it was not my original intention to compile these writings.

Fearing that I might remain silent and fail to record them, I have jotted this down at the end of the draft. On the first day of the Lantern Festival in the year of Xinyou, the layman Wuzhu, Li Bing, wrote this atop the Xiaoxi Cottage.

Chancellor Zhang (Deyuan), through great skillful means, protected and sustained the True Dharma. The majestic and sublime reality transcends birth and extinction; it is like the surging and tumultuous flow of rivers.
Like dragon-elephants trampling and treading; I observe the Master’s countenance and speak thus:

since the True Command has been put into practice, the heavenly Māras have lost heart. In every place, the light of the Dharma shines resplendently; yet there are those who, though having such a son, do not recognize him.

This means that when the Master establishes the self, he gazes upon the vast void; there, the roar of thunder and flashes of lightning become a profuse rain of Dharma, from which all equally receive its bounty.
Observing the Master in this way, one sees that no distinction exists between self and others.
The Dharma-eye transmits the mind; the worldly eye transmits the form. Yet both form and mind are fundamentally not true. To truly understand Great Wisdom, look at the blue sky and the white clouds.
Prime Minister Li (Boji) had heard of the name of Furi but had not yet beheld his countenance; he had seen the appearance of Furi but had not yet heard his words.
The mind may be in accord and spirits may commune; it is possible that we have not yet met face-to-face. The Way may exist through direct perception; it is possible that we have not heard your words.
Like the moon in the water, though it is not seen in reality, there is already a sense of refreshing clarity. Like the lion’s roar, though the sound has not yet been uttered.
Having already given rise to a heart of awe and reverence, were it not for one who is truly such a person, capable of discerning such matters and esteemed by all, who could have attained this?
Nevertheless, on the summit of a solitary peak, one may revile the Buddhas and scold the Patriarchs—this is the Sun of the Buddha.
Yet, within a single scroll of painted colors, there is silence and no speech—this too is the Sun of the Buddha. As for which is right and which is wrong, those with clear eyes will surely know.
Regarding the assessment [of this matter]:
Minister Yi Han-ro’s service to Yuanwu was like that of Guan Zhong in serving Qi; first it was "Father Zhong," and second it was "Father Zhong. Master [Yi]—*duo*.

In discerning the heterodox from the orthodox, he was like Zhongni (Confucius) honoring the Zhou dynasty; "Those who understand me are the Spring and Autumn Annals; those who condemn me are the Spring and Autumn Annals.
Observing his method of teaching, it is like thunder and lightning; at its essential points, it is like a compact or a covenant; in its application, it is like the sun and the moon.

Where they met, they were like father and son; thus, the eminent, extraordinary, and profoundly learned scholars of the time all revered his virtue and conduct, following him in a life beyond the mundane world.
Even those of the lineage who had once held their own nostrils high toward heaven and sat upon thrones to preach the Dharma submitted themselves to his teachings and called themselves his disciples.
Alas! It was by this means that he gave rise to the orthodox lineage of Linji, making it radiant and magnificent.
As for this world, it truly possesses its own significance.

With a cranial protuberance as lofty as a mountain peak and brilliant eyes like flashing lightning, his countenance is as harmonious and melting as spring, and his solitary bearing is as pure as frost. He serves as a pillar and beam for the Dharma.
Acting as a bridge and raft for the world, revered by humans and devas, and causing demons and heretics to tremble with awe—there is yet one more phrase;
who can discern it? To say "it is" would blind your eyes; to say "it is not" would stammer your tongue. Puhua, do not perform your somersaults;
Zhaozhou, desist from saying "I would kill you. Ānanda and Kāśyapa both knit their brows; since you have not yet understood, I shall now act for your sake.
A Secret Instruction. Formerly, Minister of State Li (Tae-baek) once beheld the Elder Vimalakīrti;
today, he has suddenly donned the robes of a monk. For what reason does his portrait fail to capture this?
Accomplished. It is simply because from the beginning there has been no face. Chancellor Qian (Chuhe):
[illegible] heaven and earth are not clear and peaceful. This old man extinguishes the world. A fine time for Great Peace.
Sitting with feet upturned upon the sea—tell me, what supernatural powers does he possess? Seizing him by the face, he spits right in his eyes.

Whether one intends to go to the wheel of gold, the wheel of wind, or the wheel of water; to the realm of desire, the realm of form, or the formless realm; or to Pūrvavideha in the east, Aparagoyānī in the west—[where can he escape?]
Jambudvīpa to the south, Uttarakuru to the north, circling the heavens eighteen times— seeking such a venerable and compassionate one,
appearing in such a multitude of strange, marvelous, and extraordinary forms, and yet fundamentally there are not two of them (a shout).
With nothing at all within his belly, he made a great show before his eyes. Of the more than a thousand people beneath his seat, he reviled them all from start to finish.
