For a time, he felt a sense of lofty satisfaction; thus, his ill repute spread far and wide. One would imagine that among the biographies of the Jin and Tang dynasties, there could never have been such a high monk;
how could there be such a Bodhidharma in the *Jingde Chuandeng Lu*? Truly, what a spirit-filled patch-robed monk!
Upon seeing him, he liked to spit directly in his face.
Official-Conferrer Feng (Jichuan) wished to know the Elder of Mount Jing;
his stubbornness was peerless. He settled fifteen hundred followers and took charge of the monastery’s permanent assets.
Originally there was not a single grain. If one discusses Chan or speaks of the Way, indeed it is纵横 (zōnghéng) and difficult to oppose; its singular flavor and temperament are not constant.
Even the Buddha could not fathom it. Seeing it across the river and immediately returning—truly, I can guarantee this is the highest and greatest good fortune.
There were fifteen hundred stewards of rice and gruel, and more than three hundred spiritual friends across the various provinces. Within his room, he used a bamboo staff;
he simply wanted to bend the crooked and make it straight. If you can bring this forth completely in this very moment, you will see the news of the Buddhas and Patriarchs.
If you can believe it, you shall become a Buddha standing right where you are, without expending even a hair’s breadth of effort.
This is the Abbot of Jingshan. Whether acting in opposition or accord, his myriad ways are beyond compare: when he is joyful, even Bodhisattvas cannot equal him;
when he is enraged, even asuras cannot be mentioned. With his own will, he roams freely in every direction, leaving people at liberty to turn their backs or face him.
Though empty space might still be possible to sketch, this fellow has always been without pretense.

The Brahma-like features of the World-Honored One cannot be carved; the countenance of Master Zhigong cannot be traced. If one wishes to achieve a complete and total likeness, neither brush and ink nor chisel and carving will suffice.
This body is solemn as if dwelling in meditative absorption, yet it is also like a verse on the emptiness of all things.
Nonsense! To take this and show it to people in the world is like walking backward out the door.

Before Zhaojun Wang (Biao-zhi) had even poked his head out, he encompassed heaven and covered the earth; as soon as he lowered his hand, he startled heaven and shook the earth. One must not seek after such a family style.
Constantly discussing Chan, they produced divergent views. Those with discernment gazed upon the mountain and offered praise; those who harbored doubts took it to be mere abuse.
Unless one has previously walked upon this mountain peak, one cannot understand the swallowing of words and the holding of one's breath.
Throughout his life, Assistant Minister Liu (Shao-mei) towered over the Buddhas and patriarchs; he could scold them until their worth was not even half a coin.

Yet, when others brought him before the "Cat Painting," there was not a single word he could utter. Because he could not speak it, he did not hear it. Just this much encompasses heaven and earth. Therefore—
Scholars from the four quarters gather at his gate like clouds; when he reaches the point where there is nowhere left to turn, he even turns his trousers inside out to make them into a loincloth.
I have no prior grudge against this old man, yet the moment we meet, he becomes a thorn in my eye. There is no need for me to go everywhere exposing his ugliness and clumsiness.
The rivers are clear and the seas are calm; the autumn sky is high. In whose jar is there no bright moon?

Provincial Inspector Wu (Yuanzhao) possesses an air of heroic spirit like a jade mountain; his compassionate countenance is filled with the autumn moon. To say he is the true Jingshan is to call him "sand-steamed rice."
The Way is not at Mount Jing; there is flour even within the wheat. Unless one is a person who recognizes the mind, they will concern themselves with neither right nor wrong.
This stagnant merchandise has lingered for a thousand years—a wheel-rut from the time of Qin.
He has revived the true lineage of Linji; the handle of the ladle must be returned to this man. From of old he has roamed freely across the seas;
do not take offense at his lifelong carrying of a wooden board. I now join in rejoicing and extolling him, yet this is merely a temporary expedient.
Should you turn your head back to look at him, you would blind the eyes of all people in the world.
Minister Liu (Jigao), Gautama Xi, was forty-nine years old.
This eminent descendant was rare in his generation; his appearance was like that of a celestial being, and he was as lofty as the Dipper.
For seventy-five years he roared the lion’s roar, a compassionate parent who received beings and benefited all living things. To depict him in ink and color ensures his legacy shall endure forever.
This old master, Official Cai (Ziying), has realized nothing in his entire life. His countenance is not worth looking upon, and his speech is not worth listening to.
He speaks one-sidedly of the "Great Emptiness of Liberation. Furthermore, his mind is driven by the affliction of craving, agitating the monastic communities throughout the world.
He reviles the sages and saints of both past and present; how can such a person be a master of our own time? Yet he possesses so many defects. Among them, there is one particularly pitiable instance:
when asked whether a dog has Buddha-nature, he merely shouts, "No! (Duh!).

Zhang Huigou (Zhaoyuan) possessed the mechanism of a rushing thunderclap and a flashing lightning bolt; he bore the spirit of lifting up mountains and leaping over the stars. Whenever he encountered someone, he spoke of the wondrous and discoursed on the profound mysteries.
In their fundamental state, they possess no handle at all; sometimes they blow sand and scatter stones, which is originally their playful sport.
Were it not for those who are true masters with the eye of discernment, one would surely fall into such a trap.
His spirit was lofty and imposing; his natural endowment was preeminent. His sharp, piercing wit surged like thunder and flashed like lightning.
With a hammer beyond the conventional, he forged both patriarchs and Buddhas. Alas! The Treasury of the True Dharma Eye has been extinguished within this blind donkey.
The Way of the world has fallen into ruin;
the King of Evil Demons reigns supreme. May the Sun of Yao sweep away the miasma, and the Sun of the Buddha shatter delusion amidst the chaos and separation of rivers and lakes.

Providing for and preparing against decline and weakness, you, Master, have come seeking people. You preach the Dharma according to their capacities; when people remain, I depart, and when people leave, I stay.

What does the *yuánluán* (pheasant) seek? It is like the owl that caws at a rotting mouse. Whether by tending the fire-seed or plowing with the blade, if one were to spend one’s entire life thus, there would be no obstruction in the waters and clouds.

Mountains and seas are traversed at will. The Patriarch crushed the six schools; the Master distinguished the heterodox from the orthodox, discussing only the One Truth and not inquiring after the five houses.

Dwelling in the present yet practicing according to antiquity, he set aside conventional rules. He revived what was fallen into ruin and pierced the blindness of the ignorant, seeking only to bring about a single awakening. This is for those long-time practitioners.
He cannot be turned away by a mere wave of the hand. They carry their provisions and take him to heart; what need is there to compel them?

With a little stimulation, they all become lively and agile. Released into the monastic groves, none dare to obstruct him. That the great masters and eminent sages harmonize with him is as natural as Heaven; they see no cause for anger or suspicion.
Upon seeing this, one is set at ease. It is like Huangbo’s rest, like Dadian’s recovery. The arrival [of the truth] is yet to cease; its transmission shall be brilliant and far-reaching.
The Way lies in discussing reality, not in competing with the mouth. Paths diverge and branches spread; each views their own longevity. Like grass bowing before the wind, all shall hasten toward it.
Thunder crashing and rain pouring down—this teaching was propagated without waiting for thirty years later.
State Councilor Zheng (Yugong) was truly a descendant of Linji;
he penetrated the Three Mysteries and Three Statements and brought forth Danxia’s head-wrap. North of the River...
Unrivaled in the Jiangnan region: Deshan sings, He Shan beats the drum, Xuefeng plays with the ball, and Yantou dances.

A heap of bones on level ground—this is the ultimate deployment of the Way. How can these compare to the idle man who alone fills the four seas? His refined bearing flows freely as his sleeves are lightly raised.
Only when the General on the Frontier recognizes the *biu* does he know there is a true tiger.
People say this old man delights in discussing Chan. Who would dare to transmit this matter? Before the peak of Shaoshi, there were no superfluous words;
the elegance of the Second Patriarch pervades the great thousand-fold world. Let us set aside for now the story of standing in the snow with his waist even with it.
But what of it before the Hall of the Bright Moon? The fragrant breeze blows as it did of old; it is precisely the right time to open one’s chest and stroke the strings of Shun’s zither.
Censor Chen (Cizhong): "Magnificent indeed is this elder!
He possesses a refined elegance that moves others and a majestic presence like that of a king. With his correct knowledge and vision,"
He championed the Great Dharma with great power, shouldering the burden of the patriarchs. His verbal discourse on Chan was like thunder and lightning;
his unrestrained reviling of others was like wind and rain. His discernment of the heterodox and the orthodox was like that of upright men and noble officials in the imperial court;
his ability to kill or give life according to the occasion was like that of a strategist or a valiant general facing the ranks. Those who were self-styled elders were jealous of him.
To those of true lineage, he was like an enemy; yet to the monks of his own school, he was as dear as parents.
That the Yangqi lineage flourished with such radiant glory for five generations relied upon this old man as the master of the Dharma path—until the time the "donkey saddle" finally arrived.
He restrains and refines those who have recently entered the study of the Way; his realization transcends ordinary sentiment.
That which no one is able to conjecture or deliberate upon is nothing other than this single black bamboo staff. "Ren, Zen! Ren, Zen! You must, by all means, realize it.
Fu Jinggan (Zhonghou) was a towering figure at Jingshan, a paragon among men.
While the whole world slandered him behind his back, I alone confronted him face-to-face. Others have called him a modern-day Ji An.

Not holding office at court, his pen moved with unrestrained mastery, like thunder rolling and wind sweeping across the heavens. People said that Dongpo was not in the Han-yuan (the Imperial Academy);

I knew this man to be a teacher of both men and gods—his majestic virtue could not be bowed, nor could he be shifted by poverty or low station. He sat upon the *pútuán* (grass mat) and held his staff.
Laughing at Xuanyuan and Fuxi.
A Memorial for the Court Scholar.

Special Advance, Right Vice-Director of the Department of State Affairs, concurrently Acting Director of the Secretariat and the Chancellery, and Participant in Deliberating State Affairs, as well as Director of the Bureau of Military Affairs...
Secret emissary, Duke of Rong, Tang Sita: Alas! The Way was founded in India;
its transformation spread throughout the world during the Putong era. Seven patriarchs passed through the ages, and the lineage branched into five schools.

Masters from all quarters stood like horns jutting out, contending for preeminence. When it grew obscure and diminished, it was bound to flourish and prosper once more. How great is the Chan Master—Buddha after Buddha!

I am one with you. Our practice and realization correspond; person and environment are both fused. Like the sun of Zhongni and the dragon of Laozi, you illuminate ten thousand *li*, riding upon clouds and driving the wind.
For seventy-five years, your Dharma-gift has been inexhaustible, shaking the lands of China and the barbarians. People look up to you as they do to Mount Heng and Mount Song.

Now that your fruit is full and your conditions exhausted, you have ended your life in accordance with the world. Humans and devas sigh in lamentation; the mountains and forests change their countenances. Oh, Master!

Master Daodian: Having long been in accord with Your Imperial Acumen, You have bestowed upon me a decree of appointment, such that Your bounty is exceptional and Your rites are abundant. Recently, I encountered the Master, who awakened my ignorance and dispelled my delusions;

yet I have only caught a glimpse of his outer precincts, not yet having entered his inner palace. The Master has suddenly passed away—whither shall I now turn? Bound by the silken cords of official service, I am unable to attend the offerings in person.

I have composed these words and entrusted them to a friend to express my inner sentiments. The Master now dwells in profound stillness... *Note: The final character "常" (cháng) appears to be an incomplete or truncated ending of the original text.*
Within the realm of tranquil light, birth is without attachment, and death is likewise not emptiness. Why then do I harbor such persistent concern in my heart?

May you enjoy this offering. [This is for] Zhang, Duke of Wei, the Special Advancement (Tejin) and Chief Secretary of the Imperial Chancellery (Shumishi), and Commander-in-Chief of the Military Forces of Jianghuai, who was specially invested.
(Jun) Alas! My relationship with the Master was one of fundamental mental resonance from the start. We conversed at ease, forgetting ourselves beyond the realm of material things.

Yet the Master’s heart relied solely upon loyalty and filial piety; his concern for the state and the people never strayed onto other paths. Who could have recognized that this true monk would so skillfully display [his talents]?
He was slandered in the interim and cast away at the edge of a ridge. He sought only to satisfy his own private whims; yet how could a speck of dust defile the vast void?

How could a fierce fire alter the nature of true gold? That he met with such fortune in his final years was entirely due to the Way of Heaven. The Master did not linger long, and for this reason, I shed tears on his behalf.
May he enjoy [this offering].

The aforementioned Chen Hui, Grand Master for Court Audience, Director of the Zhifuwen Pavilion, Prefect of the Military Administration of Lin’an, and Recipient of the Purple Gold Fish Bag, [observes that] the Buddha-dharma has gradually declined and divergent views have come to clash with one another.
Were it not for one who stands out preeminent, who could revitalize its school? How magnificent is Da-hui!

The Way is lofty yet accessible; Confucius, Laozi, Brahmā, and Śākyamuni blend together as inner and outer teachings. With their powerful eloquence and noble bearing, they are like a river bursting its banks toward the east.

Those who lift their robes to follow them find no request that is not fulfilled. Below, they move the common folk of the villages; above, they incline the hearts of kings and dukes. Thus it has been for fifty years.

Do not encounter his sharp edge. Returning late to Longjing, he showed the end of his life with a smile and conversation. How could the Master truly have departed? This is a source of grief for both the clergy and the laity.
These meager offerings of food and drink are merely to express my innermost thoughts. May you still enjoy them. *Shangxiang*.
Liu Cen, Chamberlain for the Left, Grand Master of the Hall of Auspicious Virtue, retired from office:
Alas, Great Wisdom! You manifested in this world and taught the Dharma to deliver sentient beings for seventy-five years. Whom can compare to the greatness of your Way?
You stand shoulder to shoulder and side by side with the ancient Buddha, the Yellow-Faced Gautama. As the True Dharma has become desolate, who else could do so?
Supported by you, it relied upon my great wisdom to be revitalized and transmitted once more. With such a Dharma-eye, humans and devas turned toward you in devotion.

We were now just beginning to rely single-mindedly upon your compassionate protection—like a child longing for its mother, like a sick person obtaining medicine, like a traveler finding a carriage, or like one crossing water finding a boat.
Sentient beings are as numerous as clouds; having a karmic affinity with you, they listened to the Dharma without weariness. How could you suddenly depart? Although...
Upon hearing that he had entered parinirvāṇa, I still hoped he would remain in this world; yet, he did not tarry for even a moment but passed into final extinction.
As lofty as our Master was, his coming and going within birth and death were like dreams, illusions, bubbles, and shadows—all taught as provisional means. Where now is that celestial and human form?
When I recall his voice and laughter, they seem as clear as if before my very eyes. It is only I, an old man, who recognized the Master in the capital and encountered him there.
From the time he chose this hall among the trees until his departure upon the ridges of Mount Wu, nearly fifty years have passed since we last counted the days.
Our hearts and eyes have shone upon one another, free from the fluctuations of worldly affairs. Grieving for all sentient beings, I can only imagine him at his sacred altar;

though his physical form has passed away, as he responds to conditions and manifestations, he shall surely never leave the Bodhi seat, but will be present throughout the trichiliocosm. Thus do I entrust my feelings to him.
These writings—how can they be described? May they be enjoyed.
Written by Xu Lin, Rectifier of Studies at Fuwen Pavilion, Left Court Gentleman for Imperial Service, and Director of the Taiping Xingguo Abbey in Jiangzhou.
When the True Teaching was first transmitted, it was like a single flower with five petals. Once the fruit had ripened, the branches divided and the lineages branched out.
Yangqi was the orthodox successor, and Yuanwu was his heir. From within the lion’s den, another lion was born; its roar and vigorous display shook the great trichiliocosm.
While the demonic hordes lay in ambush, his great function manifested before us; the multitude gazed up at him like the bright sun in the midst of heaven.

When the Master fled to Hengyang and I was transferred to the southern lands, I sent a letter to inquire after him, and he joyfully gave his heart’s consent. In the year of Jimao (1099), I finally beheld his compassionate countenance.

Desiring to transmit his mind, he did not rely on verbal instruction. Suddenly he manifested parinirvāṇa, returning to truth and the source. At the twin śāla trees, he entered extinction; the fire of samādhi arose.
Returning westward beyond the Pamir Mountains, only a single sandal remains. The fourfold assembly is shrouded in grief, as if they have lost their sole protector.
In my devotion to my teacher, my longing knows no end. How can I give vent to my grief? I offer this pure water as a memorial.
May you still accept it. Bestowed the title of Left Zhaosan Dafu, Fuwen Ge Waitzhi, Consultant to the Jiahuai Provincial Military Command: Tang Wenruo.

Alas! This very source is the Dharma-less Dharma. Through the transmission of dharma-to-dharma, one attains the Dharma-less Dharma. Pointing to emptiness to show others, it is called the Seal of Bodhi;
it is called the Army of the Demon King. To divine and clarify it, all things are laid bare.

Before the time of Bhīṣmagarjitasvara, who carved the doors and windows? Kāśyapa’s single laugh was the transmission of the tally. Linji attained his teacher and cast it aside, refusing to cling to it. The giant tortoise swallows...
The whale leaps; its spirit is peerless. It looks back at its mother with a gaze of profound compassion and filial piety. Majestic and dignified, it realizes great sovereignty.
Its scattered speech overflows like the surging waters of the Bohai Sea. Having finished speaking for you, believe and accept this without reservation.

Whether in rites, music, military expeditions, or punishments, if one smiles yet frowns, how could one give rise to anger or resentment because of such obstacles? Let the overturned halberds and raised battle-axes all return [to their sheaths].

O Benevolent One, for seventy-five years we have looked up and down together in this manner. Now that the teachings of the Image-Period are withering and the dragon-deities are languid, a Great Sage appears once in ten thousand ages.
With the wisdom of Yao and the sagacity of Shun, you have realized the truth of this Way; thus, your lofty name and magnificent titles are here bestowed as an honor.
Since the Dharma is not extinguished, how could you, O Master, have departed forever? I reflect upon our past, that I was never equal to you, [as we traveled] toward the West...

To the west of my house, to the east of my neighbor’s house—how could I have known you would come? To wrap rice for you was no longer possible; I strung my lute and played it by the bright moonlight in my chamber.
May you still accept this offering.
Zuo Chaofeng Dafu, Director of the Office for the Administration of the Normalization of Grain, Tea, and Salt in the Two Zhejiang and East Circuit Regions (Yu Chu):

"The Great Being’s attainment of transformation makes it difficult to fulfill both [worldly and spiritual] principles simultaneously. One may attain the Buddha-dharma, yet lack worldly connections; or one may possess a foothold on a famous mountain."

His followers were like clouds; though the fourfold assembly looked up to him, his reputation for the Way was rarely heard of elsewhere. Possessing both of these qualities, he was truly a Guiding Teacher.
He did not conform to worldly things, yet all things followed him. Raising his whisk and striking the mallet, he reviled the Buddhas and scolded the Patriarchs, his voice like thunder.

A thunderclap resounds across the eastern lands; its transverse and vertical wondrous functions, I dare not claim to know. When the momentum reaches the power of the Buddha, it becomes even more extraordinary:
the paper robe falls away instantly, and Yinfeng passes into extinction while upside down. Viewing such death and birth, they are truly like day and night. As I gaze upon Mount Jing, I behold this.
The stupa rises loftily; I bow my head before this enduring model. It is the refuge for those of later learning.

May it be honored. Written by Wang Yingchen, Left Grand Master of the Court of Imperial Ceremonial, Acting Director of the Fuwen Pavilion, Governor of Fuzhou Prefecture, Supervisor of Educational Affairs, and Pacification Commissioner of Fujian Circuit.
Alas! The Way of Linji was nearly severed like a single thread. Those who pilfered and peddled it were numerous, each boasting of their own understanding.

Yet the Way did not remain forever obscured; a man of extraordinary character appeared. With transcendent insight and unhindered eloquence, he seized upon every opportunity as a sharp blade meets its mark, leaving no room for even a blink of an eye.
Through laughter, jesting, scolding, and reviling, he employed all manner of skillful means—like thunder from hibernation, like sunlight in the darkness. Upon hearing him once...
The correct sound does not fall into false views. For seventy years, I have witnessed further changes in the world; I have maintained this purity and subjected it to a hundred refinements.
It is the same with birth and death—how could one truly be subject to transmigration? Why am I alone so distressed that I cannot even swallow my food?

I recall our past excursions together, when you dispelled my delusions and confusion. When I was still at court, I sent letters to reprove you for your failings, yet now I hear nothing more. I, for my part...
I offer my own condolences. Having traveled a hundred *she* with calluses upon my feet, I respectfully present this libation.
May you still accept it. Zhang Xiaoxiang, Court Consultant of the Left, serving as Editor-in-Chief of the Jiying Hall and Prefect of Pingjiang Prefecture, overseeing educational affairs.
O Master, your Way is vast and your virtue complete; you are the teacher of devas and humans. You penetrate the finest motes of dust, your subtle essence pervading the entire realm of sands.

There is nowhere you do not reach; all is unified within you. Yet when words attempt to praise you, they fall ever further short. When the twin śāla trees announced the change, you departed with but a single sandal.

The bridge of compassion has been severed across the sea, and men have gouged out the eye of wisdom. Who shall now open the path of nature? The Buddha-lamp is forever extinguished. In this age of Semblance Dharma...

In his decline, who would not grieve? Xiaoxiang has been honored by entering your teacher’s gate and being deemed worthy of instruction; a single word of your teaching was like a needle for a chronic ailment, raising the dead.
In midsummer you entrusted me with a letter, saying you would come to visit; day after day I listened for the sound of your boat, yet it was with the news of your passing that it finally arrived.
The sun alone dwells in the heavens; among men there is both light and darkness. Throughout my daily life—whether rising or reclining, eating or drinking—I have always been with you, O Master.
Whether you were present or have passed away, your vision remains as it was before. I now offer these sacrificial delicacies, likewise for your sake. May you still accept them.

The aforementioned Chao-yi Dashi (Court Consultant of the Third Class), Zhi Fuwen Ge (Director of the Fuwen Pavilion), newly appointed Governor of Ezhou and concurrently Commissioner for Internal Pacification,

Fang Zizhi, was a master of subtle discernment whose extraordinary brilliance emerged from amidst the common. Having received the three calls of Master Zhantang, his literary talent was fully manifested.

Having realized the single word of Yuanwu, his numinous light shone through with penetrating brilliance; his virtue and reputation resounded throughout the four seas, and Zen disciples flocked from all directions.
Although he once encountered waves in unfathomable depths, he remained like pine and cypress, maintaining their austere integrity even when others wither.
My words cannot cease; I preserve this record so that it may not be lost. The Way is eternally nameless, beyond the reach of praise.
Looking down upon my own record of decline and indolence, I recall our early discussions on the Way and its principles.

I remember the beginning of our friendship when you rushed out of your shoes to greet me, and the time you humbled yourself by holding an alms bowl before me. Having visited your door to pay my respects, I repeatedly ascended Mount Heng to stay in your humble thatched hut. There, changing places with you, we forgot all worldly distinctions many times over.
I have received your letters from afar across the Yangtze River; by the time you returned to the regions of Wu and Yue, how many years had passed?
Yet, lacking the karmic affinity of Pang Yun, you were unable to enter the profound depths of Zhongnan Mountain. Nevertheless, you have continued to guide and lead those of duller faculties.
The words of your Dharma teachings shine forth clearly; yet looking upon them now, I feel a sense of profound insufficiency. My affection for you is deep and enduring.

Alarmed by the news of your passing as I traveled abroad, I imagine your stupa is already complete, yet I have no way to wail in the empty hall where you once dwelt. The Great Gate of the School has been grandly established, yet I see its lofty ridgepole suddenly collapse.
The ocean of suffering flows wildly, and we have lost the compassionate vessel that could ferry us to safety. I reverently present these meager offerings, merely to send my condolences.
My private thoughts: may you still enjoy [this offering].

The aforementioned Fengzhidagu Zhimige (Yi), our late Master, formerly made his name renowned in the southeast through the Way and its Dharma. As the leader of ten thousand monks, his fame filled the heavens. Although he was a follower of Śākya...

His outward appearance was that of a monk, yet his mind was truly Confucian. He had mastered the teachings of the hundred schools; his spirit was as formidable as ten thousand men. Because his words ran counter to the world, he suffered a fall for many years.
Yet regarding life and death, or poverty and success, he remained as immovable as a mountain. Though his body was beset by hardship, his Way became ever more luminous.

A guide for the four seas, he was the one man south of the Northern Dipper. Formerly, when I stayed at Mount Heng, I first beheld the Master. At the very first sight, it was as if we were old acquaintances; our hearts and minds...
Tanyi: Throughout my life, I have reflected that the trials I have encountered have been exceedingly difficult. My inner depth and outer integrity have made my followers truly numerous.

Yet, upon speaking but a single word with you, Master, my eyes were cleared and my mind was opened. Although I have not yet fully mastered the wondrous purport of the West’s transmission, its great principles have been deeply understood by you, Master.
Now that you are gone, who will instruct me? Alas! When you first returned from illness, I nearly lay in the Nine Springs.

Sengyue suddenly arrived to report the Master’s passing. He struck his pillow and lost his voice, wailing and sighing as he wept: "I have known you for several hundred years; have you been reborn as my teacher once more?
You, Master, are indeed transcendent, yet my heart is filled with longing. This single offering of incense—were it not for you, there would be no one to present it."
Vast and expansive is the Xiang River; though it may turn ten thousand times, it must flow eastward. My longing for my teacher—how could it ever come to an end? May he enjoy this offering.
By Huang Yue, Grand Master of the Left, Director of the Chongdao Abbey in Taizhou.
Majestic and imposing is our teacher; his Way is as vast as heaven. People know only its height, but who can see its entirety? He has appeared in this world.

His voice shook the great trichiliocosm, and he traveled to the four quarters to release others from their bonds and untangle their entanglements. Kings, dukes, and high officials received his teachings with profound reverence.
Late in life, he was favored by imperial brilliance; edicts were repeatedly proclaimed, and his precious calligraphy shone forth, illuminating forests and springs.

Just as all expected him to enter the imperial presence to clarify and expand the source of the Way, the Master did not remain, suddenly following the conditions of the world. The ocean of suffering is vast and boundless; the Great Dharma has been lost.
The Master’s practice was austere and simple; the gentleman feels sorrow for this. I, Yue, came to know the Master late in life, yet I was fortunate enough to enjoy his company.

Since our parting in the past, many years have suddenly passed. I have been unable to visit him because I am entangled by worldly concerns. His letter arrived last summer, and now the news of his passing has suddenly been transmitted.

I am struck with such shock that I lose my voice; I can do nothing but weep in silence. The Master was like a precious moon, full and perfect throughout the long kalpas. Rising in the east... [it sets] in the west.

Sinking into stillness, how could day and night be partial? This wheel of purity—how could it ever undergo change? Sealing these words and sending them a thousand miles away, I offer this as a token of my devotion.
Though mountains and rivers separate us, you, Master, are ever present before me. May you accept this offering.
Rightward, Li Duanmin, Acting Director of the Directorate of Works and of the Third Rank, Scattered Official:
Alas! The great function of Linji and the orthodox lineage of Yangqi—were it not for a preeminent man, who could have explored their depths?

This majestic Chan Master was a beacon for the Śākya school. Having shaved his head and received full ordination, he mingled with dragons and snakes; wandering through the four quarters, he was like a gem.
He gathered stones. Upon seeing Yuanwu for the first time, their karmic conditions met directly. Regarding the "dog has Buddha-nature," he reached its ultimate limit;

the whole body manifested before him, mind and form merging and boundaries dissolving. It was neither encased in diamond nor entangled in brambles. What was once dark and murky became the blue sky and the bright sun;

what was once dull and stagnant became a flash of lightning and a clap of thunder. The contents of his bag were no longer trivial fragments, and the old molds were no longer dense and restrictive—there was only radiant light.

Universally illuminating, he was profoundly clear and lucid. Once the ancestral style had been revitalized, he extensively opened the dharma seat. Seated at Shuangjing, he brought both demons and heretics to their knees;

as his orthodox command was put into practice, he completely swept away all pestilence. Who was this man that caused him to be exiled and banished, cast into the wilderness ten thousand *li* away to a remote land of yellow reeds?
Though his person could be suppressed, his Way remained unerring. Carrying his bundle, he returned home, leaving nothing behind.
A Single Object: The Great Lord has issued his mandate; the Dharma King [Śātavāhana] shook his staff, and disciples flocked from all directions across the fields and roads.
He returned to Mount Jing, where the level paths were opened once more. It was said that he would dwell in this world to perpetually succeed as the true heir.

How could it be that he did not prosper? He has returned to the West, leaving but a single shoe behind. Alas, how lamentable! The elders have withered and passed away; the pure sound is now solitary and desolate. Since the time of Fengxue, [the lineage of] Shishi...

The Iron-Spined Gut: Once one departs from this world, what benefit is there in grief and lamentation? Reflecting on my later years, I have leveled all boundaries. Even amidst the flourishing weeds and tares, you, sir, were not cast out.
Moving according to the free mind, I have excised remaining prejudices. Floating slanders flow like a river; often there is doubt and confusion.
Like flies in vinegar or summer insects, they speak of their own "every night" (the trivial); how could they know Great Wisdom, the single flavor of reality? Only...

That person of ultimate realization was fundamentally free from joy and sorrow. Birth was not something he created; death was not something he brought to rest. Whether right or wrong, who among ordinary minds could discern it?
Whether acting contrary to or in accordance with the flow, even Heaven could not fathom him. Whether reviled or praised, he made his own choices.

Alas, how tragic! I alone am left fragmented and solitary. For a long time I have admired his fame and virtue; yet in the intervening years, we have looked toward one another across a surging sea of clouds. How could...

My thoughts have long been directed toward the East. Having finally had the honor of meeting you in person, we recounted our past experiences with a friendship as close as that of those who cannot bear to oppose one another.

Since arriving at the imperial court, we have met face-to-face with knees pressed together; yet, throughout these four years, we have been constrained by the burdens of worldly affairs. My dreams have yearned for the famous mountains, separated from them by but a few steps. From time to time, when the west wind blew, I would occasionally receive a letter from you.
Recently, hearing that you were ill, I was filled with both anxiety and joy, still hoping for a recovery without the need for medicine. Thus I speak.
In the midst of his laughter, he departed with a graceful flight. This "Harmony Jade" (Hebi) is now hidden away; with the departure of this Dragon-Elephant, my sorrow is as consuming as hunger.
The Dharma-milk grows thin, and the Peak of Wisdom crumbles. Who will now wield the axe to carve the essence of Ying? I have heard by report that his sacred relics rest within a magnificent stupa.
Standing before the wind, I am filled with grief and regret; like wings drooping toward the heavens, I reverently prepare pure offerings to express my profound anguish. I burn...
Incense is sent by this humble messenger. With painstaking detail, I have set forth these words to establish a spiritual communion and pour out the depths of my heart.

May the enlightened spirit clearly perceive them and, in response to this vow, accept this offering and come with grace, to comfort my grieving heart. Alas, how lamentable! I humbly pray that you will graciously accept this. May it be enjoyed.
Vice Commander of the Right Gate Guard, Defense Commissioner of Changzhou, and Director of the Youshen Observation, Zhao Buei, lamented: "Alas!
I did not know the Master in person;
I only looked up to his loftiness from afar, constantly fearing that I would fall before him. Throughout my entire life, I was unable to associate with him. Now that he has passed..."

Upon seeing him once, I grasped the essence of his voice and meaning. As he sat with dignified composure upon the lion throne, my mind and eyes were in perfect accord; the Master also granted me his seal of approval, allowing me to enter his chamber.

He laughed heartily, and the obstruction that had weighed upon my chest was cast off. I am truly dull-witted and base, yet I relied on the Master to enlighten me. Before long after we were separated, I remained anxious in my heart.
Having met with this unjust misfortune, I was too preoccupied with saving myself to attend to anything else. Suddenly hearing of his peaceful passing, I have been unable to go and pay my respects.

A few moments passed. As the seasons turned and the year drew to a close, all things appeared desolate and figures seemed to vanish. Facing these words, my throat was choked with emotion; old tears flowed like a river.

May you enjoy this offering. Submitted by Zhang Juqing, Right Attendant-in-Council, Administrator of School Affairs and Agricultural Promotion for Lin’an County under the Jurisdiction of the Prefecture of Lin’an, Recipient of the Scarlet Fish Bag.
[Seal of] Mo Zhang, Right Assistant in the Office of Merit, County Magistrate of Lin’an;
and Zhou Youliang, Right Assistant in the Office of Merit, County Commandant of Lin’an.
Their insight is alert and awakened, their endowment is eminent and exceptional. They are pillars of the Chan school and masters for those in later learning. [Seal of] Samādhi.
With the six supernormal powers, he traverses myriad paths and a thousand diverging ways. Like a *maṇi* jewel, he responds to all things according to their nature.

His verbal acuity is sharp and penetrating; wherever he encounters an opportunity, he strikes it with precision. He shatters delusion and releases bonds, dissolving the doubts of the multitude. Like drawing from a vessel that never runs dry, his application is inexhaustible. Like the eastern ocean, he cannot be fathomed.
Those of shallow understanding and heterodox views each follow different teachers; they cling to the literal text while harming its true intent, becoming mired in rigid rules.

Following established rules, he realized that polishing a brick would not produce a mirror; what then was the purpose of his "driving in the needle"? As the rain of Dharma was universally bestowed, all was cleansed into emptiness.

Having encountered censure and expulsion midway, he traversed treacherous and pestilential mountain ranges; alone and beset by difficulties, he journeyed ten thousand *li*. Though broken, he did not yield, remaining serene and self-composed.

His power of meditative concentration stood firm like a mountain—whom could it possibly deter? At the former hermitage of the Benevolent One (*Śākyamuni*), he repeatedly upheld the essential principles; thus he received [the mandate].

The Imperial Decree has looked down with compassion to console the thoughts of the people; divine dragons have assisted in the offerings, and even the grasses and trees radiate brilliance. The *nāgas* and *elephants* from the four quarters have all followed him with devotion.

Vimalakīrti manifested illness and withdrew according to his convenience; in the space of a single finger-snap, he returned to the West in his single sandal. He has departed into the distance, and my heart is filled with sorrow.
I present this meager offering with utmost sincerity, hoping that you may deign to accept it. May it be enjoyed.
Right, Xiu-zhi-lang, Acting Assistant Commissioner for Observation of Lin’an Prefecture, Luo Gongdan:
Alas, how lamentable! Did the Master truly have no intention for this world? Or was it that the Way of the Buddhas and Patriarchs was destined to sink into oblivion with none to succeed it?
Why did he suddenly cast off his mortal coil through illness? Though humans and devas sought to detain him, such hope could not be realized. O Master!
He was seventy-five years of age at his passing; one cannot say he did not live long.
Yet, as the Great Dharma rests upon him and he is venerated by scholars, even a hundred years would still not have fully satisfied them.

Since the time of Linji, there have been countless teachers who manifested the Way and established the teachings, yet none has been as radiant, eminent, and magnificent as this Master. When he first led the assembly in the capital...
The Master established a hermitage on Yang-yu; though his prominence had not yet been revealed to the various quarters, his thunderous resonance had already startled the ears of the multitude.
This was because that which the Master attained was the profound and secret essence of all former sages, and his talent and vigor were moreover far superior to his peers.
Observing how he opened up the mysteries of the Way and how his discourses issued forth with vigorous brilliance, one finds him as vast and inexhaustible as the rivers and seas.
Furthermore, when he dabbles in calligraphy, a single stroke yields a thousand characters; he takes Confucius and Laozi as his words and unifies the Three Teachings into a single principle.
The world all praises the Master for his superhuman intelligence, his vast learning, and his powerful memory, yet they do not realize that these are merely his minor traits.
He grasps the essential pivot of a thousand sages and holds up the bright mirror to see through all things; from the common studies...

Among those who followed the Way, there were none passing before him who did not have their depths and shallows, their greatness and subtlety, fully grasped by him without waiting for even a single word.
Thus, the Master’s power to transform others surpassed what his predecessors had ever achieved; consequently, the world was stirred at once and the four quarters responded like echoes.
Men of outstanding talent and extraordinary character flocked to him from all sides like clouds gathering or rivers meeting, as soon as they set foot in Mòu.
Ling served as the abbot of Mount Jing-shan for two terms; those who followed him as disciples under his seat numbered approximately twenty thousand.
His fame reached the imperial court, such that from princes and dukes downward, all paid him homage with bared forearms and treated him with reverence.

Formerly, before he had appeared in the world, the assembly desired to establish him in the position of their teacher; later, when he was exiled for having offended the state, they looked toward his return day and night.
Having returned, he was already old. Those who carried their provisions on their backs and followed him as shadows would go directly to wherever he was headed.
When he declined medical treatment and retired to his bed, the crowd surrounded him without dispersing, still hoping for the instruction of even a single word.

Alas! Who could have known that he would suddenly and abruptly vanish, never to be seen again? The Dharma drum split at dawn; a shooting star fell at night. [He] wrote a slip of paper the size of a *shàn*.
This memorial was submitted. You departed in auspicious splendor, yet I have been ill-fated. My habitual karma has left me obscured and dull;
you were my guide who cleansed and purified me, and I relied solely upon you as my teacher. Now that you have passed away, jackals howl in confusion and frogs croak in discord;
where shall I find a place of rest? I reverently present this meager offering, following it with tears of snow-like purity—not only out of grief for my own misfortune, but...
It follows. This is surely intended to inspire awe among the scholars of the world. May it be honored.
Written by Wang Mingfa, Acting Assistant Magistrate of the Lin’an Prefecture, who holds the rank of Left Chengzhilang.
The Master’s Way fills the four seas; ten thousand monks have but one teacher. He has cut off the continuity of past and present, leaving not a single thread behind. It is manifestly clear.
He moves as if lifting the sun and moon to show people without doubt; he is vast like the boundless Milky Way, such that no one can fathom his limits.
Thus, he was able to continue the life-vein of the Buddha and revive Linji when it had nearly vanished.
The Master has now passed away; upon whom among gods and men shall we rely? Those who hear this and those who see it are filled with profound sorrow.
Alas! To abide is non-abiding; to depart, what need is there for action? Within the interval between these two, the Master remains serene and unmoving.

Alas, I, a mere youth of shallow capacity and humble understanding, have failed to advance with you; do not cast me far behind in your departure. I have come to pay my respects to the awakened spirit, yet I have already arrived late. I brew this tea...
I present this offering. May you briefly set down my thoughts;
may you still accept them. Pure and Tranquil Layman Li Chenwei:

Your Way is great and your virtue complete; your insight is clear and your conduct pure. Your brilliance was like the roar of a great thunderclap shaking the world; your purity was as bright as the moon.

If one views the autumn moon reflected in a clear, azure pool, regarding birth and death as mere comings and goings, and encompasses the workings of creation within the scope of brush and tongue—such a person is truly what is called a master of the Linji lineage, a preeminent hero of the Buddha-vehicle. Alas!

When I met the Master in Hengyang, we frequently enjoyed leisurely conversation; grasping hands and revealing our innermost feelings, we were indeed like two kindred spirits who opened their hearts to one another, making it all clearly manifest.
Beholding the radiant light from within a thatched hut, one is suddenly refreshed as if grasping a burning fever and bathing in a cool breeze.
In the spring of the year of Xinsi, he struck his mendicant’s staff and ascended into the air at Yangxian. I happened to be on my way to the capital when we coincidentally met for a brief moment;
yet, after following his tracks back, I was eventually delighted to behold him again. He was just about to pull me out from the common flow of worldly custom.

Within this, you have comforted me regarding my lifelong aspirations. How is it that a letter of but a few inches has been sent from afar, reaching down to the nine generations of ancestors, where the painted images remain solemn and dignified?
You have sent a verse and a detailed explanation, sealed in layers, sufficient to reveal your intent. Yet before the ink of these writings had even dried, you suddenly passed away.
My gratitude for your virtue is ever-increasing; how could I not shed tears? When one speaks of the Master’s passing, the realm of spirits seems vast and mysterious. When one speaks of...
While the Master was alive, his white jade remained without a single blemish. Whether hidden or manifest, his Way grew ever more honored.
He snapped the golden chain to shatter the dark barrier; he withdrew the sword’s edge to conceal Mount Kunlun. I, Chen, am humbled by our long-standing friendship and have thus offered this labor.

With complete purity and sincerity, I exhaust my intent, hoping that the memory of the Elder Miaoxi shall not be forgotten. Alas, how tragic! I prostrate myself in deep thought. May you rest in peace.
Offering.
By the Pure Wisdom Layman Huang Wenchang. Alas!
Born in a distant land, I have been obscured by conventional learning; my meager knowledge and experience consist only in clinging to mere words, busily engaged in toil.
In this worldly realm, there is nothing but fame and profit; I had never even heard the Master’s name, let alone tasted the flavor of the Dharma.
I harbored doubts for many kalpas, yet profound meditations and wondrous verses occasionally moved me in my dreams. In the second month of summer in the Guiyou year, I fell ill and nearly collapsed.

In a state of trepidation, I was suddenly awakened and turned my heart toward the ultimate truth. Only then did I realize that the Master’s Way filled the heavens and the earth. Three years later, it was truly at this point that—
We met by chance. At first, beholding his physical marks and signs (*lakṣaṇa-vyañjana*), I felt great joy and comfort. A single spark of resonance suddenly ignited a wondrous accord.
The Master smiled and asked me, "From where did you obtain this? Strive on without negligence; become a vessel for the Dharma.

The entire school turned to him in reverence; fathers, sons, brothers, and even children ran to serve him. When the Master was about to depart for Changsha, we took our leave at Xiao Temple. I, having already...

He wept silently, and the Master also shed tears. "How is it," he said, "that even a Guide is not yet free from the burdens of emotion? Thus I know that our karmic convergence has not been limited to a single lifetime.
When you resided at Mount Jing, I visited three times; this spring, I finally obtained the opportunity to serve as your attendant.
Yet you did not tarry for long, but passed away with serene composure. As for Cunda’s final offering, I have no cause for shame. The compilation of the Dharma-treasury has long since been completed."
The Master’s intent—how could I dare be disrespectful and thus fail the Great Benefactor? The Master’s virtue and realization are beyond all discussion;
whether one praises or slanders them, it is like flies buzzing in the air, coming and going, arising and ceasing—neither one nor two. Why do I alone sigh with such deep emotion?
Heretical views tower high, the True Lineage is in decay, and the Dharma-path of Linji lies desolate—whom can it rely upon? It is only this...
In grief for this, he shed clear tears day after day. May you still enjoy [this offering].
Wu-zhu (Unabiding) Layman Yuan Zuoyan. Alas!
Though heaven and earth are vast, they manifest only as forms; though the sun and moon are bright, their cycles can be measured. Only I—
"O Mahāmati, what constitutes 'direction'? If one were to posit such a thing, it would be the beginning of slander.

In years past, when I went to pay my respects, I stayed at Sian, where I personally received his Dharma discourses and enjoyed the full joy of my life. Who would have expected that his final instructions would so suddenly become our eternal parting?
Māra and the non-Buddhists will all rejoice; let them clamor as they will—it is like pouring hot water on snow. Who knows that my Teacher did not [use]..."

"Speech itself is originally unborn; how could it now cease? With awareness in all four directions, we shed tears and choke with sobs, stretching our necks to wail long and loud, offering oblations to part from you. May you still enjoy them."
Alas! Even the utmost clarity in the world is insufficient to fathom the subtle mystery of the Master’s Way;
even the entirety of the world’s speech [is inadequate]. —Written by Wang Zhongfu, Right Cultivated Official and newly appointed Judicial Assistant of Hongzhou.
This is insufficient to describe the full extent of the Master’s sublime virtue. What is roughly visible in the world is the merit of his supreme benevolence:

like a wondrous cloud of compassionate shade, it merges with the primordial ether to cover the three realms; his unimpeded eloquence is like the waters of the celestial river, bursting forth from ten-thousand-fathom heights to flow across the nine regions.
By this means, the wise and the ignorant alike know where to find their refuge, while foxes and wild beasts likewise [cease their howling].

Hold your breath! When he first stepped into the worldly net, he was exiled to the lands of the Yi and Mo barbarians; yet he did not disdain his dwelling there, and those who reached him still recognized him.
While that region was still ablaze with calamity, who could have fought and prevailed? He returned from ten thousand li alive, with a withered neck and yellowing beard.
The Emperor held him in his innermost thoughts, and imperial edicts were repeatedly bestowed upon him. He was honored with a magnificent title, his auspicious radiance shining brilliantly.
Retiring to the forests and springs, he became a model for the world. Why did he not live a hundred years to bring peace to the southern realm? Alas!

Though birth and death, departure and arrival, are like a dream from yesterday, the Master remained composed therein and was certainly without regret. What is truly to be lamented is that the later generations and their superficial learning [will suffer].

We shall be left without any reliance, allowing the jackals to howl through the night as the True Path is extinguished; we shall wander like those seeking a path in the mud, unable to see the North Star.
Alas, how lamentable! For more than twenty years since our meeting, you have shown me profound kindness, never disparaging my ignorance.

This force of urging and drawing me forward has led me to come north for an appointment at the Ministry of Personnel after three years of humble service. I climbed to the summit of the mountain to pay my respects;

we conversed from day until evening, and he invited me to return with him to the west. We spent several days together in leisurely ease, yet who would have expected that in just three months he would suddenly return to his rest?

Alas, his voice and countenance can no longer be pursued; sighing that the colors of the mountains and rivers have changed, I present this meager offering to manifest my sincerity, recording but a fraction of my heartfelt words.
May he enjoy long life.
Zhao Wenlin (Wenjin), Left Gentleman of the Literary Forest and Military Commissioner of Changzhou, [writes]:

Master Wei, whose Way is honored throughout the age, upholds the source of the Dharma. He eradicates the heterodox and returns all to the orthodox; those who follow the Buddha know from whom they must proceed. His teachings have been widely propagated.

Throughout the world, there was none who did not revere him as a teacher. His fame rose like the sun, shattering the ignorance of the deluded and simple. His reality was profound and his reputation vast; he reached the ears of Heaven.

The Great Wisdom conferred upon him this title, in perfect accord with the consensus of all. For a hundred generations hence, those who hear of him will look toward his influence with longing. I am sparing with my writing.

For a long time we have been close associates; you have condescended not to disdain my mediocrity, and your exceptional affection has led you to fathom the depths of my heart. Now that you have departed and cannot be detained, my thoughts for you are boundless.
Though your words remain in my ears, how can I behold your countenance? Bound by official duties in a distant land, I am prevented from personally attending to the sacrificial rites.
Spiritual awakening does not perish; may you accept this humble sincerity and continue to enjoy [our offerings]. Left:
Wenlinlang Cai Di, serving as an officer in the Hubei and Jiangsu Regional Military Command (Jianghuai Dushi Fu).
Alas! The Way has a correct transmission, and the Dharma is not lightly bestowed. It does not fall within the realm of verbal explanations, but is entirely realized through the mind. To die for...

It is delightful. Life has its limits; to hold such a view is a misconception. Only the Great Wisdom Master (Mahāmati) transcends all categories; day and night, darkness and light, are blended into a single unity.
Coming and going are of his own nature; both precepts and meditative concentration are cast aside. Throughout Min, Guang, Hu, and Jiang, he manifests a thousand million bodies.
Recalling our late predecessor, we attained silent resonance with him; at times he would manifest Zen mechanisms, [which] accorded with the Master’s.
In playful ease, my teacher of consciousness truly honored me with a prediction from my very childhood; I thought it was merely to strike away my ignorance.
Yet recently, when I visited the Master at the waters of Ningbo, twelve thousand fingers struck the bell to welcome me at the gate. Last autumn, we met by chance on the mountains of West Lake;
who would have thought that this parting would mean never returning? What is expected beyond the mundane world—how can one grieve such a final farewell? My aspirations remain.

At this juncture, with whom shall we resolve our doubts? Amidst the proliferation of heterodox interpretations, these too claim to be from the Master; the lingering influence of Linji is thus feared to decline.

If there be no one capable of upholding the lineage, who can truly revitalize it? Let the clearing away of all false views begin from now on. Though the Master has passed away, the Master lives on forever.
How could I not take refuge [in him] to make these words true? May he graciously accept this offering.
Right Tongzhilang, serving as an Administrative Assistant at the Jianghuai Metropolitan Commandery, Luo Bowen:
Alas! The teaching of Yangqi reached Yuanwu in the fourth generation, whereby the gate was magnified and the lineage was revitalized.
In the fifth generation, our Master was attained, and his Dharma became even more radiant and magnificent. Truly, our Master possessed the *śakrāloka* eye.

Employing the affairs upon the edge of a sword, he overturns the verses of "Little Splendor" and brings forth the lines of the "Warm Breeze. His wondrous functions are纵横 (zōnghéng—transverse and vertical), and his rolling up and unfolding are free and at ease.
Like Linji and Deshan, with their great capacity and great function, they reviled Buddhas and scolded patriarchs, cutting off all quarters.
Upon the head of a single bamboo staff, they forged and tempered hundreds of thousands of monks, so that each, according to their own faculties and vessels, obtained their realization.
The many senior disciples were all like *pián* and *nán* timber of the forest, or dragon-elephants at the Dharma assembly;
the prosperity of his lineage was as majestic as that of Mazu and Xuefeng in their prime. Bowen had long admired this lofty style and wished to inquire into these matters.
As soon as he conveyed his message, [the Master] granted him the meeting of needle and magnet, and spoke of having already resolved his will, saying that one day they would gather...
There was certainly no doubt in his mind. The Master traveled from Huiguan and moved again to Chengjiang; after enduring the hardships of many years, he finally managed to return south.
Carrying his book-box, he sought out the Master, traveling from Hangzhou to Mingzhou, until they were finally able to meet beneath Mount Mao (Meofeng).

Thus fulfilling his previous promise, as soon as he heard the Master’s Dharma words, he realized his original aspiration. Only then did he know that the enlightened ones of the past had not deceived him. Then...
The Master truly possessed the power to untangle my adhesions, release my bonds, extract my nails, and pull out my wedges.

I ought only to break the bamboo staff and burn the meditation board as a small way to repay the kindness of his not revealing [the truth] to me. To receive the Master’s posthumous calligraphy—how could I feel anything less than profound sorrow?
Due to official duties, I traveled far to Gan-chuan; I wept for the Master at Long-shan, yet was prevented from visiting him in person.

Before the stupa, as the year draws to a close, I have finally returned to the banks of the Huai River. With due reverence, I dispatch this offering of *īśvara-pūpa* while gazing afar toward the summit of the Double Path (Shuangjing).

Alas, that the Dharma banner has suddenly fallen; I reflect upon how difficult it is for the ancestral Way to be transmitted. Those who have attained the Eye of the Dharma must surely spur themselves on.
May the spiritual light remain unextinguished, witnessing my sincere and earnest devotion. May you accept this offering.
Tongzhilang (Court Gentleman of the Right) in charge of Anhua County in Tanzhou, recipient of the crimson fish-bag, Xiang Huan, laments:
Alas! Although my birth was late, I was still able to encounter those who have reached maturity. Master Miaoxi alone is a peerless figure for a hundred generations;

he is the one revered by humans and devas, like a dragon, a phoenix, or a qilin. His square-collared robe and round monastic shawl are merely his outward form; it is through him that the myriad things are understood as a single principle.
Who could have known its true nature? Since my childhood, I had already heard the Master’s name; when I met him in Yichun, it was like beholding the auspicious star.
The Master said I was worthy of instruction, and I attended upon him morning and evening. He instructed and guided me, offering counsel and admonitions for twenty years.

Having entered the master’s gate several times, I have been graced by the master’s never-failing remembrance of me. Over time, my diligence has increased, yet I observe that my faculties are dull; I am stubborn and ignorant, lacking spiritual resonance.
It was insufficient for me to receive the Master’s teachings, yet I have merely preserved this intention. Now that the Master has departed, the mountain crumbles and the river is choked;
who shall preside over and maintain this Way and this Dharma? I, Huan, am most unworthy, my person but a speck of dust, yet I heard of the Master’s peaceful passing.
Dropping my chopsticks in grief and alarm, I lament the security of Mount Tai and look up in sighing admiration at how this resolve of yours remains unfulfilled. Alas!
As for fortune and misfortune, separation and union, departure and arrival, life and death—the Master regards these as merely evening and morning. What more need I say?
This humble sentiment of mine, as I gaze eastward with a snap of the fingers, I set forth fully for the Master’s sake. My feelings cannot be restrained; may the Master not be angry with me. Alas!
Alas! We humbly pray that you may accept this offering.

The aforementioned Fan-yi-lang (Court Consultant), Lu Weishi, who oversees the Southern Treasury of the Left Imperial Storehouse at the Seat of Government, is the refined essence of Heaven and a model for the Way. Through the marrow of the Dharma of Bodhidharma, he has revitalized the Linji school’s tradition.
He pointed directly at people; not even a speck of dust was established. Had there been anyone who attained it, one could have known it by looking.
From antiquity until now, such a person has never been seen. Now that all living beings rely entirely upon him, why has the bridge of the Dharma suddenly collapsed?
What is called "the Master’s presence" means that while he was visible, one should have perceived that which is invisible. This is what is meant by "the Master’s passing."
Furthermore, when he is invisible to the eye, one must perceive that which is necessarily visible; only then will one know that the Master cannot be bound by existence or non-existence.
I have long received the Master’s instruction and have been most favored by his guidance and support. Now, though we are but a few feet apart, [he remains beyond reach].

Bound by the constraints of worldly affairs, he practiced this Way to give rise to compassion and offered his profound resolve as his requital. I prostrate myself, praying that he may still enjoy [the fruits of his merit].
The aforementioned Zhang Borthou, a *Didigonglang* overseeing the Nanyue Temple in Tanzhou, was preeminent in his conduct and upright in his character.
His heart was like metal and stone; his integrity was like ice and frost. He early on awakened to the Dharma-eye.
His fame resounded far and wide; he was a leader of the Gate of Emptiness and a bridge and raft for scholars. In the past, while in Lin’an, I associated with his late father;

it was not a friendship based on power or profit, but rather a meeting of kindred spirits. Our paths were the same and our virtues harmonious, our mutual affection deep and enduring. Yet, we both fell into the net of slander.
Sharing the same misfortune and blame, he accepted it as his destiny and felt no anxiety. Although we were in places of exile, we maintained a constant exchange of letters;

when we both returned, our friendship grew even more profound. When my late father passed away, the Master was filled with grief and sorrow; having performed the ritual offerings, [he continued to mourn].

Furthermore, as I stood before the coffin, I mourned for the deceased while reflecting on those who remain; your virtue was beyond compare, and your kindness remained deeply within my heart, such that I vowed to repay it.

Now that you have passed away, not even a hair’s breadth can compensate for your loss. Hearing the news of this calamity from afar, my grief reaches the very marrow of my bones. Had you been free from illness—
Near and far, we relied upon you as our refuge. Now that the Master has passed away, to whom shall we turn? O azure heavens, why do you not spare him for us?
With these meager offerings presented with devotion, may the Master perhaps take notice; may he accept them.
Zuo Chao-san-lang, Zhi-mi-ge, Director of Judicial Investigations for the Tongchuan Prefecture Circuit, Grand Master of Purple-Golden Fish Ribbons, He Qi, says:
"The Great Wisdom Master’s physical body is indestructible;
he was an old Buddha of the Unending [School] and a monk of Yunmen. Having served as my junior preceptor, his brilliance has already shone forth."

Spiritual! With his rounded skull, he startled the world in every direction; with the sound of ocean tides, he roused those who were angry. He claimed that the Buddha-sun had opened the eyes of the blind masses;
yet they perversely traced him back to Linji and dragged him down to Yunmen. He kicked over Huìtáng and shouted at Dònglín.

When I was a youth living in the barbarian lands of Jing, I stood beside the Old Buddha and recognized this man. Though the fires of the kalpa blaze fiercely, there is nothing they do not destroy; yet when the Master saw me—

Wen Zhang opened his mouth in astonishment, saying, "The Way has been inexhaustible from the very beginning. These words shown to people should be received with prostrations; dragons and elephants gallop across the heavens and seas.
In the Dharma-ending age, many Chan practitioners are like shrimp and crabs; they claim that if a master does not die, he must be feigning strangeness, yet to say he has died is equally foolish.
Those of the Two Vehicles who dwell in the world are called Arhats; those who abandon death to hasten toward life are the Mahāyāna.
The Great Void does not perish; the Master eternally endures. The Sun of Wisdom shines brightly with its primordial radiance.
Right Chengwulang, serving as Vice-Director of the Grand Treasury Bureau, Wang Zhiqui, laments:
"Zhiqui, during the final month of winter in the Guiwei year, while on duty at Mount Xian, I passed through Yuyuan and visited the Abbot."
The monk said, "Daoyan has traveled westward to report that Master Furi has passed away. He remained in a state of profound grief and lamentation for many days.
Zhizhi had first met the Master in Mei Yang; they shared hardships together for four years, their mutual respect and affection never waning over time.

Whether in the depths of winter or the height of summer, whether gathered around a brazier or enjoying the cool breeze, they spent every day together discussing the past and present and evaluating the character of men.
When we parted, I was still full of lingering affection and could not forget you. Although we met again later at Mount Jing and in the capital, it was just as it had been before;
however, because each of us was constrained by worldly affairs, our intimacy was not as close as it was in the past.

As for Master Chan, that he serves as a bridge across the sea of Dharma and is the leader of the Zen lineage is something even a child of three feet could say. Yet, I, Ruzhi, am a man of remote and simple character.
I have never before encountered such a person and dare not venture to offer idle criticism. Yet, your brilliance and resolute character are innate;
from your youth, you have associated with great elders and are able to recount their ancient words and deeds with such earnestness that they are well worth listening to.
Consequently, you look down upon the younger scholars and officials, and because of your naturally impetuous temperament, those who do not understand you charge you with insolence. Alas!
"It is indeed difficult to dwell under a great reputation; how much more so when one uses worldly affairs to judge those who stand outside the world?
Your fame already pervades the heavens, yet there have been slanders of suspicion and resemblance. However, Zhiqi has associated closely with you for four years;
observing your minute conduct regarding what is called the precept of the Gautama clan, there is not even a hair’s breadth of regrettable deficiency."
Now you have departed. Out of the sense of mutual friendship shared between us in the past, and for that which the world has yet to know, I have committed these words to paper as an offering.

I shall no longer perform the rites of the secular world. These incense, tea, honey, and torches are likewise in accordance with the principle of Xu Ruzi’s offering of fresh grass. May you still accept them.
I, Chou, have been traveling with the Chan Master Furi Daohui Pujue for over thirty years. Suddenly hearing of his parinirvāṇa, I cannot overcome my grief and sorrow.
A world-renowned master who walked alone at the head of the school has passed away; who would not lament and regret this? From—
Alas, I am decrepit and aged; having withdrawn my traces to the shores of the sea, I have had no leisure to personally present offerings of tea and fruit.
I shall merely compose this one poem to express my heart’s sentiments.

The Layman Yizhen (One-True) Mo Chou constantly grasps his bamboo staff to rouse the ancestral wind. Miaoxi roams freely throughout the four seas. From beneath the lofty peaks, he surveys all other mountains.

Small indeed; the true dragon has washed away all ordinary horses into emptiness. His fame is inscribed upon Pujue, shining alongside the bright sun; the stupa leaps with jewel-light, enshrouded by auspicious mists.
The layman dwells in seclusion, his body loath to stir; gazing afar at the bright moon, his regret is boundless.
On the ninth day of the tenth month of the first year of the Longxing era,
the Layman Shuanghuai Zheng Ji offered a modest sacrifice before the stupa of Chan Master Dahui Pujo and composed five verses to express his sentiments of longing and remembrance.
Eight years have passed since returning from beyond the passes. My tongue has no bone, and my mouth flows like a surging tide.
At times it pierces through the nine streams, surging forth the Chan of Yangqi’s crown.

Presenting the pivot within a phrase is truly marvelous; the message therein is inconceivable. It is simply because the ground of the mind is as bright as the sun that one recognizes the moment the soaring dragon leaps.
The moonlight before the Bright Moon Hall is fresh; The green mountains, after the rain, are free of even the finest dust. The pine wind whistles and breaks as the azure clouds close together;
I do not see the former master within the hall.
A cool breeze arises at the corner of the hall; with this effective phrase, one may speak vertically or horizontally as many times as there are sands in the Ganges.
Now, the wood has fallen and the vines have withered. Tell me, where does the phrase return?
On the tenth day of the eighth month, at the fifth watch of the night, the blade that could shave a hair was used and its point concealed within its scabbard.
When one contemplates this state where killing and giving life are both free, one does not envy the merit of securing victory on the battlefield from afar.

Eulogy for the Portrait of the Layman Ziyen,

a Friend Beyond the World (With Preface) The scholar-gentleman who studies the Way of the former kings must enter it through filial piety, reverence, loyalty, and good faith. Although it is said that he has not yet...

It was sufficient to stir the ears of the age and to be displayed to posterity. Desiring to select the most eminent among them to be lauded in the world so as to enrich social customs—who could it be other than Ziyán?
I first met the Master in the capital when he served as a clerk in the Court of Imperial Sacrifices.
In his leisure from official duties, he came to follow the Elder Yuánwù. His spirit was lucid and his capacity vast; his aspirations—
He was steadfast and possessed a rectified spirit; his eyes did not gaze wantonly, and his mind had no other attachments.
No words that were not the teachings of the sages ever issued from his mouth. He was luminous, serene, and profoundly silent, as tranquil and unmoving as still water.
He never engaged in jesting, frivolity, or boisterous laughter; this was truly his innate nature. Fifteen years later, they met again at Sian in Wu, at which time the Master’s body—
His reputation was already honored and his stature already great; his meritorious achievements were complete, yet he remained enlightened, serene, and profoundly silent, no different from before.
After another three years, I incurred reprimand and came to Hengyang; the Duke likewise retired from office and, supporting his mother, the Grand Mistress, resided in a new residence in Changsha.
He named its hall "Exhausting the Mind" (*Jinxin*), for he sought to exhaust his mind in serving his parents, and [there he] took his meals...
He did not forget his lord even in his rest; this manifests that loyalty and filial piety are one and not divided.
Mencius said: "He who exhausts his mind knows his nature. He who knows his nature knows Heaven. To preserve his mind and nourish his nature."
This is how one serves Heaven. I say: nature is the Heavenly nature. To nourish one's nature in order to serve Heaven is to not forget one's root.
Your Lordship’s dedication of heart—if it were indeed different from this teaching, it would be something beyond my understanding.
Lord Liao of Hengyang has painted a portrait of you and come to seek a eulogy from me. I share with you a bond beyond the mundane world; thus, in accordance with our duty, I cannot decline.
I respectfully set forth these brief accounts. To compose a eulogy, I say: How magnificent is Mount Ziyi!

A seer and a mirror for this enlightened age. Girding his sash at the imperial court, he expanded the majesty of the state’s ceremonial regalia. Having achieved his great service, he retired in peace.
He concealed his brilliance and devoted himself to a single valley. He provided delicious food for his parents at home, exhausting the heart of a filial son in serving them;
