He possesses the heroic spirit of the maiden Yueyang, yet does not flaunt his sharp wit; he resembles Lingzhao’s transcendence of the crowd, yet does not boast of his strategic prowess.
He has leaped over the deep pit of the heterodox masters’ "silent illumination" and rises far above the very crowns of those two men.
Her backbone was forged from cast iron, and her two feet were hammered from solid steel.
She is a true great man among women, one who cannot be turned by the eight winds or the five desires.
Eulogy on the Portrait of Protector Yang:

People say this is Protector Yang; I say it is the Dharma-protecting deity of Mei County. By nature loyal and righteous, without flattery or crookedness, he possesses a single heart of pure sincerity and uprightness.
Eulogy for the Portrait of Minister Sun:

He exhausted the investigation of principles and reached the fullness of human nature; he entered the Buddha’s wisdom and vision. For seventy-eight years, like a flash of lightning in the void, was his life.
Praise by the Layman Without Stain, Minister Zhang.
Churning throughout the entire trichiliocosm, buying and selling all by oneself; now both principal and interest have vanished at once.
Yet one goes back to the place of the poor child to collect the debt; his livelihood I know all too well.
Half-deaf, half-dumb, half-stupefied, half-deluded, he still seeks advantage with empty hands. He constantly uses a broom to paint the brows of a beauty.
Eulogy for the Portrait of Minister Zheng, the Layman of the Twin Huai Trees:
The mind is vacant and empty; gazing at the cascading waterfall, there is no external object to be perceived, nor is there anything internally received.
Sitting upon a rock, leaning against a withered pine, let those who know him try to fathom his depths. Both the mundane and the supramundane are caught all at once in a single net.
In the *Eulogy on the Portrait of Minister Han*:

Wearing informal robes and a simple headcloth, he carries a staff and lets his sleeves hang loose. His gaze follows the wild geese on their journey; his mind receives nothing. Truly a worthy man for a hundred generations.
This official’s master was a descendant of the Changli lineage for ten generations; he acted solely according to what was right, never being confined by literary conventions.
Magnanimous and forthright, this great man’s handling of affairs was like the sun at its zenith during the day.
Eulogy on the Portrait of Vice-Minister Qian:
He does not crave birth and death, nor the pleasures of the various desires; he does not follow the perversions of thought, the perversions of view, or the perversions of mind.
Truly, such a person is called a Great Man of both the mundane and supramundane realms. Seated upon his meditation platform, grasping his whisk, he remains solemnly present before all people.
Within the eyes, there is no need to seek elsewhere. Who is it that spoke these words? It was Zonggao of Miaoxi from the Mingyuetang on Mount Shuangjing.
This is the eulogy for the portrait of the Layman Miaoyuan, Prefect Zhang.
Within his breast, he originally possesses the Five Chariots and the Classic of Documents; he accommodates the rivers and lakes within the scope of his capacity with ample room to spare.
Vast and expansive like ten thousand acres of reservoirs, he does not yield to the son of the ox-herder from Jiangxia. This is what is called the Layman Miaoyuan.
To study the wondrous joy and aspire together to this Way is something rare in the world.
A Praise of the Buddha Śākyamuni’s Appearance upon Leaving the Mountains.
The thirty-two marks and eighty minor characteristics; beneath the Bodhi tree and in the Deer Park, rising and falling by himself.
When Mañjuśrī inquired after his illness, he knew only how to praise non-duality and lost one of his eyes. Claiming for himself to be the teacher of the seven Buddhas, he departed and never returned.
The worldly Han people have brought trouble upon themselves; they have needlessly inserted their beaks and incited litigation that remains unresolved even to this day.

Entering meditative absorption, Avalokiteśvara sits upright with eyes closed, manifesting the *nāga* posture. With the wondrous wisdom of Avalokiteśvara, a single blow achieves two purposes, as he abides in the ground of tranquility.
It should be as numerous as the atoms within a buddha-field, for such is the nature of the Dharma.
Unobstructed and unimpeded, the body remains unmoving while the mind enters into meditative absorption (*samāpatti*). A single point of numinous light is like the sun at midday.
Vimalakīrti Layman (2):
The Buddha’s illness and the Dharma’s illness—swept away both at once. Pass on these words to old Vimalakīrti: "Spare your wretched life!"
Emptying all that exists, one enters deeply into non-duality. Raising a single needle-point stirs heaven and shakes the earth.

When Avalokiteśvara and Bodhidharma face each other, Bodhidharma is Avalokiteśvara; when Avalokiteśvara and Bodhidharma face each other, Avalokiteśvara is Bodhidharma. "I am you; you are me. One body, two names.
The nostrils and ears—neither speaks to the other; they sit facing one another in silence. Sitting or not sitting? (A shout! How very hot it is!
For over fifty years, the Ninth Patriarch, Vimalamitra, sat in meditation;
what was he waiting for? Even if lords and attendants were to interlace like a net, one could not avoid it.
If you miss it at the very outset, you have failed.

When the Great Master Bodhidharma sat beneath the withered pines upon the stone platform, he focused his intent yet let go of all attachments; thus, neither side was missed. Those who come must simply keep their eyes wide open.
The Eye: Raising his gaze, the hawk flies to Silla;
in India he found no place to stay; with a shamed face he crossed the shifting sands, knocking out the teeth right before the gate—yet they still speak of the "five-petaled flower."
The Second Patriarch exchanged his skull; for no reason he changed his name again. Severing his arm in deep snow, he made those on the other side laugh to death.
— Sixth Patriarch Dajian Chan Master.
"Hey, you old fellow! Go pound your rice for now. What is this talk of transmitting 'bowls and robes'? You have made the four seas boil with your chatter.
Today, seeing your true form, it turns out you are nothing more than this."

A calendar of many years tied at the waist—knowing with whom one might engage in dialogue. Setting down the strainer and raising the hands high in greeting:
why must one prattle on to respond to the occasion?
Non-arising is fundamentally beyond speech; to speak of it is to fall into verbal error. With his bones and flesh gathered into one head, this Great Tiger gazes at the water mill. Bagu Monk (4):
Bowing to the Buddha of the Dragon Flower who is next in line for succession, he refuses to dwell peacefully in Tuṣita Heaven, but instead comes to the bustling marketplace seeking [the Way].
This person is called a "white-handed thief" among men. With his bare legs thrust out, he sits in a sprawled posture;
he flaunts his hemp sandals, displaying his eccentricity. From time to time, he mutters to himself, chanting, "I am the true Maitreya."

Rough and coarse, it preserves no ritual protocols; there is neither grandeur nor solemnity. The entire ten directions, the dharma-realm, and empty space are all contained within a tattered cloth bag.
Suddenly, in the midst of a bustling market, it is untied and scattered toward every street and alleyway.
*Namo Maitreya Bhagavān*. Such is the family style.

With a staff of tangerine peels, he pries open the straw mats; he lies prostrate in the streets and by the roads, begging for alms. Who would have known that the Tuṣita Heaven originally has no such news?
Rough and coarse, he lacks all discipline and measure; at the crossroads, he is defiled by the public gaze.
Master Linji (III): His countenance was like a heap of ash drenched with water; his shout was like thunder shaking a cloudless sky.

Within a single phrase lie the Three Mysteries; within each Mystery lie the Three Essentials. To see the temple wall behind one’s head—what a rustic monk! This is the Ultimate.
There is yet another aperture:

Attained! Yet he comes back to the marketplace acting like a madman.
This lacquer bucket, Zen Master Xuefeng Zhenjue, also knows how to burst open. To settle the case according to the facts, he receives but a single wedge. What is that?
A single stake. Cold pines atop the ridge; the white moon at the edge of the sky. Vanishing, vanishing.

Regarding the true and the false among the human kings and Dharma-kings—such as the Dharma-eye King Li—the Celestial Eye and the Dharma-eye possess not the slightest obscuration. A single scroll of painted silk captures both.
Ultimately, they all converge upon the same ultimate truth (*paramārtha*).

It is said that the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka* is a crude and disordered practice, with those practitioners constantly wandering through streets and alleys; though they recite the Lotus Sūtra with their mouths, within their bellies—
I have long been thinking about what you eat. People say that neither ordinary nor sage can peer into your depths, yet Miaoxi alone has recognized you. Pshaw!
You fallen village monk—take off those pair of wooden clogs!
The Fifth Patriarch, the Venerable Master, was a peddler of cheap wooden boards. "Three pounds of hemp, equal to its weight"—how many seekers of the mystery have mistaken the zero point on the scale!
To say "I" when it is not "I," and to claim "true" when it is not true—even if one transmits [the teaching] as such, one has still not discerned its spirit.
Chan Master Yuanwu (4): Two prominent teeth protrude from the gate;
the root of the tongue surges like a spinning wheel. Within the spark struck from flint, he reveals his ugliness and clumsiness;
amidst the flash of lightning, he again becomes obscured. Pressing down his knees and bracing his body, he fashions a mold and strikes a pattern, playing at the false.
A mere semblance of truth! Even if one possessed such skills today, to whom would one intend to entrust them?
To slander the Buddha and destroy the Dharma—utterly coarse and entirely reckless, with a countenance so loathsome one should strike him dead.
The Eye of the True Dharma has been extinguished by this blind donkey! (A shout! Offer this very body and mind as service to all lands of dust.
He no longer conceals or covers anything; he opens his mouth and shows his gallbladder. Yet the student does not understand, and instead becomes like a flat wooden board.
Alas, you coarse monk from Luochuan! You especially wish to deceive the people of Lu. Though you exhaustively employ infinite spiritual powers, you cannot avoid returning home to die.
You thought there was something so extraordinary about it, but your skillful means turn out to be merely this.
Chan Master Juefan Hong penetrated Yun’an’s "Single-Word Barrier" and delighted in discussing Caoshan’s "Three Kinds of Falling. From his brush-tip, ocean waves surged;
whether speaking horizontally or vertically, he was entirely without fault. He won himself a towering reputation, yet nearly incurred the calamity of death.
In literary composition, he did not yield to Confucius; in discussing Chan, how could he have been inferior to Bodhidharma? Do you all see him yet?
Cease searching for that bald official; just look at this scholar among monks.
Master Sishin’s Chan was not understood;

The world of Jambudvīpa has been emptied; such a monk as this is difficult to find. If you understand him through words, you will surely be detested by others.
He reviles the Buddhas and reviles the Patriarchs, yet who knows that he has never done so at all? I ask you to shake up your spirit and look;
do not mistake this fellow for the Buddha-lamp.
Master Nanhua Bing’s lifelong eye at the crown of his head shines through without a single speck of obscuration. When Taiping and Nanhua meet on the stage, they perform their play.
On the morning of the sixteenth day of the seventh month, the sound of thunder shakes heaven and earth. I observe the Dharma of the Dharma King; such is the Dharma of the Dharma King.
The inner mind of Master Zhong of Muguan was tranquil; external conditions were severed. His realization was precise and true; his application was intimate and direct. "One blow leaves a scar;
one slap draws blood"—this is the lineage style of Master Zhong. It must be spoken by Miaoxi: a tortoise in the fire.
Soaring into the heavens, in the sixth month, auspicious snow falls in profusion.

Master Fāng of Heshan sits cross-legged upon a low couch, wearing his *kāṣāya* robe; he gazes like a tiger at the monastic groves, where all manner of monsters hide. Do not say that Sīxīn has already passed away.
Death. The one who possesses the mind of death has never perished.

Master Ying Puzhao beats the poison-drum and preaches flavorless Chan; he takes awakening as his seal, sealing the minds of all beings with awakening, and attains the [Dharma] of the Buddhas and Patriarchs.
This is essential and subtle. It penetrates the source of all phenomena; upon mountains of knives and trees of swords, it seizes the very life-force of the monks;

Master Puzhao Qin shattered the "poison-drum" of Mount Huishan; he passes this life moving freely and spontaneously. Do not blame the world for failing to recognize him;

His strengths were such that he could explain how to ride a horse inside a bowl.

Patriarch: What demons or heretics would dare to clamor so?

This is what is meant by Master Min: one who brings forth inexhaustible merit and benefit, yet remains free from self-conceit.

Master Zhengtang Bian transmitted the Way of Master Foyan and expounded a Zen of transcendent caliber—neither establishing fixed patterns nor lingering in words and phrases—thereby achieving his own realization.
The Patriarchal Founder. This constitutes a beautiful tradition for the monastic community. Such is what is meant by the Elder of the Main Hall;
he is one who has caught the fish and forgotten the trap. Master Jin, Huiyun of Shandong.
